Taipei Chinese Orchestra unveils season of Taiwanese stories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:03:11 UTC
21:03:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taipei Chinese Orchestra will bring contemporary works and cross-cultural collaborations to audiences in its new season, with a focus on Taiwanese composers and stories.
The orchestra will present 56 performances through June next year. The season continues its focus on contemporary Chinese music by Taiwanese composers, with this year’s program highlighting composer Su Wen-cheng (蘇文慶).
The program will feature works from different periods of Su’s career, showcasing his distinctive approach to contemporary Chinese music and his long-standing engagement with Taiwan’s culture and society.
The season will also extend beyond contemporary Chinese music to explore Taiwan’s performing arts traditions. One of its highlights is the Taiwanese opera “The Sisters” in December.
Set against the world of a traveling Taiwanese opera troupe, the production follows several women whose lives take different paths while remaining closely intertwined. Their stories offer a glimpse into the experiences of women and performers during a period of social change.
The program will also bring together musicians from different backgrounds and musical traditions. An October concert will open the Taiwan International Cello Festival, featuring four cellists from around the world under the direction of conductor Chang Yin-fang (張尹芳). The concert will pair the cello’s rich, resonant sound with Chinese music, exploring different cultural and regional influences.
“Indelible Love Stories” will explore the ties between people and their homes, loved ones, and country. Three stylistically distinct works will offer different perspectives on the emotional world of Chinese folk traditions through combinations of piano, voice, and erhu.
In November, the orchestra will spotlight younger Chinese instrumentalists performing on the erhu, flute, and yangqin. Another concert will revisit music from earlier periods through performances by acclaimed erhu and pipa players.
A December concert will turn to the works of composer Ng Taikong (吳大江), an early advocate of developing Chinese orchestral music in a more symphonic direction. The program will span different stages of his career and feature the zheng, erhu, and other traditional instruments.
The new year will extend the season’s international focus. A January concert will bring together musicians from Singapore and Malaysia for a program that blends Chinese orchestral music with Southeast Asian musical traditions.
Taiwan has developed its own diverse musical traditions, including nanguan and beiguan traditions long associated with temple communities, as well as Indigenous instruments such as the jaw harp and wooden drums, according to Taiwan Md.

Taiwan Cement Corporation buying Ukraine's 2nd largest cement maker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:03:05 UTC
21:03:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan Cement Corporation said Tuesday that it will acquire major Ukrainian cement maker Ivano-Frankivsk Cement and expand further into Eastern Europe, according to a press release.
Taiwan Cement said its subsidiary TCC Dutch Holdings will execute the acquisition for no more than 750 million euros (NT$27 billion). It said the transaction has not been approved by the two countries’ governments yet.
Taiwan Cement Executive Shelly Yeh (葉毓君) said the acquisition includes the cement firm itself, roofing materials company Ivano-Frankivsk-Dakh, plaster manufacturing firm Kru Gips, and dry-mixed mortar maker Kru Mix. She added that the settlement amount will be adjusted after net debt and capital.
Taiwan Cement said the firm is Ukraine's second-largest, with a 36% market share. It makes cement, pre-mixed mortars, and additives, with production located in western Ukraine, about 760 kilometers from the nearest combat zone. It noted that the war has not halted production.
According to the Ukrainian firm's 2025 annual report, its revenue grew 20.3% in 2025, with a net profit of NT$4.56 billion, a 40.3% increase each year. Gross profit margin grew in 2024 from 34% to 39.6%; after-tax net profit grew 44.5% each year, with a 26.4% net profit margin.
Taiwan Cement said it has hired Morgan Stanley for ratings, with other firms conducting due diligence investigations on risks from sanctions, labor practices, and operations.
Taiwan Cement Chair Nelson Chang (張安平) toured the facility in the first half of the year. The site has installed 50 megawatts of solar power and 19 megawatts of gas-powered installations to reduce reliance on the nation's power grid.
Taiwan Cement said the firm exports mainly to Poland and Romania as well as Moldova, Slovakia, and Hungary. It plans to introduce more efficient production to Ukraine after the sale concludes.
Ukraine's cement consumption was 10.6 million tonnes in 2021 and plummeted to 4.5 million tonnes in 2022. It has since rebounded to 6.2–6.5 million tonnes per year.

SAPO serves new suspicion to SBGSU official for bribery in drone supplies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:02:51 EEST
21:02:51 KST

Under the procedural guidance of a prosecutor from the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), detectives from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) have served new suspicions to an official of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine (SBGSU) and the owner of a private company in a bribery case concerning drone supplies.
In a Telegram channel on Wednesday, the SAPO reported that in May of this year, the official and the company owner were exposed for extortion of $1 million.
"Today, they have been additionally incriminated with the provision of an undue advantage and the legalization of illegal funds (Part 2 of Article 369, Part 2 of Article 209 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine)," the message reads.
According to the SAPO, the pre-trial investigation established that an official of the SBGSU Administration arranged for public procurement procedures for unmanned aerial vehicles to be conducted by SBGSU units.
"He determined the conditions of the procurement in order to ensure the victory of a company controlled by his accomplice. Despite the accomplices' plans, another enterprise joined the tender, the head of which offered a more advantageous proposal – to supply 270 unmanned aviation systems for UAH 825 million," the report says.
The SAPO notes that upon learning of this, the businessman approached him with a request not to lower the prices for the mentioned technical equipment, since there were already agreements on the victory of his specific enterprise.
However, as the anti-corruption prosecutor's office clarifies, the new participant nevertheless submitted an updated proposal, according to which the total cost decreased to UAH 760 million.
"As a result, it was the new participant who won," the SAPO explains.
According to the report, since the plans to obtain profits from the controlled company were thwarted, the individuals decided to extract a benefit from the tender winner.
Thus, the businessman began to convince him of the necessity to provide a bribe for the trouble-free conclusion and execution of the future contract. He even organized a telephone conversation with an SBGSU representative to finally assure him that all demands were being made with the agreement of the agency's Administration, the SAPO emphasizes.
The amount of the undue advantage was $1 million, i.e., 5-10% of the total amount of the future contract; the individuals planned to divide the funds among themselves and SBGSU officials.
According to the anti-corruption prosecutor's office, the director of the winning company put forward his condition – to meet personally with SBGSU officials.
"During the further investigation, it turned out that in order to maintain ties with the border guards, the owner of the competing company decided to provide a part of these funds by transferring 50,000 Tether (USDT) units to the SBGSU official's cryptocurrency wallet, which amounts to over UAH 2.1 million at the NBU exchange rate," the SAPO clarifies.
Also, as informed by the anti-corruption prosecutor's office, it was established that the SBGSU official repeatedly received and legalized illegal income.
"Thus, throughout January – April 2026, he transferred over UAH 15.4 million into Tether USD (USDT) cryptocurrency. He converted part of these assets into cash, with which he subsequently bought a Mercedes-Benz GLC 300 car, registering it in his wife's name," the report states.

The launch of the plant's first phase, with investment of about $1 million, took place in 2022, several months after the full-scale invasion.
Lviv Ventilation Plant produces air ducts, sound attenuators, as well as components for ventilation systems intended for the needs of industry, retail, hotels and business centers.
According to YouControl, in 2025 the plant increased net sales revenue by 20% compared with the previous year, to UAH 50.1 million, while net profit decreased by 34.6%, to UAH 1.6 million. In the first half of this year, net sales revenue amounted to UAH 19.6 million, and net profit to UAH 0.71 million.
The owner of 100% of the company's shares and its head is Serhiy Vozhomenchuk, a resident of Rivne region.

ECO Film Week brings diverse regional cinema to Tehran
TEHRAN- The ECO Film Week is underway in Tehran, bringing together a selection of films from member states of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) in a program highlighting the region’s diverse cinematic traditions and cultural narratives.
Organized by the ECO Cultural Institute (ECI), the four-day event features films from Iran, Tajikistan, Pakistan, the Republic of Azerbaijan, Türkiye and Kazakhstan, providing audiences with an opportunity to explore different cinematic approaches and stories from across the ECO region.
The event opened at the ECO Cultural Institute in Tehran on Monday with the participation of Mehrdad Rakhshandeh, Executive Director of the ECO Cultural Institute, and Raed Faridzadeh, Head of the Cinema Organization of Iran.
Following the opening ceremony, Iran’s “Whisper My Name”, directed by Rasoul Sadrameli, was screened as the first film of the program. The 109-minute film marked the beginning of a series of screenings featuring works from six ECO member states.
“Whisper My Name” is about Ziba, a teenage student working girl. Living in a dormitory with no bonds to her parents, she dreams of moving to a room of her own. She’s struggling to find a path to be independent, but everything becomes even more complicated when her dad, Khosro, shows up. He has escaped from a psychiatric hospital to celebrate his daughter’s birthday with her.
The 2025 drama stars Amin Hayai, Juliet Rezai, Mehran Ghafourian, and Setareh Pesiani. It won the Best Film Award at the 2025 Fajr Film Festival.
The program continues on Tuesday with two films from Tajikistan and Pakistan. “Looking for Truth,” a 97-minute Tajik film, is scheduled to be screened at 4 p.m., followed by Pakistan’s “Nayab” at 6 p.m. The latter has a running time of 153 minutes.
On Wednesday, the program will feature “Meryem” (2023) from the Republic of Azerbaijan at 4 p.m. and “Once Upon a Time in Anatolia” from Türkiye at 6 p.m. The films have running times of 95 and 157 minutes, respectively.
The final screening of the event will be held on Thursday at 4 p.m., featuring Kazakhstan’s “Dawn of the Great Steppe,” a 138-minute film.
All screenings are taking place at the ECO Cultural Institute in Tehran.
A special exhibition featuring a selection of film posters from ECO member states will also be held alongside the screenings. The exhibition will offer a visual overview of the history and development of cinema in the region, highlighting the artistic diversity of film poster design and its role in promoting and preserving cinematic heritage.
The ECO Film Week is being held as part of the ECO Cultural Institute’s efforts to strengthen cultural cooperation among member states and provide greater opportunities for interaction among filmmakers, artists, cultural professionals and audiences across the region.
The event will continue through September 24 in Tehran.

“Macbeth of Zar” to represent Iran at Tunisia’s Carthage Theater Days

“Macbeth of Zar” to represent Iran at Tunisia’s Carthage Theater Days
TEHRAN- Iranian theater production “Macbeth of Zar”, written and directed by Ebrahim Poshtkuhi, is set to take part in the 27th edition of the Carthage Theater Days, which will be held in Tunis, the capital of Tunisia, from November 21 to 28.
The production, staged by Iran’s Titovak Theater Troupe, is an Iranian adaptation of William Shakespeare’s “Macbeth”.
“Macbeth of Zar” draws on the traditional Zar ritual and indigenous cultural elements of southern Iran, while incorporating influences from a range of international performance traditions, including Kabuki, Kathakali, Butoh and commedia dell’arte, as well as Vsevolod Meyerhold’s biomechanics.
The production explores Shakespeare’s tragedy through a theatrical language that combines local cultural traditions with diverse performance techniques. Through this approach, Poshtkuhi has developed an adaptation that places the familiar story of “Macbeth” within a distinctive Iranian cultural and ritual context.
“Macbeth of Zar” has previously been presented at a number of international theater events, with performances in Russia, Germany, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Hungary and Iraq. The production has also received several awards and accolades during its international career.
The play had previously been invited to participate in the Avignon Festival in France. However, it was unable to take the stage at the event due to difficulties related to embassy coordination and visa issuance.
The Carthage Theater Days, one of Tunisia’s major international theater events, will bring together theatrical productions and artists from Tunisia and other parts of the world during its 2026 edition.
“Macbeth of Zar” offers a novel fusion of the ancient Zar ritual and William Shakespeare’s timeless tragedy "Macbeth.". The production reimagines Macbeth's story set on Hormuz Island, where he becomes embroiled in a fateful struggle to transform into the "Great Zar Father."
Macbeth is one of Shakespeare's finest plays, and presents a man's conscience and the effect of guilt on his mind. A dark and bloody play, Macbeth explores reality and illusion; witchcraft and the supernatural; ambition and kingship; the natural order; light and life, darkness and death; blood and dead babies.
Zar is a legacy from slavery as it was performed by African slaves who were brought to southern Iran. They performed it on weekends in order to gain energy to enable them to bear the burden of bondage for the rest of the week. Over time, ordinary people also joined in their musical rite comprising ecstatic dance with dammam (tom-tom) playing.
Today, Zar is mostly performed by workers in a group named ahl-e hava, which is conducted by a leader called a babazari.
In this play, Scottish general Macbeth commits a crime to join an ahl-e hava to become a babazari.
It was previously staged in Iran under the title of “Hey Macbeth, Only the First Dog Knows Why It Is Barking”.
The troupe performed the play at the 41st Fajr International Theater Festival in Tehran in 2023. The play brought Poshtkuhi an honorable mention in the best play category. In addition, musician Behrang Abbasi won the award for best composer for his collaboration in this play.

How to turn leftover roast chicken into a brilliant midweek meal – recipe | Waste not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:00:48 UTC
21:00:48 KST

It was my gran’s funeral a few weeks ago, so today’s recipe seems rather fitting, because coronation chicken was one of the few savoury dishes she cooked, and also one I loved. This homage to her glorious personality and astonishingly sweet tooth (add extra mango chutney for sweetness) is a wonderful way to use up leftover chicken from a roast, barbecue or whatever. I make the mayo from scratch, because I don’t keep mayonnaise in my larder, but I do have eggs and extra-virgin olive oil.
Leftover roast coronation chicken
Coronation chicken was a genius solution to a common caterers’ conundrum, and was created by Rosemary Hume and Constance Spry for a 350-person banquet at Westminster school to mark Queen Elizabeth’s coronation. I take a similar approach, whether I’m cooking a dinner party for five or feeding 500 at a festival, and generally go for simple recipes that can be finished with little effort (and have my mise en place ready, of course). This dish is a brilliant use of Sunday’s leftovers, be it as a delicious stand-alone supper or a superior sandwich filling. Don’t be precious about which bits of leftover chicken you use: thigh meat, wing meat, the oysters, skin, and any last scraps clinging to the carcass – all of it goes in.
Serves 2
1 egg
  1 heaped tsp wholegrain mustard, or to taste
Flaky sea salt and black pepper
Juice of ¼ lemon, plus the finely grated zest if the fruit is organic and unwaxed
About 150ml extra-virgin olive oil, or enough to emulsify and thicken the mayo
Finely grated zest and juice of ¼ unwaxed lemon
  A few coriander sprigs, stalks finely chopped, leaves left whole 
1 tbsp mango chutney
  1 tsp mild curry powder, or a pinch each of a few warm spices such as turmeric, cinnamon, cumin, fenugreek, mustard seed, ginger, black pepper and nigella seeds – whatever you have to hand
300g cooked chicken or turkey scraps, pulled off a roast
1 handful flaked almonds, toasted, to serve
To make the dressing, crack the egg into an immersion blender jug and add the mustard, a pinch of sea salt, the lemon juice (and zest, if using), the finely chopped coriander stalks, the chutney and the curry powder. With the motor going, slowly pour in the oil and blend until the mixture emulsifies into a thick mayonnaise, then taste and adjust the seasoning. The curried mayo will now keep in the fridge for up to four days.
To make the coronation chicken, pull any leftover chicken or turkey scraps – 200-300g should feed two generously – into rough pieces, then mix in a bowl with enough mayonnaise to coat the meat well. Serve topped with toasted flaked almonds and the coriander leaves.

Men with less modest self-views are more likely to feel victimized and support men’s rights activism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

Men with a less modest view of themselves tend to feel that men as a group are unfairly disadvantaged compared to women. This sense of victimhood predicts a greater willingness to support and participate in men’s rights activism, according to new research. The findings were published in Personality and Individual Differences.
To understand this connection, it helps to look at two psychological concepts at the center of the research: trait modesty and group-based relative deprivation. Trait modesty refers to how people evaluate themselves in relation to others. People with high trait modesty generally view themselves as being no better than anyone else. On the other hand, people with low trait modesty tend to feel superior and entitled to special privileges, viewing themselves as better than those around them. This shapes how they interpret situations involving social comparisons.
Group-based relative deprivation is the perception that a person’s own group is being unfairly treated or disadvantaged compared to other groups in society. This feeling often triggers anger and resentment. To experience it, an individual has to compare their group to another, appraise their group as disadvantaged, and view that disadvantage as unjust. In the context of gender, it captures a sense that men are losing power or status they are rightfully entitled to.
Researchers have increasingly documented how men adopt a sense of victimhood and how entitlement fuels backlash against gender equality. For example, a 2021 study indicated that many people now believe sexism primarily targets men rather than women, capturing a core grievance of the men’s rights movement. Building on this idea, a 2022 study showed how men in the men’s rights movement construct a sense of victimhood to build a collective identity that justifies their protests and organizing.
Adding to this picture, a 2024 study provided evidence that male entitlement predicts a willingness to engage in both peaceful and aggressive actions to defend men’s societal status. Similarly, research covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that traits like narcissism and psychopathy were associated with lower support for feminist attitudes.
The new research, led by Joanna Lindström, a psychology researcher at Uppsala University, and Morgana Lizzio-Wilson, a lecturer in social, political, and feminist psychology at the University of Exeter, sought to pinpoint whether low modesty is a specific personality trait linked to these feelings of unfair deprivation and a willingness to engage in men’s rights activism.
“I was initially interested in understanding why some (but not all) members of structurally advantaged groups perceive that their group is unjustly disadvantaged, despite statistics and history suggesting otherwise,” Lindström told PsyPost. “This led me to show that low modesty was linked to feeling deprived among men (but not women), and among White Americans (but not Black Americans),” she explained, referring to a previous study she conducted. “We then wanted to examine whether modesty and feeling deprived as a man could also explain men’s willingness to engage in men’s rights activism.”
The researchers tested this idea in two separate stages. In the first study, the team recruited 195 White American men through an online platform. The participants completed a standardized personality questionnaire designed to measure trait modesty. They also answered a series of questions measuring group-based relative deprivation, indicating how frustrated they felt about men being supposedly disadvantaged in modern society.
Next, the researchers measured the participants’ support for and intention to engage in men’s rights activism. They separated these potential actions into two distinct categories. Conventional political actions included activities accepted within a social system, like advocating for law reform or joining a men’s rights organization. Extreme or non-traditional actions included behaviors that deviate from societal norms, like participating in a protest that might turn violent or supporting those who use physical aggression for the cause.
The team found that men with lower trait modesty were more likely to report feeling that men are an oppressed group. This feeling of deprivation, in turn, predicted higher support for both peaceful and extreme activism. Deprivation was a stronger predictor of conventional activism, while having low modesty itself was a stronger predictor of a willingness to engage in extreme, non-traditional activism. The results suggest an indirect pathway: low modesty leads to a heightened sense of relative deprivation, which then fuels a desire to engage in activism.
“Aspects of men’s personality and perceptions of social context both have a role to play in shaping men’s support for men’s rights activism,” Lindström said. “That is, trait modesty predicts how men appraise their treatment as a group in society more generally, which, in turn influences whether they support and want to personally engage in actions that further men’s ‘rights and opportunities.'” “Put another way, the findings highlight that high modesty may protect men from perceptions of deprivation and men’s rights activism in turn,” she added.
In the second study, the researchers expanded the project to include 492 men, split almost evenly between White and Black Americans. The authors wanted to see if the connection between modesty and activism existed across different racial groups. While the men’s rights movement is often stereotyped as being exclusively White, emerging scholarship has highlighted the presence of a Black manosphere, where Black men engage in online conversations about men’s issues and articulate similar narratives of gender-based disadvantage.
The researchers also tested whether making the idea of male disadvantage highly visible would alter the results. Participants first completed the same measure of trait modesty used in the first study. Half of the men were then asked to take a minute to reflect on the ways men are disadvantaged relative to women, and write four sentences about it. The other half acted as a comparison group and wrote four sentences about their morning routines. After this writing task, all participants completed the measures of deprivation and activism.
The experimental writing task did not change the underlying personality effects. Across both White and Black participants, low modesty consistently predicted a stronger sense that men are unfairly deprived. Just as in the first study, this sense of group deprivation predicted a greater willingness to support and engage in men’s rights activism.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that personal feelings of disadvantage drive hostile sexism toward women. However, the new study specifically measures how group-based deprivation predicts support for collective men’s rights activism rather than individual sexist attitudes.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the results. The experimental writing task in the second study did not actually increase feelings of relative deprivation compared to writing about a morning routine. This suggests the specific writing exercise might not have been strong enough to affect participants’ views, or that trait modesty exerts a stable influence regardless of the immediate situation.
Also, the researchers note that low modesty shares some overlap with narcissism. Future research is needed to untangle exactly how much of this effect is driven by low modesty alone versus related narcissistic traits, like a desire for authority or a tendency to exploit others. The study also focused exclusively on White and Black men. The authors point out that other minority groups, such as Asian American and Latino men, face unique racial and cultural pressures that could alter how modesty and feelings of deprivation interact.
Finally, the studies were conducted entirely in the United States. Cultural norms around modesty and gender vary widely across the world, meaning these patterns might look different in other countries. More research is needed to see if these psychological pathways hold true in different cultural contexts.
“Given the correlational nature of the data, we also cannot determine a causal link between personality, perceptions of relative deprivation, and men’s rights activism,” the researchers noted. “We know that these things are linked and have explanatory power, but we need to conduct a further experimental study to determine if one variable causes the other, and in which order.” For instance, they explained, “does heightened relative deprivation causally increase men’s rights activism, or does engaging in men’s rights activism/collective action color men’s perceptions of their group’s status in society.”
“We don’t want to convey that the manosphere and men’s rights activism can be explained purely by personality,” the researchers emphasized. “It’s also important to remember that personality is malleable – just because men lower in trait modesty are more likely to perceive men as deprived in society and support/engage in men’s rights activism doesn’t mean that their modesty perceptions can’t change. Cultivating higher modesty may be a key avenue for protecting men from the manosphere’s influence.”
Looking ahead, the researchers are continuing this line of inquiry, including work with the EMMELO project an EU-funded initiative examining the role of masculinity in extremist movements. “We are currently conducting research where we show that modesty and feeling deprived (individually and as a man) predict men’s support for manosphere figures in the U.S. context,” they said. “We aim to design interventions that may decrease men’s support for—and engagement in—the manosphere, which are informed by our ongoing work on the role of modesty and relative deprivation in underpinning endorsement of the manosphere.”
The study, “Low modesty and feeling deprived as a man: A psychological explanation of men’s rights activism,” was authored by Joanna Lindström and Morgana Lizzio-Wilson.

Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home
Unknown

2026-09-23
12:00:20 UTC
21:00:20 KST

There were violent scenes in Madrid on Wednesday as riot police fought with protesters trying to prevent the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her apartment in the Retiro district.
Hundreds of protesters had gathered, many of them overnight, in an effort to block the fourth attempt to carry out the eviction. Activists from the Madrid and Barcelona tenants’ union, and celebrities including the actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actor Ana Belén, joined the protest.
Police fired rounds of teargas and made repeated baton charges as they tried to open a path for a judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed on Wednesday morning. The tenant, known simply by her first name, Maricarmen, is about to turn 88.
Demonstrators chanted “Ayuso’s attic for Maricarmen”, a reference to the scandal surrounding the Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso’s alleged purchase with public money of a €6.3m residential apartment for her use as a temporary office.
Behind the building’s locked door, more protesters occupied the staircase leading to Maricarmen’s flat while neighbours handed out snacks and offered the demonstrators the use of their bathrooms.
When a developer bought the building Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years, she was offered the chance to buy her apartment for €247,000 (£212,000), an impossible sum for a pensioner.
They then raised her rent from €500 to €1,650 a month, while she receives a state pension of €1,350. An unnamed “prominent” writer offered to pay the €1,150 difference indefinitely but their offer was ignored.
In a video recorded by the local tenants’ union before the eviction, a tearful Maricarmen said: “Good morning, everyone, I thank you for the action you are taking, spending the whole night sleeping in the street. Please, keep going, but don’t hurt one another. This has to be peaceful.
“I can still hear all your noise. A hug to everyone and to all the people who are supporting me in this cruel struggle against a person who wants to make money but who should not forget that they have parents and that one day they could find themselves in the situation that unfortunately I am in.”
The original 1956 contract for the flat was in Maricarmen’s father’s name. When he died, the apartment passed to his wife, and on her death in 2008 it was then sublet to Maricarmen. The landlords, Urbagestión SL, successfully argued in the supreme court that this subletting was invalid and that the contract was no longer valid. Urbagestión SL has been approached for comment.
Speaking at the scene, Aldo Reverte, a spokesperson for the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, said: “Maricarmen’s case is just one more example of what happens when housing is put in the hands of landlords. The difference is that a lot of people have become aware of her situation and the tenants’ union has shown that we can fight this type of barbaric behaviour.”
However, for all their efforts, the protesters were unable to stop the eviction. Beatriz Duro, the lawyer representing Maricarmen, said: “The owner isn’t prepared to negotiate or accept any sort of offer. We have asked for a place where we can take Maricarmen’s personal belongings.”
So far this year, 4,000 evictions have been carried out in Spain.

US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:58:11 UTC
20:58:11 KST

NEW YORK, United States -- The United States is set to unveil the next stage of its effort to develop the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP, a planned transport and infrastructure corridor through southern Armenia that Washington says could open new trade routes between the South Caucasus, Central Asia, and Western markets.
Senior State Department officials told reporters that the New York event on September 23 will focus on the institutional and financial mechanisms needed to move TRIPP from last year's Armenia-Azerbaijan peace initiative toward implementation.
The event is expected to bring together the foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan, representatives of the five Central Asian states -- with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan showing particular interest -- US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Republican Senator Steve Daines, and executives from more than 40 companies, many of them American.
Officials said the event will highlight how TRIPP aims to "pop the cork" on the Middle Corridor, unlocking a westward trade route that connects Europe to Central Asia while reducing reliance on transit through Russia, China, and Iran.
The gathering will also feature the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund, which officials said will invest in opportunities arising from TRIPP and the wider Trans-Caspian trade route. The fund operates at arm's length from the US government under a White House-appointed board and receives grant funding from the State Department. It is distinct from the TRIPP Development Company, the joint US-Armenian corporate entity being established to develop and oversee the corridor.
'A Major Security Issue'
TRIPP is intended to provide unimpeded access between Azerbaijan proper and its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory while respecting Armenia's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security.
"This becomes a major security issue for us," the official said, describing the removal of existing trade "choke points" as a central objective.
The transit route will be developed and managed by a US-controlled company, giving Washington exclusive rights while effectively excluding Russia from a strategically important project in one of its traditional spheres of influence.
The project emerged from an August 2025 White House summit at which Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a US-brokered joint declaration aimed at ending decades of conflict between the two South Caucasus neighbors.
Armenia and Azerbaijan fought two major wars over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that for decades had a predominantly ethnic-Armenian population. Azerbaijan regained full control of the territory in 2023, prompting almost all of its ethnic Armenia population to flee. The two sides agreed on the text of a peace treaty in March 2025, but a final agreement has yet to be completed.
Officials said there have been no cease-fire violations since the August summit and pointed to limited trade in fuel and agricultural products as evidence of growing economic integration. According to them, Azerbaijani fuel supplies have contributed to an estimated 20 to 30 percent decline in Armenian fuel costs.
They noted there had been more interaction between Washington and Baku during the previous 13 to 14 months than during the preceding 13 to 14 years.
A senior State Department official said Yerevan and Baku were acting as though peace were "inevitable," although additional steps remain before a final agreement can be completed. Washington intends to develop TRIPP in parallel with that process, arguing that greater economic integration could help remove remaining obstacles.
Physical Construction Still Some Way Off
Despite plans to move TRIPP toward implementation, construction of the roughly 43-kilometer section through Armenia is not yet ready to begin. The section is expected to include a railway, road, pipelines, electricity infrastructure, and digital data links.
The senior State Department official said Azerbaijan has already been building infrastructure toward the Armenian border at its own expense, while Turkey is similarly developing infrastructure up to the border. The remaining section through Armenia is still to be developed.
“We're not there yet,” the official said when asked how soon physical construction of the Armenian section could begin. The administration hopes to begin looking for business and investment opportunities by the end of 2026 or the first quarter of 2027.
The railway will take longer. A feasibility study is expected by the end of 2026 or early 2027, after which companies will be able to bid. The official said completing the railway would likely take at least 18 months, complicated by difficult topography.
Electricity connections could come sooner. Discussions are already underway, with officials expecting electricity operations to begin in 2027, potentially linking the Armenian and Azerbaijani grids with wider Central Asia, Turkish, and European regional networks. Passenger rail is also planned.
TRIPP Leadership
The briefers provided more detail about the planned structure of the TRIPP Development Company (TDC) but no names for its future leadership.
The TDC is being established as a corporate joint venture between the US government and Armenia. The senior State Department official described it as a first-of-its-kind arrangement in which the US will hold a majority stake, with its own board, voting procedures, and management. Several legal matters still need to be finalized before the company can formally be announced.
Projects involving rail, roads, electricity, oil, gas, and data will go through regular tender processes for construction or concessions. The US Development Finance Corporation (DFC) has been involved in the legal and institutional setup, but the TDC itself will operate as a separate US-Armenian corporate entity.
The United States is prepared to invest once feasibility studies establish that individual projects are commercially viable. The State Department is financing part of the feasibility work, with engineering firm AECOM set to present investors with projects unlocked by TRIPP during the event on September 23.
'A Difficult Neighborhood'
Officials described TRIPP as an alternative to existing east-west routes, with the proposed corridor offering Central Asian trade another route to Western markets that bypasses Russia and Iran.
The senior State Department official said Washington had held discussions with regional competitors but declined to characterize their private views.
"There have been numerous conversations with all of the competitors in the region," the official said, adding that Washington was aware of the potential for "hard conversations" in what officials called a difficult neighborhood.
The event is intended to mark a shift from the 2025 peace initiative toward implementation, with more than 40 companies attending.
The project still requires completing feasibility studies, legal arrangements, financing, tendering, and ultimately construction.
While Washington says Armenia and Azerbaijan are on an "irreversible path to peace," their final peace agreement has yet to be completed.
The US nevertheless intends to develop TRIPP alongside the peace process, arguing that greater economic integration could help remove remaining obstacles. As the senior State Department official put it, the focus is on "what happens the day after the piece of paper."

Singapore’s entry-level job market shrinks despite salary growth, data shows
Aon data published last month shows a 3.2 per cent drop in entry-level headcount in the city state, amid a rise in AI use in the workplace
Data published last month by global professional services firm Aon showed a 2.5 per cent year-on-year salary increase for entry-level employees, alongside a 3.2 per cent drop in entry-level headcount.

UK to review Chagos deal after Trump tells Burnham it is 'terrible'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:57:56 UTC
20:57:56 KST

Britain has suspended its €139 million-a-year lease payments for the Diego Garcia base while ministers try to reshape the agreement into one Washington can accept, with the Conservatives calling for it to be scrapped altogether.
Britain will go back to the drawing board on its agreement to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said on Wednesday. The move comes a day after US President Donald Trump attacked the deal during his first meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The two leaders met on Tuesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. With Burnham sitting beside him, Trump said he expected the British leader to reconsider the "terrible deal". Burnham nodded and replied "yep".
Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer in July, later told broadcasters that Britain would "work hard" to resolve the issue and that he was "confident we can find it working with our US partners".
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting said Trump's objections were "not news to us". But he said the president's latest remarks "provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing".
"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where we can support it," he said.
Streeting also confirmed that Britain would not "at this stage" make the annual payments of at least £120 million (€139 million) it had agreed to pay Mauritius to lease back the military base on Diego Garcia.
Months of US opposition
The agreement, reached last year between Starmer and the Mauritian government, would hand the Indian Ocean archipelago back to Britain's former colony. Britain would then lease the strategic US-UK base on Diego Garcia for 99 years, with the option to extend. Britain announced in April that the plans were on hold.
Trump first backed the pact but later turned against it, calling it "an act of great stupidity", and it has caused friction with his administration for months.
Starmer defended the agreement by arguing that international legal rulings had cast doubt on Britain's claim to the islands, and that only a deal with Mauritius could secure continued US and UK use of the base.
Britain held on to the Chagos Islands when Mauritius became independent in the 1960s. It removed thousands of islanders, who have since brought a series of compensation claims in British courts. In 2019, the International Court of Justice concluded that Britain unlawfully separated Chagos from Mauritius when ending colonial rule..
'Ostrich strategy'
James Cartlidge, defence spokesman for the opposition Conservatives, said the agreement "should be binned entirely".
Streeting rejected that approach. He told Times Radio: "The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it (will) go away ... is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world."
Jack Pannell, a senior researcher at the British Foreign Policy Group think-tank, told AFP that Burnham's focus with Trump would be on "the big international issues", such as AI regulation, Ukraine and the Middle East.
"Success for Burnham means avoiding this issue becoming a millstone around his neck while he pursues his other foreign policy priorities and focuses on his domestic agenda," Pannell said. "The chances of a breakthrough on this issue are slim, and that may suit the prime minister just fine."
Also on Tuesday, Trump signed a security agreement with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark that will allow the US to build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland.

Russia’s use of jet-powered drones has spiked eightfold within three months since June, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.

Hacker arrested over cyberattacks on at least two Latvian companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:55:16 UTC
20:55:16 KST

On the 15th of September, Latvian State Police arrested a hacker born in 2003 on suspicion of carrying out cyberattacks against at least two Latvian companies for financial gain.
One attack against a company was recorded as early as February this year, while another cyberattack with a similar modus operandi was detected in early September against household appliance and smart device repair company TSC, which is part of the LMT group, the State Police reports.
The hacker gained unauthorised access to some of the personal data stored in the database and attempted to extort money in exchange for not disclosing the data further. Information available to the State Police indicates that the suspect did not distribute the data obtained in the cyberattacks.
In both cases, the man born in 2003 has been formally recognised as a suspect, and investigations in the criminal proceedings are continuing.
While investigating criminal proceedings concerning a cyberattack on a company’s website in February this year, the First Division of the State Police Cybercrime Combating Department analysed the nature of the attack and the attacker’s “modus operandi”, which indicated a connection to the recent attack on the TSC website.
Investigators established that the suspect used an automated attack tool to identify a vulnerability,
after which he gained access to the website’s database and exported information, including restricted-access data.
The attack was carried out using virtual masking tools to conceal the attacker’s actual location. After completing the attack, the hacker contacted the company using an anonymous email account created specifically for this purpose and demanded payment in exchange for not distributing the stolen data further.
By analysing and investigating the cyberattack on the TSC website, with support from the LMT Security Service and CERT.LV, investigators were able to quickly establish and verify the circumstances of the case. This enabled the State Police not only to identify a potential suspect, but also to link the two incidents and determine the suspected hacker’s location.
On the 15th of September, law enforcement officers arrested the hacker, a man born in 2003, and carried out several other procedural actions, including a search at an address in Riga.
During the investigation, police obtained evidence and information concerning other cyberattacks
allegedly carried out by the suspect against various companies in Latvia and abroad. Investigations into these incidents are continuing.
Based on information obtained during the investigation, there are grounds to believe that, thanks to the swift action of the State Police, the personal data obtained without authorisation was not passed on to third parties.
The First Division of the State Police Cybercrime Combating Department succeeded in linking the two cases, and the detained man has been formally recognised as a suspect in both criminal proceedings.
The cases are being investigated under Section 241, Paragraph two of the Criminal Law for unauthorised access to an automated data processing system for financial gain; Section 183, Paragraph one for extortion; and Section 243, Paragraph three for disrupting the operation of an automated data processing system and unlawfully handling information contained in such a system for financial gain.
In investigating the suspect’s motives, police established that the cyberattacks did not target specific companies. Instead, automated attack tools were used to scan various websites and online resources in search of vulnerabilities.
The State Police therefore urges all companies to assess their online resources and ensure that appropriate security measures are in place to minimise the risk of similar incidents occurring in the future.

Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:55:03 UTC
20:55:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
A relative pause in fighting between the United States and Iran that ended in early September has brought the region back into a state of geopolitical tension.
As the exchange of strikes, retaliations, and signalling between Washington and Tehran continues, there is a heightened expectation from Washington that the US pullout from Iraq should coincide with Iranian-backed militias in the country being disarmed.
A looming US withdrawal
At a meeting at the White House in July, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, met with President Donald Trump and indicated that Baghdad would work to disarm the pro-Iranian Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).
“The fact that both Trump and Zaidi are following through means this is a bipartisan vision in the United States and a continued commitment from Zaidi, who took over the premiership from Sudani as the Coordination Framework’s candidate,” Hamzeh Hadad, an Adjunct Fellow with the Center for New American Security, told The New Arab.
The withdrawal of US forces now places a greater burden on the government in Baghdad to determine the future of the PMF.
“The US pullout removes a key lever for Baghdad and forces tougher bargaining at home,” Dr Inna Rudolf, Senior Research Fellow in the War Studies Department at King’s College London, told The New Arab.
“Coalition forces had been both an excuse some factions used for pursuing greater autonomy but also a tool Washington could use to push for change.”
The US continues to pressure Baghdad for the disarmament of the PMF through diplomatic channels, but the threat of further sanctions and tariffs has been floated by the Trump administration.
On 21 September, Zaidi requested more time beyond the 30 September deadline agreed with the United States, and the next day it was announced that it would be pushed back to 30 June 2027.
Baghdad will now have nine months to continue negotiations with the factions while avoiding potential US financial or economic sanctions.
“The Iraqi government needs to have a more honest dialogue with Washington about its situation and vision,” Haddad told The New Arab.
“But this needs to take place without wishful statements from the Iraqi side that they backtrack on, as they already have to deal with strong foreign pressure on the issue.”
The plan to dismantle and reorganise the PMF fighters into existing brigades and retire older commanders who have served since 2014 will reportedly start implementation in January 2027.
The government also intends to establish a new directorate to monitor the integration.
Zaidi's disarmament push
Iraq’s new prime minister has sought to strengthen Baghdad’s image as a government that can rein in corruption, ensure security, and pursue economic development with the international community.
“Zaidi, entering politics, a new face, with no prior experience in public office, wanted to build on the US backing that saw him come to power, and so he boldly stated that he would enforce a deadline for armed groups outside of the state apparatus to disarm,” said Hadad.
The Iraqi government is currently waging a campaign to curtail the PMF’s power in the country. In mid-August, Iraqi security forces detained a senior commander from the Nujaba Movement, one of the primary Iranian-backed militias that make up the PMF coalition.
“There is a different understanding between what constitutes armed groups outside of the state apparatus in Iraq than in Washington,” Hadad noted.
Hiba Abdulwahhab, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, told The New Arab, “The relationship between the Iraqi government and these factions resembles a Catholic marriage, a union with no easy divorce. They are deeply intertwined politically, institutionally, and economically”.
An uncertain security situation
The US military will also be removing the air defence systems, including Patriot and C-RAM systems, from the Kurdistan Region. The depletion of US air defence system interceptors during the conflict with Iran has contributed to the declining security situation.
In March 2026, Kataib Hezbollah, one of the key factions of the PMF, released a two-minute video that went viral showing an FPV drone flying over the Camp Victory complex near Baghdad International Airport, a site that continued to host US and NATO-linked facilities.
A drone attack that Saudi officials reported originated from Iraq struck the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia on 11 September. Baghdad later confirmed the pipeline attack came from Iraqi territory and dismissed security officials responsible for Maysan Province near the Iranian border and closed the area’s border crossing.
Still, some PMF groups have sought out a political advantage by appearing to adhere to the government’s calls. One militia, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, announced over the summer that it formally withdrew from the PMF coalition and handed over its weapons to the government.
Other groups, such as the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement, have stated they will not turn over their weapons, saying that certain conditions had to be met before they did so.
“[Zaidi’s] reasoning is that there will be no more American forces present in Iraq and therefore no more excuse for armed groups to exist after that,” Hadad told The New Arab.
Dr Rudolf agrees. “Losing that pretext gives negotiators cleaner rhetorical space to press for stricter control as it strips the factions of their usual talking point that foreign troops justify armed resistance outside the formal chain of command.”
Finding a path to disarmament
Iraqi leaders have advocated for the PMF to function as a state security institution and slowly reduce their political nature.
In May, the militia of prominent Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, Saraya al-Salam, announced it would begin disarmament and integrate into the state. While this group is not technically part of the PMF and Shia Coordination Framework, it could be interpreted as a sign of the direction the wind is blowing in Iraq.
However, it is likely that the groups will utilise this approach to reposition themselves without totally surrendering their arms.
“The most likely outcome is therefore adaptation and repositioning rather than genuine disarmament,” Abdulwahhab told The New Arab.
“Weapons could remain in faction-controlled depots, be transferred to affiliated units, or be placed nominally within the PMF’s official structure without being brought under effective government command.”
Observers of Iraq are right to be sceptical that the PMF will do little else other than rebrand and retain their loyalty to informal chains of command and external ties with Tehran.
Regarding the extension of the disarmament deadline, Abdulwahhab said, “The progression raises serious doubts about the government’s ability to act against factions deeply embedded in Iraq’s political and security institutions”.
She added, “The extension is more likely to give Iran-aligned factions time to reorganise and protect their networks than to give the government the power to disarm and dismantle them,” further noting that Baghdad had to take concrete steps now, otherwise June 2027 may bring another postponement rather than a resolution.
Some positive steps have been taken, but it is still early in the process to understand how far Baghdad can go.
“Without tangible incentives and accountability mechanisms, ‘integration’ will feel like administrative rebranding,” Rudolf said. “The public will see it as window dressing.”
The long-term outlook will depend on the future of the financial and military support from Iran as well as Baghdad’s own ability to assert control over the militias.
For now, the government in Baghdad will have to navigate the post-US withdrawal environment on its own.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)

British lawmakers urged banks and financial institutions Tuesday to avoid new financial commitments linked to Israel's E1 settlement project as the government prepares to ban trade with illegal settlements.
The lawmakers, members of the all-party Britain-Palestine group, made the call in a letter to financial institutions warning of potential legal, sanctions and reputational risks.
The letter follows Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's announcement two weeks ago of plans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlements, alongside new sanctions on those involved in their construction.
However, the secondary legislation needed to bring the measures into force could take six to nine months to pass through Parliament.

The E1 project involves plans for thousands of new homes in the occupied West Bank, with the Israeli government seeking bids for two tenders covering as many as 3,400 homes.
More than 1,300 of the homes are covered by a tender due to close on Oct. 25, two days before the Israeli elections.
Financing, insurance and guarantees are required before construction can begin.
The project has been delayed for years because of concerns over its impact on prospects for a two-state solution, which is backed by many Western and Gulf states.
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. The international community considers Israeli settlements built on occupied land illegal under international law, a position rejected by Tel Aviv.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 settlement outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

Burnham survived his first Trump meeting. His nice hair may have had something to do with it | Emma Brockes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:54:08 UTC
20:54:08 KST

Watching footage of Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly on Tuesday was like watching your child from behind a tree in the playground. Are they making friends? How normal do they seem relative to the average? How will they react when they come into contact with that hulking great child who seems to be running things? Burnham’s first face-to-face with Donald Trump was billed as a knife-edge encounter that, due to the latter’s capriciousness, could go either way. In the event, it was drama-free, leaving observers to ask: was it Burnham’s brilliance or simply the weather in Trump’s head?
To viewers at home, Burnham’s performance at the press conference looked like that of a man who had worked out his best approach was to go for the sheepish, slightly cheeky air of the junior partner. Burnham is 24 years younger than Trump, on top of everything else – which can afford a certain licence to the less powerful person in any exchange. At the last minute, the meeting had been moved behind closed doors and afterwards, in a windowless room at the UN, the two men appeared side by side, mirroring each other’s body language: just two guys, legs akimbo, shoulders hunched, hanging on a bench in the locker room.
It was intriguing to guess what Trump saw when he looked at the UK’s new prime minister. British people can’t always parse class or regional difference in Americans and one assumes Trump can’t distinguish Burnham’s accent from that of someone from Melbourne, or Torquay. Still, something in the British prime minister’s bearing clearly appealed to him. “Thank you, Mr President,” said Burnham after Trump praised this country as “special” and Burnham’s tone – “That’s wonderful. We really appreciate that. This relationship matters so much to us” – hit just the right note of warm condescension that probably struck the president as flattery.
Other factors in play: it seems ridiculous to mention, but knowing how superficial Trump is, it seems to me that Burnham’s extremely impressive coiffure for a man of his age – which appears to exist without augmentation – won’t have been missed by a US president who spends an awful lot of time on his hair.
There were also a couple of contextual factors that may have given Burnham an easier ride than some other, less fortunate world leaders. First, the run-up to the meeting had seen Trump on absolutely top chaotic form while addressing delegates at the UN, threatening the destruction of Iran and going on a whimsical detour to try to get the acronym SI (“superintelligence”) as opposed to AI off the ground. Perhaps, by lunchtime, he had burned himself out and was ready for a bit of quiet time.
We know Trump gets bored quicker than a toddler spoilt for toys and Burnham’s shiny newness will have, briefly, diverted him. The replacement of Keir Starmer in relatively brutal fashion also gave Trump an opportunity to do something he loves more than anything else in this world, which is to kick a person when they’re down. When asked about recent rockiness in US-UK relations, the president replied, “No, I think they’re up … well, they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.” In that moment, one saw a tiny endorphin rush of meanness light up his face.
And finally, I guess, the president is fresh out of friends at the moment, as the fight with Canada continues and he falls out with his European friend Giorgia Meloni, formerly known as the “Trump whisperer”. As a result, Burnham was lavished with the highest praise Trump can summon, namely: “I think he’s a natural businessperson.” An astute reader of weakness, he perhaps sensed in Burnham someone more sure of himself than Starmer was. And the prime minister passed Trump’s do-you-think-you’re-better-than-me? test, in which anyone who displays any kind of overt intellectual curiosity is instantly a threat to be vanquished. Even his name, Andy, gives regular-guy vibes that probably helped.
Burnham weathered all this with equanimity, although it was tempting to detect behind his poker face the shadow of a smirk while, surely, he thought to himself, “God, this guy”. “News is fake!” said Trump, and, in reference to the Chagos Islands, “they’re a very important piece of real estate!” Meanwhile, Burnham smiled slightly as if appeasing a lunatic. “He gets it,” said Trump and for once, one had to agree.
- 
  Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

WHO pledges to support health ministry to turn global patient safety commitments into action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:53:46 UTC
20:53:46 KST

WHO pledges to support health ministry to turn global patient safety commitments into action
TEHRAN – Commemorating World Patient Safety Day 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) Country Office in Iran reaffirmed its commitment to turn global patient safety commitments into practical action across hospitals, primary health care and communities as the Ministry of Health and Medical Education advances its patient safety agenda.
Hosted by the Health Ministry, the hybrid event brought together senior officials, including Deputy Ministers and Vice-Chancellors for Curative Affairs and Public Health from universities of medical sciences, as well as hospital and primary health care managers, university focal points, and WHO colleagues. Participants reaffirmed the importance of patient safety as a core component of quality health services and resilient health systems, the WHO website announced in a press release on September 21.
WHO provided technical and advocacy support for the commemoration, sharing the global messages and priorities of World Patient Safety Day and highlighting the need to integrate patient safety across all levels and settings of care. In his remarks, Dr Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative and Head of Mission in the Islamic Republic of Iran, reaffirmed WHO’s commitment to making safety an integral part of every health care interaction. He underscored that safer care contributes to improved health outcomes, prevents avoidable harm, and strengthens trust in health systems.
The event also highlighted the need for safe and continuous care for people living with non-communicable diseases (NCDs) during crises and emergencies, when disruptions to essential health services can put patients and communities at greater risk.
A message from the WHO Regional Director for the Eastern Mediterranean, delivered by Dr Adham Ismail, Officer-in-Charge, was presented during the ceremony, with subtitles in Farsi, reinforcing the regional and global commitment to advancing patient safety.
The ceremony highlighted several priorities aligned with the global patient safety agenda, including: strengthening reporting and learning systems for patient safety incidents; building a culture of safety among health care providers; engaging patients, families and communities; improving health literacy; addressing medication-related risks such as polypharmacy; and extending patient safety efforts beyond hospitals to primary health care and other levels of care.
The commemoration also provided an opportunity for WHO and the Ministry of Health and Medical Education to identify areas for continued technical collaboration, including: knowledge exchange; strengthening patient safety assessment; and follow-up on capacity-building under the Hospital Patient Safety Assessment Manual and the Patient Safety Assessment Manual for Primary Care.
These discussions reflect WHO’s role in bringing global evidence, standards and tools to the national context, facilitating knowledge exchange, supporting capacity-building and convening partners around practical actions to strengthen patient safety.
World Patient Safety Day is observed on September 17 every year and serves as an opportunity to raise public awareness, enhance collaborations among healthcare stakeholders, and expedite measures to reduce preventable harm associated with the delivery of health services.
Each year, the day is observed under a specific slogan. In 2026, it focuses on safe care for NCDs, under the theme ‘Safe care for life!’.
NCDs such as cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases are among the most significant global health challenges, accounting for 74 percent of deaths worldwide; they affect people of all ages and require constant, lifelong care. Patients’ frequent interactions with the healthcare system can put their safety at risk. These risks are also influenced by health system challenges and the broader determinants of health.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 1 in 10 patients is harmed during health care, with around half of this harm being considered preventable. People living with NCDs are particularly vulnerable to harm due to the long-term nature of their conditions, ongoing treatment needs, and frequent interactions with health systems.
With some conditions, such as cancer, up to 1 in 3 patients experience adverse events during care. Many people also live with multiple chronic conditions, further increasing the risk of harm.
Addressing NCDs is a global priority, reflected in the United Nations political declaration on NCDs and mental health, which calls for strengthened prevention and long-term management of NCDs. Achieving these commitments requires access to safe and quality care.
Improving safety in NCD care requires addressing risks related to the complexity of care, strengthening health systems through a primary health care approach and tackling wider determinants that can increase the risk of harm. The day also highlights the importance of engaging people with lived experience in the design and delivery of NCD services and in their own care.

MOSCOW - At least six people have been killed in bear attacks in Russia’s vast Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk in a month, prosecutors said on Sept 23, as an official in a neighbouring region reported bears had put one town “under siege”.
Prosecutors said they had opened a probe into criminal negligence, accusing local officials of failing to control bear numbers.
Russia’s brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to Russia’s natural resources ministry.
While the number of bear attacks across Russia has remained constant at around 20 to 30 a year, according to the ministry, local media and officials have expressed alarm about the rising numbers.
Despite numerous warnings, local officials “failed to take measures to regulate the predator population or prevent them from appearing in areas inhabited by people”, the Investigative Committee of Russia’s sparsely populated Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia regions said on its website.
The bodies of two pensioners were found mauled in a forest near the remote town of Podtyosovo earlier in September, followed by the death of a 40-year-old factory worker who walked through the forest on Sept 6, according to local media.
Three others were killed in the following weeks. The latest victim was a 39-year-old logger guarding machinery in the forest early on Sept 23, investigators said.
The deputy head of the neighbouring Khakassia region, Dmitry Buchenik, said on Sept 23 that the forest town of Abaza – home to around 10,000 people – was surrounded by bears “on all sides”.
“It was an alarming night in Abaza. The taiga (coniferous forest) town is effectively under siege by bears,” he said.
“Some of the animals were chased off, but three were killed (one of them was huge),” he added.
Unverified social media videos purported to show a bear swimming across a river beside the town, while another showed a group of three bears leaping across a road in front of cars.

Legal & General plans to cut 1,000 jobs by the middle of next year, about a tenth of the British insurance and pensions firm’s workforce.
António Simões, the chief executive, is wielding the axe as part of his attempts to create a “leaner organisation” since taking over from longtime CEO Nigel Wilson in January 2024. L&G described the move as “the next stage of that transformation”.
The London-headquartered firm told staff on Wednesday that it had begun moves to eliminate about 1,000 roles by mid-2027, which had first been reported by Bloomberg News. Most of L&G’s 10,000 employees are based in the UK.
The programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but L&G will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up.
The fund management division, which oversees £1.2tn in assets, is excluded as it has its own restructuring plan.
Simões, who previously worked for Santander and HSBC, announced a sharper focus on L&G’s booming pensions arm in June 2024 and reduced the group’s four businesses to three, by merging its asset management divisions. It sold several “non-strategic” assets, the biggest of which was the housebuilder Cala Homes, along with legacy land and real estate.
He also brought in a new executive team and pledged to return more than £5bn to shareholders between 2025 and 2027 through dividends and share buybacks.
Simões told employees in an email: “Over the past two-and-a-half years, we have made significant progress executing our strategy, simplifying L&G, establishing three core businesses, and creating a more focused business.
“However, over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be… we need to change how we work today and, through this, become a leaner organisation.”
An L&G spokesperson said the changes “will help us focus our resources and investment on the areas where we see the strongest opportunities for long-term growth”. The spokesperson added: “We recognise and take seriously the impact on colleagues and are committed to supporting our people throughout the process and consulting with our unions.”
The company expects £500bn of transactions in the UK pensions market over the next decade, as employers transfer their old defined benefit pension plans to insurers and pension companies. L&G said it was also benefiting from strong auto-enrolment of staff in their companies’ pension schemes, with about £1bn of new inflows each month.

The enhanced agreement is intended to replace the existing Türkiye-UK trade pact that came into force after Britain left the European Union.
Services and technology take centre stage
The latest negotiations covered digital trade, telecommunications, investment, legal services and market access, while officials also discussed intellectual property, public procurement and sustainability.
Chris Gaunt, chairman of the British Chamber of Commerce in Türkiye, described the negotiations as a positive step and said expanding the agreement to services could open new opportunities for both economies.

Gaunt also pointed to agriculture, education, advanced engineering and technology as areas with potential for deeper commercial ties.
“Türkiye has always been a priority market for the UK,” he said.
Trade reaches $38 billion

Gaunt said British companies remain interested in increasing their activities in Türkiye despite geopolitical challenges that can affect inflation and living costs.
He also described Türkiye as a platform for British businesses seeking access to markets across Central Asia, the Middle East and Africa, citing the country's geographic position and established commercial links.
Tech partnerships offer new opportunities
The digital economy is another area expected to gain prominence under an expanded agreement.
Gaunt said Türkiye's technology startup ecosystem has grown rapidly, while Turkish technology companies are increasingly looking to international partnerships to expand globally.
He said the chamber is encouraging British businesses to explore opportunities in Türkiye and plans to organize side events in Antalya during the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, which Türkiye will host.
“Don't ignore Türkiye. Türkiye's got enormous potential, and you don't want to get left behind,” Gaunt said.
He added that the expanded agreement could give UK companies a clearer understanding of Türkiye's business environment and help them make more informed investment decisions.

ICC convicts CAR ex-rebel leader of crimes against humanity
September 23, 2026
The International Criminal Court on Wednesday convicted a former Central African Republic rebel commander on four counts of crimes against humanity committed while he was in charge of a detention center in 2013.
The court found that Mahamat Said Abdel Kani, 56, oversaw beatings and maltreatment as the country was gripped by sectarian violence.
Said also faced three counts of war crimes but was acquitted of them. During his trial, he pleaded not guilty to all charges for the crimes, which were carried out between April and August 2013.
A sentence, which could be life imprisonment, is to be handed down at a later date.
What was Said charged with?
Said was a top commander of the mainly Muslim Seleka rebel group that ousted President Francois Bozize in 2013 amid a civil war.
He was put in charge of the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry (OCRB), a prison unit in the capital, Bangui.
Prosecutors allege that prisoners at the facility, who were suspected supporters of Bozize, were subjected to various forms of torture, including whippings and body mutilation.
According to the court, inmates were also denied food or water, with some drinking their own urine out of desperation.
One cell, dubbed "the hole," where prisoners were held in dire conditions, was said by the court to be directly under Said's office.
Said stood accused of overseeing this maltreatment and personally participating in the beating of at least one prisoner, the court found.
First trial of a Seleka member
Said was extradited to the ICC by Central African authorities in 2021, with his trial beginning in September 2022.
It is the first time that a member of the Seleka group has stood trial at the ICC.
The ICC, established in The Hague in 2022, is the world's only independent tribunal capable of prosecuting those accused of the world's worst crimes.

Ban on Russian diesel increases EU fuel market vulnerability — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:49:57 UTC
20:49:57 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Restrictions on Russian energy supplies and a decline in domestic oil refining have increased the vulnerability of the European Union’s fuel market, whose structural problems predate the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, deputy director of a center at the HSE Institute of World Military Economics and Strategy Nikolay Novik told TASS.
A sharp rise in diesel prices in Europe means that European drivers now pay 40% more every time they fill up than they did at the beginning of the year, the Financial Times reported. Amid record fuel prices and emerging shortages, French President Emmanuel Macron appealed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to temporarily relax certain EU fuel regulations in an effort to bring prices down.
"Macron’s letter essentially exposed a systemic vulnerability and acknowledged that the model of less refining within the EU and greater reliance on imports of finished petroleum products is no longer viable under current conditions," Novik said. The expert explained that European refineries have historically focused on gasoline production, relying on imports to cover diesel shortfalls. "Before 2022, the European Union received around 700,000 barrels of Russian diesel per day, accounting for half of its purchases in this category," he stressed.
The 2023 embargo prompted the EU to shift toward suppliers in the Middle East and Asia, the expert continued. "The ban on imports of petroleum products made from Russian crude oil refined in third countries, which took effect in January 2026, further restricted this supply channel. At the same time, Europe was reducing its own refining capacity," he noted.
According to Novik, the Middle East accounted for 36% of European kerosene imports and 18% of diesel imports. "The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, but the structural problems facing the European market emerged long before that," he concluded.
