Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:08:01 UTC
20:08:01 KST

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

'UP ke ladke' in for political 'brawl'? SP, Congress spar over who can beat BJP in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:06:43 UTC
20:06:43 KST

'UP ke ladke' vs each other? SP-Congress spar over who can beat BJP in 2027
NEW DELHI: The "UP ke ladke" bonhomie is beginning to look less like a united front and more like a contest for the upper hand, with Congress and Samajwadi Party leaders trading jabs over who can take on the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. With the 2027 assembly election approaching, are cracks emerging in the INDIA bloc's battle plan against Yogi Adityanath's BJP?
Iqra Hasan’s remarks trigger Congress pushback
SP MP Iqra Hasan set off the latest bout of sparring by saying Congress "can't achieve much on its own" and projecting party boss and former CM Akhilesh Yadav as the only leader capable of defeating the BJP in Uttar Pradesh.Her remarks drew a quick response from the Congress, with party leaders pushing back against the suggestion that the SP could take on the BJP by itself.Congress MP Imran Masood said, "She (Iqra Hasan) also cannot do it alone. What is the problem with that? Iqra is our child. She is like our niece.""People from the Trinamool Congress were also saying a lot. Look at what happened in Bengal. Let us move together, and we will remain in peace," he added with a reference to Mamata-led TMC's big defeat in Bengal after contesting solo.Congress leader Udit Raj pointed to the SP's performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha election while questioning Iqra's claim."That may be her (Iqra Hasan's) own statement, but we can understand this through an example: when the alliance was formed in 2024, the Samajwadi Party won 36 seats. What was its performance before that? The Samajwadi Party had only six MPs in 2019. So, in politics, one plus one does not always make two; one plus one can make eleven.
Therefore, I think she should correct her understanding," Udit Raj told IANS.
BJP joins SP-Congress war of words
The saffron party, meanwhile, was quick to weigh in on the disagreement. Uttar Pradesh BJP vice-president Neeraj Singh said, "Congress will not be able to achieve anything on its own across the country. And even if it forms an alliance with the Samajwadi Party or any other party in Uttar Pradesh, the people of Uttar Pradesh have already formed an alliance in their hearts with the BJP government..."Iqra, who made the remarks on Monday, had said, "It is an absolutely foolish statement. I think that if there is anyone in Uttar Pradesh who can defeat the BJP, it is only Akhilesh Yadav. Congress will not be able to do anything on its own. If the alliance remains, it will be very good; if it does not, it is a loss for them (Congress), not for us."
SP-Cong face a new test: Who gets how many seats?
The "UP ke ladke" chemistry that helped Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav pull off a striking upset in the 2024 Lok Sabha election has yet to turn into a clear seat-sharing formula for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly polls.The two leaders have continued to share the stage on occasions, including protest for students, maintaining a public show of camaraderie. But behind that familiar chemistry, the alliance arithmetic is still taking shape.There has been no concrete discussion on how the 403 assembly seats could be divided between Congress and the Samajwadi Party.
How 2024 ‘UP ke ladke’ formula worked
Their partnership took shape months before the 2024 Lok Sabha election, and the results that followed gave the alliance a strong political imprint.The SP contested 62 of the state's 80 Lok Sabha seats and won 37, including Faizabad, the constituency covering Ayodhya. Congress fought 17 seats and won six. Together, the two parties crossed the halfway mark of UP's Lok Sabha tally, handing the BJP a major setback in a state that sends the most MPs to Parliament.For the SP, it was very much the bigger share of the alliance pie. Akhilesh's party emerged as the largest opposition force in the state, and second largest in country, while Congress revived its presence with six seats.
Ayodhya loss added to BJP’s UP setback
The result also had a powerful political backdrop. Uttar Pradesh is the home turf of chief minister Yogi Adityanath and the parliamentary constituency of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The BJP had also invested enormous political capital in Ayodhya, where the Ram temple consecration took place in January 2024 in the presence of PM Modi and RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat.Yet, months later, the BJP lost the Faizabad seat to the SP.The result turned Rahul and Akhilesh into the "UP ke ladke" of the 2024 campaign, a political pairing that seemed to have found the right formula for the state's electorate. But as the next election approaches, the partnership is facing a different kind of test: Seat-sharing.Akhilesh has repeatedly said that the SP will contest the 2027 election with the INDIA bloc partners with whom it fought the 2024 Lok Sabha polls, effectively keeping the door open for Congress. But Congress has not made a similar formal commitment. Neither Rahul Gandhi nor party president Mallikarjun Kharge has publicly announced a seat-sharing arrangement with the SP.
SP gets its 403-seat election machinery moving
Meanwhile, the SP is already getting its electoral machinery moving.Sources told TOI that the party's top leadership has finalised candidates for more than 100 of the 403 assembly seats, while the process is under way for the remaining constituencies. The party has not yet released a formal candidate list.SP strategists say the early exercise is deliberate, giving prospective candidates time to prepare their constituencies, build networks and hit the ground running once the campaign begins.The strategy is not entirely new. Political observers point out that the SP followed a similar approach before the 2022 assembly and 2024 Lok Sabha elections, beginning the candidate-selection process well ahead of polling but releasing the actual lists only a few months before the election.
Congress prepares for all 403 seats too
Congress, meanwhile, has indicated that it is preparing to contest all 403 seats. That ambition could make the eventual negotiatins with the SP considerably more interesting.
Owaisi offer adds another variable
And there is another piece on the chessboard. AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi has made an open offer to Akhilesh, potentially bringing another party into the opposition's seat-sharing calculations.
AIMIM's performance in Maharashtra, UP and Bihar
If the SP chooses to engage with Owaisi, the equation could become even more complicated for an alliance that has so far largely revolved around SP and Congress.
What happened in 2022 assembly polls
The Lok Sabha 2024 friendship was a renewed one. Just two years earlier, the grand old party and Akhilesh Yadav’s Samajwadi Party had contested the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections separately, as they sought to take on Yogi Adityanath, who was then seeking a second term as chief minister.Yogi comfortably retained his Lucknow throne, while the Samajwadi Party increased its numbers. The Congress, however, suffered a major setback, winning just 2 of the 403 assembly seats.
Big heart or bigger share?
Rahul, personally, also appeared hesitant when it came to announcing the Mahagathbandhan’s chief ministerial face in Bihar last year.He also appeared to have reservations about Tejashwi Yadav’s eagerness to project himself as the alliance’s face, as well as over seat-sharing, with a large chunk of seats going to Lalu Yadav’s Rashtriya Janata Dal.A similar story could now unfold in Uttar Pradesh, where the Congress may look to expand its footprint with an eye on the next Lok Sabha elections. Uttar Pradesh remains at the heart of national politics, making a strong presence in the state crucial for any party with larger ambitions.Akhilesh Yadav, meanwhile, would be looking to return to power in Lucknow and reclaim the chief minister’s chair.Congress’ delayed decisions and its cautious approach towards trusting allies have also been visible more recently in Tamil Nadu. Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav have previously urged the Congress to show a “big heart” and back “regional players” in their home turfs.
What next for UP ke ladke?
So, while the Rahul-Akhilesh bond now may still look intact in public, the real test could come away from the cameras: How many seats each party wants, how many it is willing to give up, and whether the "UP ke ladke" formula can survive the hard arithmetic of 2027.
The BJP under Yogi Adityanath, meanwhile, is preparing to defend its position in Uttar Pradesh and seek another term in the state's 403-member assembly, ensuring that the opposition's alliance arithmetic will remain under close watch.With a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, Yogi would match former CM Mulayam Singh Yadav's record of three consecutive terms in the state, while he already holds the record for the longest uninterrupted tenure as UP chief minister, having been in office for nearly a decade.

US AI Force being created after same pattern as Space Force — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:05:31 UTC
20:05:31 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. The creation of the US AI Force follows the logic behind the creation of the country’s Space Force, which was largely formed in the interests of Elon Musk’s SpaceX and key giants of the military-industrial complex, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
"This move, again, is comparable to the earlier creation of the Space Force, when entities de facto affiliated with [US President Donald] Trump’s inner circle became key contractors. The Space Force was created largely in the interests of Elon Musk’s SpaceX and key giants of the military-industrial complex, including Boeing, Northrop Grumman, and other companies that are implementing the US military-space program," the expert said.
Stepanov emphasized that the creation of the new agency legitimizes the participation of the largest US high-tech giants in government policy and will grant them access to massive US budgets. Among the key beneficiaries, he singled out Palantir, a major player in the field of security and intelligence analytics.

Iranian flight lands in China despite U.S. sanctions threat, says tracker
A Mahan Air flight from Tehran landed in China's Guangzhou, tracking data by FlightRadar24 said on Wednesday, according to the AFP news agency, on the day Washington had threatened to "shut down" Tehran's carriers and punish anyone doing business with them.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned this week that any countries which provided Iranian planes with "landing services" would be "knocked out of the dollar system," but did not give further details.

Around half of Iran's damaged South Pars gas field capacity restored, says official
Around 50% of the damaged production capacity at Iran's South Pars gas field has been restored, according to a senior oil ministry official cited by Iran's semi-official Fars news agency.
Ahmad Zeraatkar, Deputy Oil Minister for Planning, told Fars that efforts to restore production capacity began following damage to South Pars facilities early in the war, with some units back online ahead of schedule.
In March, Israel struck South Pars, part of the world's largest natural gas field, spiking global energy prices and drawing a rebuke from President Trump.
"By the end of September, around 50% of the damaged capacity had returned to service, and production in this section had resumed," Zeraatkar said.
Zeraatkar said the planned restoration targets had been achieved and that all scheduled measures would be completed before the start of winter.
He also called on consumers to help the effort by reducing energy consumption.
Countries suspend Iranian airline flights as U.S. sanctions take effect
Several countries began suspending flights operated by Iranian airlines to their airports on Wednesday as new U.S. sanctions targeting the country's aviation sector took effect.
The Trump administration announced earlier this month that Iran's entire air transport sector would be subject to sanctions. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Iranian airlines would face difficulties operating globally from Sept. 23.
Georgia has banned flights operated by Iranian carriers from the country, while Iran's Mahan Air suspended flights to Turkey at Ankara's request.
Azerbaijan has also suspended Iranian flights, citing the new U.S. sanctions.
Iraq ordered the suspension of Iranian flights to Baghdad International Airport from Wednesday, according to the Reuters news agency. Iraqi authorities were, however, considering redirecting the flights to the central city of Najaf, an important Shiite Muslim pilgrimage destination.
"The decision does not mean a complete suspension of flights to Iraq, and that flights to other airports, including Najaf airport, will continue to operate as usual for all Iranian airlines," Iraqi Civil Aviation Organization spokesman Majid Akhavan said in remarks to Iranian media.
Iran's Civil Aviation Organization said flights from Tehran to Baghdad and Muscat, Oman, were canceled from Wednesday, while other remaining international flights, including those to Istanbul, would continue according to schedule.
It added that Iranian passengers were not being allowed to enter Oman's airport, with consultations underway on the issue.
Houthis threaten to target U.S. interests in Mideast if Washington intervenes in Yemen's civil war
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen will attack U.S. interests in the Middle East if Washington intervenes in the conflict in support of Saudi Arabia, including by attempting to thwart Houthi efforts to blockade Saudi shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a military adviser for the group told the AFP news agency Wednesday.
"If America dares to intervene militarily with its fleets or tries to take control of Bab el-Mandeb, it is a red line for them and anyone else … we will fight over it," Houthi military adviser Abed Mohammed al-Thawr told the AFP.
The Houthis have dislodged Saudi-backed government forces from Yemen's Red Sea coast in recent weeks in fighting that has left hundreds dead. Houthi drones and missiles have also targeted Saudi sites, including the capital Riyadh, for the first time in years.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested help from President Trump in fighting the Houthis earlier in September, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. Yemen's government also made the request, a well-placed source told AFP.
The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of strikes in Yemen since fighting resumed in July, effectively ending a four-year truce.
"If America gambles on supporting Saudi Arabia with airstrikes or air support ... We will consider any American interests around us to be targets and we will not exclude anything," Thawr told AFP, adding that the group would "close Bab el-Mandeb completely to American ships."
Thawr denied receiving directives from Iran, but said they were "one alliance and one body."

Iran and U.S. held peace talks Tuesday, Trump says

Tigray rebels seize airport and clash with federal forces as fighting in Ethiopia reignites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:03:33 UTC
20:03:33 KST

TPLF forces took control of Mekelle airport and fought federal troops at two locations in the Afar region, while Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to three Tigray airports in an apparent collapse of the Pretoria Agreement that ended the 2020-2022 war in the country.
Tigrayan rebels in northern Ethiopia seized control of a key airport and clashed with federal troops in the neighbouring region of Afar on Wednesday, as long-standing tensions spilt into open battle.
Fighting escalated "since last night in Abala and Erebti (in Afar) between TPLF and federal forces," an NGO source in the region said, requesting anonymity.
"We are expecting it to expand. We just sent a truck with food to help the people displaced," they added.
Abala lies in the mountain ranges that mark the border with Tigray. Erebti lies around 100 kilometres further into Afar.
Another humanitarian source confirmed clashes in the two locations, as did a foreign security source in Ethiopia.
A former TPLF senior official said the rebels were in control of Berhale, Erebti, Abala, Megale, Dalul and Konoba in Afar.
The federal forces are "fast-retreating", he added.
Meanwhile, local and security sources said Tigrayan forces were in control of the airport in the regional capital Mekelle.
Ethiopian Airlines said it had suspended flights to three airports in Tigray — Mekelle, Axum and Shire — "due to the current situation".
"While we were on our way to the airport for work, our supervisor called the driver and told him that the airport had been taken over by Tigray forces. Since there were no flights, he told us to return home," an employee at Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle said.
A foreign security source based in Ethiopia confirmed the information.
A small number of federal police guard the airport and their situation was unknown.
Between 2020 and 2022, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fought a devastating war with the federal government that resulted in the deaths of some 600,000 people, according to African Union estimates.
Sporadic clashes in recent months have raised fears of a return to war.
Abiy under fire
Ethiopia faces multiple insurgencies, including in its most populous regions, Oromia and Amhara.
On Sunday, the TPLF announced it had joined a seven-group military alliance dubbed Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival aiming to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and install a transitional administration.
The alliance also includes Amhara nationalist Fano militias — who fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF during the last war — and the Oromo Liberation Army, an active insurgency in Ethiopia's most populous region, along with four groups from three other regions, making up half of the country's 12 regional states.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, which eventually triggered the war in 2020.
The Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the war and maintained an uneasy calm until late 2025, when clashes resumed.
The federal government has since launched drone strikes in Tigray and massed troops at the regional border.
Rights groups have accused the TPLF of a campaign of forced recruitment this year as it prepares for renewed fighting.
The region has not recovered from the last war, with around 1 million people still displaced and many parts of the peace deal unfulfilled.
Abiy won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 partly for brokering a peace agreement with neighbouring Eritrea.
Good friends and neighbours
The federal government has a significant military advantage, having ramped up production of military drones since the last war.
Yet the TPLF's Tigray Defence Forces retain a significant inherited arsenal from their years at the helm of Ethiopia's military before 2018, including tanks, artillery, long-range guided rockets and ballistic missiles documented by open-source military analysts during the 2020-2022 war.
Ethiopia's Foreign Minister Gedion Timotheos said in June that TPLF hardliners had been "actively accumulating and acquiring new arms" in violation of the Pretoria Agreement.
Neighbouring countries have also been implicated in backing the rebels.
ACLED conflict monitoring group assessed earlier this year that Eritrean forces had moved troops toward western Tigray in coordination with the TDF and that Eritrea was providing weapons and hosting Tigrayan fighters.
Ethiopia's government formally accused Sudan's armed forces in May of providing "arms and financial support" to TPLF-linked forces and described Sudan as "a hub of anti-Ethiopian forces". Sudan denied the allegation.
Locked in a long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, Egypt is assessed by analysts at the Soufan Center as providing diplomatic cover and logistical support to Ethiopian opposition factions, although no direct weapons transfers to the TPLF have been documented.

AI and ski to cruises and Gen Z: dnata’s CEO on the trends driving travel in the UAE and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:02:25 UTC
20:02:25 KST

From AI-powered travel offers to growing demand for ski holidays, cruises and food experiences, dnata’s new Group CEO Nabil Sultan Al Murr says consumer habits are evolving rapidly.
Travel in the Middle East is evolving rapidly, with shifts in technology and consumer behaviour transforming both the industry and how people explore the region and beyond.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is already changing how holidays are planned and sold, while ski trips, cruises and experiences are gaining popularity among Middle Eastern travellers, according to the new Group Chief Executive Officer of global aviation and travel services company dnata.
Nabil Sultan Al Murr, who took over the role in June 2026, told Euronews Travel that these changing preferences are pushing companies to adapt more quickly, while technology is influencing everything from inspiration and booking to the airport experience.
Part of the Emirates Group, Dubai-based dnata operates across several divisions in aviation and tourism, including ground handling, cargo, travel services, catering and retail.
Overseeing its businesses across 162 cities in 37 countries, Sultan says the company has been assessing opportunities in emerging markets, including the Middle East, Africa, the Indian subcontinent and Eastern Europe. But it is technology and changing traveller behaviour that could have some of the biggest impacts on how people plan and experience their holidays.
How could AI change the travel experience?
AI has quickly become one of the biggest talking points in tourism, with travellers increasingly using tools to research destinations and plan their next trip. Sultan believes new technologies also have the potential to improve the passenger experience by allowing travel companies to process information and get relevant offers in front of customers much more quickly.
“I honestly think that AI and technology will bring in huge advantages in terms of improving the whole passenger experience and being able to put out the best offers and products,” he told Euronews at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai.
One example is the thousands of hotel contracts handled by dnata. Sultan says information from these contracts was previously processed manually, meaning getting deals into the system could take months.
“Now with AI we've adapted the whole thing and of course everything happens in almost real time,” he said. “That just shows the importance of how AI actually brings in that agility and speed and improvement in the whole work process.”
Ski holidays and winter travel grow in popularity
Technology isn't the only thing changing. Where – and how – people want to holiday is evolving too. One of the most noticeable shifts dnata is seeing in the UAE is growing demand for winter travel. “People going out for skiing, which was never the trend almost four to five years ago, is becoming such a huge trend,” Sultan says.
Responding to that interest, dnata has launched a winter programme featuring around 10 ski destinations. The company is also looking beyond conventional ski holidays towards other winter experiences. Sultan gives the example of Finland and seeing the Northern Lights as the types of trips attracting interest.
“These are all new kinds of features and experiences that we're trying to bring to the traveller and actually meet their emerging demand that we continue to see,” he said.
How cruises, Gen Z and food will drive the next era
Sultan expects traveller preferences to continue changing quickly over the next five years. Cruising is one area already gaining momentum in the Middle East and Gulf, he says, despite historically being a less established form of holiday in the region.
“I think the tourism and travel industry has been so dynamic and has been changing so rapidly and we've been seeing that,” Sultan said. “I think the key thing, of course, is to keep up with all of these changes and continue to introduce new elements in the whole entire experience.
“We see cruising now is becoming a huge trend. And you know that was never the case in this part of the world.”
The next major shift could come from younger travellers and how the industry adapts to their preferences. “Five years from now there's probably going to be a whole new trend, especially with the Generation Z, who probably look at different sorts of priorities in their travel experience,” he said.
Sultan points to food tourism as one example of how those priorities could change. “Food and healthy food is becoming a real trend,” he said. “So how do we bring that element into travel? It is a revolution and we're staying very close to the customer to really understand how we position our product offering.”

German state election losses risk snarling Merz’s reform agenda
Unknown

2026-09-23

German state election losses risk snarling Merz’s reform agenda
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz faces a political challenge after his conservatives suffered historic losses in eastern German state elections, risking delays or dilution of his tax, pension, and health reform agenda.
- Coalition partner SPD, also weakened in elections, demands a new policy approach to address voter concerns over inflation, living standards, and early retirement rules, especially affecting eastern states.
- Economic experts warn that reworking reforms risks undermining policy confidence amid Germany's modest growth, while far-right gains highlight political fragmentation complicating Merz's efforts to revive the economy.
AI generated
BERLIN - Chancellor Friedrich Merz may have survived the triumph of the far right in September’s state elections in eastern Germany and Berlin but the shock to his coalition could force him to water down his promised reform agenda.
Merz took the unusual step of announcing immediately after exit polls showed his conservatives were on course for their worst-ever defeat that he would stay in office to get a raft of reforms to the tax, pensions and health systems through Parliament.
His partners in the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), who also lost heavily in elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin while holding on in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, also pledged to continue their alliance with his Christian Democrats (CDU).
But there has been increasing pressure from within the coalition for the government to do something to reflect the votes.
“There can’t be a simple carrying on as normal after the state elections,” an SPD strategy document circulated this week said, calling for a “German ‘New Deal’ that doesn’t leave people alone in a period of transition”.
It said a special party meeting would be called in December where the leadership would issue new policy proposals.
Despite stronger-than-expected growth in the first half of the year, surveys showed Sept 20’s election results were heavily influenced by squeezed living standards and voter worries over economic issues, notably rising inflation.
Aware of the mood of the electorate, two days before Sept 20’s votes in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Merz announced a €2.5 billion (S$3.65 billion) tax cut and plans for a price cap to help motorists deal with fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war.
There has also been pressure from his partners to change sections of the reform package that have drained support for the ruling parties in the eastern German states which voted in Septemberh, including plans to change the rules on retiring early.
The SPD letter said there were “open questions” about the proposed scrapping of the option for people to retire on a full pension at the age of 63 as long as they had paid contributions for at least 45 years.
The measure was recommended by a government-appointed pension commission as part of a package of measures that included adding a capital markets element to public pensions to keep the system affordable as the population ages.
But many in the east, where people typically have lower savings than in the west and lots went through long spells of unemployment in the wake of German reunification in 1990, feel such a change would hit them disproportionately hard.
Eastern state premiers from both the CDU and SPD have already called for the proposed change to be scrapped and the SPD letter said the proposals had caused “enormous uncertainty” among both workers and employers.
Surveys after the elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania showed many voters feared for their personal economic security and mistrusted Merz, whose ratings have hit historic lows.
Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, who has argued strongly against changing the early retirement rules, said this week Merz needed to regain the trust of voters. “I don’t know if he will succeed,” she said.
Reform pledges
In the wake of the defeats, Merz himself recognised that the government needed to acknowledge that many voters did not feel it was being “fair” in its reform plans.
But already there have been warnings that picking apart reform plans agreed over the summer would undermine confidence in German policy planning just as Europe’s largest economy looks like achieving modest growth after years of recession.
“If we start this whole process again now, it just delays these reforms and we need them,” said Martin Jacob, a professor at Spain’s IESE Business School and a member of the German finance ministry’s scientific advisory board.
“And this matters, because international investors, German investors, companies in Germany need to know what policy environment they’re in,” he said.
However, opinion polls this week showing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party with almost 3 per cent% support across the country underline the political realities facing the government.
Merz, an instinctive pro-business fiscal conservative, came to power in 2025, pledging broad reforms to revive a German economy which has seen its industrial base steadily eroded by relentless competition from China and by the abrupt loss of cheap oil and gas from Russia due to the Ukraine war.
Turning his back on years of German fiscal orthodoxy, he unleashed a €500 billion spending package to rebuild Germany’s creaking infrastructure and its shrunken armed forces and, after months of wrangling, approved the reform package in July.
But the political crisis laid bare by September’s elections could now put those reforms at risk, said Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING.
“Years of economic stagnation helped produce that fragmentation. Now the fragmentation will make the stagnation harder to escape,” he said. REUTERS

MOL has completed construction work at the AV3 unit of the Danube refinery which was damaged by a fire in October last year, the company said.
"Once the construction equipment has been removed, the gradual restart of production can begin. Following the commissioning and testing of the AV3 unit, MOL's Szazhalombatta refinery will once again be able to operate at full capacity, further strengthening the security of fuel supply for Hungary and the entire region. MOL carried out a comprehensive restoration over the past year - it dismantled and reassembled the damaged reinforced concrete structure and restored the damaged equipment, control and power supply systems. The refinery in Szazhalombatta is one of MOL's main facilities. It is the largest refinery in Hungary and one of the largest in Central and Eastern Europe. Its capacity is 165,000 barrels per day (8.1 million tonnes per year). The plant processed Russian oil supplied via the Druzhba pipeline.

The Latvian prime minister said that "the goal should have been to achieve an outcome in which Latvia would not become the last country in Europe left alone".
He noted that all EU member states had reached an agreement, leaving Latvia as the only country opposed to the lifting of sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman.
Kulbergs added that, to his surprise, Lithuania and Estonia had already agreed to remove the two men from the sanctions list. He stressed that the Baltic states should maintain a common position and that the issue needed to be resolved.
"The choice was tough: either a really bad situation or simply a bad one," the prime minister said.
He was also surprised that Latvia's interests had effectively never been discussed.
The prime minister said Latvia had remained firm in its position and had not given its consent, but had been forced to abstain rather than vote against the decision as a whole.
Background:
- The EU extended restrictive measures against individuals responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for another 36 months, but removed Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list.
- It was reported that France planned to "exchange" Usmanov's delisting for the release of several French citizens who are currently in prison in Azerbaijan.

Nazi jokes and ‘cum trophies’: meet the Texas gunfluencer who could soon represent Uvalde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:00:47 UTC
20:00:47 KST

The video begins with Brandon Herrera staring intently into the camera. He is filming himself in a hotel room seated between twin beds, his black hair slicked back and beard neatly trimmed. He is wearing a T-shirt branded with his trademark nickname, “The AK Guy”, above the image of a semi-automatic rifle primed for action.
Three days earlier, on 3 August 2019, a white nationalist armed with a semi-automatic firearm not dissimilar to the one stamped across Herrera’s chest entered a busy Walmart store in the Texas border city of El Paso and opened fire.
Within minutes the shooter had unloaded about 90 rounds, killing 23 people and injuring 22 more.
With the massacre still dominating headlines, most public figures were limiting themselves to vanilla expressions of “thoughts and prayers”. Not so Herrera.
He opened his video with a warning: what viewers were about to hear might sound “a little harsh”. But, he assured them, it was “data driven” and came from “a place of empathy”.
Then he said: “With these terrible mass shootings, you should be really glad that some of these people are using guns to do this … I think we are fortunate that these people are using guns.”
Had the perpetrator of the El Paso massacre used a truck, or a fertiliser bomb, the death toll might have been much higher, Herrera opined. He then attempted to back up the argument with statistics: the average victim count in mass shootings is 15; the Oklahoma City bombing killed 168.
Such sophistry could not disguise his core argument, however. With the blood barely dry on the Walmart floor, Herrera was urging his viewers to celebrate the choice of weapon used in the carnage – a military-style AR-15 semi-automatic rifle.
Herrera, 30, has made a name for himself producing such extreme out-of-the-box pro-gun statements. It is what launched him as a prominent “gunfluencer” with 4.27m subscribers to his YouTube channel, where his videos have been viewed almost 860m times.
And now, he is the frontrunner in the race to represent the border district of south-west Texas in November’s midterm elections. Texas’s congressional district 23 is being closely watched as potentially decisive in the battle to control the House of Representatives through Donald Trump’s final two years in the White House.
Democrats are hoping that such an extreme candidate, even by Texas’s standards, could be vulnerable at the ballot box. They aim to flip the seat that has been in Republican hands since 2015.
Should he win the midterm election in Texas’s congressional district 23, Herrera will take what he calls his “second amendment absolutism” to Washington, with possible ramifications for nationwide gun laws and debate.
Locally, the implications are even more poignant. It would mean that a Republican committed to loosening America’s already lax gun laws would become the voice in Congress for those who live in the outskirts of El Paso, the city left devastated by that 2019 Walmart mass shooting.
More chillingly still, Herrera would also represent the town of Uvalde where, in May 2022, an 18-year-old former student killed 19 children and two teachers.
Shannon Watts, the founder of the gun safety group Moms Demand Action, has been a target of Herrera’s aggressive use of social media. Should he win, she says, there could be long-lasting consequences.
“His idea that somehow we should be grateful that firearms are being used in mass killings is a very cynical ploy to numb people to gun violence, to make them expect it and even accept it. The more Brandon Herreras we elect to Congress, the more likely that will be our destiny.”
Herrera has been presenting himself on the campaign trail as a Trump-endorsed “America First” Republican. He has promised the more than half a million voters scattered across the sprawling, majority-Latino district that he will impose no new taxes, double down on the border crackdown and oppose government funding for abortion.
But it was guns – and specifically the Uvalde school shooting – that brought him into politics.
Herrera grew up in a military family in Fayetteville, North Carolina, and dropped out of college to build his own firearms manufacturing business, focusing on the growing market for semi-automatic rifles. He spent years developing his own spin on the Soviet Kalashnikov rifle, the AK-47. He scaled up the weapon so that it was capable of taking huge 0.50-caliber cartridges, ammunition developed for Browning heavy machine guns more than a century ago.
He called his invention the AK-50, and began marketing it through his company, The AK Guy Inc. Citing frustrations with state-wide Covid restrictions, Herrera relocated the company to San Antonio, Texas, in 2020.
Two years later, Uvalde became the site of one of the worst school shootings in American history. The massacre lasted 77 minutes, the shooter killing his victims at close range as police held back for more than an hour before they finally broke into the classroom and killed him.
Riding the ensuing wave of revulsion, Joe Biden signed into law the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, which strengthened background checks for buyers under 21 and tightened restrictions on firearm possession for some domestic-abuse offenders. Eric Ruben, an expert on gun policy at the SMU Dedman school of law in Dallas, Texas, says that Uvalde “jolted Congress into passing its first major piece of gun safety legislation in a quarter of a century”.
Herrera had a starkly different response. Furious that Tony Gonzales, the Republican congressman representing Uvalde, had backed Biden’s Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, Herrera decided to challenge him for his seat.
“If you vote against our interests, if you vote against gun rights,” he warned Gonzales in 2024, “we will primary you, and we will take your fucking job.”
He did challenge Gonzales that year, losing to the incumbent narrowly, and was repeating the effort this April when Gonzales abruptly resigned from Congress in a sex scandal.
His departure has cleared the way for Herrera to claim the Republican nomination. He is now free to blast his extreme view of gun rights across Uvalde, across the district, through the state of Texas and, should he be successful, nationwide.
Energised by his vast YouTube following and the large sums it passes his way, Herrera is in a position to weaponise his gun rights absolutism. He has vowed to resolutely oppose any new gun safety laws, including raising the age of ownership of an AR-15-style weapon from 18 to 21 or introducing so-called “red flag” laws that allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people who pose a threat to themselves or others.
Both measures have been championed by families of Uvalde victims, some of whom have devoted themselves to pushing for stricter gun laws in the hope of preventing other mass shootings.
Veronica Mata, a founder of the gun safety group Lives Robbed who lost her 10-year-old daughter, Tess, in Uvalde, has put it this way: “Just like we can never turn around and see our daughters again, we’re not going to turn around and walk away.”
To people outside Texas, and beyond America, one of the state’s enduring mysteries is its fierce loyalty to the most extreme form of gun rights, especially in the wake of such human suffering.
There are more than 1m gun licenses in Texas – twice as much as the next state, Florida – with about half of all households in possession of at least one weapon.
But as Ruben, the law professor, points out, until the 1990s Texas was relatively restrictive in its gun laws. In 1995, George W Bush, then governor, signed a law allowing licensed Texans to carry concealed handguns in public. He said it would make Texas a “safer place”, an argument that meshed well with the state’s culture of rugged individualism.
Herrera’s position echoes that logic: he has argued that the way to protect children is to hire more armed security officers and turn schools into “hard targets”.
Since then, Texas’s policies have taken a pro-gun turn in lock step with the tightening grip of an increasingly hard-right Republican party. “Texas has largely tracked the broader effort of the gun rights movement to relax policies on firearms,” Ruben said.
And yet, Texans are not universally wedded to the idea of firearms supremacy. A 2025 opinion survey by the Hobby school of public affairs at the University of Houston found that 85% of Texans support raising the age of buying an AR-15-style rifle from 18 to 21. The reform is especially relevant to Uvalde, given that the shooter legally bought two AR-style rifles with 30-round magazines just days after his 18th birthday.
The same survey showed a clear majority of Texans wanting firmer background checks on gun buyers, a ban on all AR-15 style rifles, and supporting red flag laws.
After the El Paso mass shooting, Republican lawmakers introduced permitless carry, allowing anyone to pack a concealed, loaded handgun in public without a licence or training. It was the polar opposite of the gun safety measures they had promised immediately after the massacre.
The law was the end result of an intense lobbying campaign from hard-right gun activists. When he signed permitless carry into law in June 2021, the Republican governor Greg Abbott did not refer to the El Paso shooting. Rather, he presented it as a defiant act to stop the federal government taking Texans’ guns, arguing that arming yourself was a form of self-defense “against attacks by others”.
Herrera wants a similar law to be imposed across the country. He wants what he calls “concealed carry reciprocity”. It would override regulations in states that take a more stringent approach to gun safety.
Watts, the Moms Demand Action founder, described the end result Herrera is seeking: “His goal is that if you can carry a gun in Texas, no questions asked, then you should be able to carry that firearm down into the New York City subway.”
Shannon Watts had already experienced Herrera’s particular style of political combat first-hand. He unloaded a stream of obscene invective at her on X in January 2023.
Speaking directly to her in a video posted on the platform, he ridiculed the group she had founded. Rather than debate her on gun policy, he opted for vulgar phrases drawn from the pornography industry.
“Just because you let somebody creampie you doesn’t mean I have to give a shit about your political opinions,” he said. Referring to her role as a mother and an activist, he continued: “The fact that you kept your cum trophy doesn’t make you any less wrong about the dumb shit that you say.”
Watts told the Guardian that she was unsurprised by his virulent attack, as she has been frequently assailed over the years by male gun rights activists.
“It has always been about misogyny. How dare a woman and a mother use her voice. That strikes at the heart of every gun extremist, that women could take away their manhood.”
Herrera’s ascent and its impact on the gun discourse bears comparison to what Trump has done to the Republican establishment. Herrera and other “guntubers” have filled the void left by the self-implosion of the once almost monopolistic National Rifle Association (NRA), the gun rights group that held an iron grip on Republican politicians and used that power to resist public safety measures.
Over the past few years, the NRA has been badly weakened by financial scandals and internal disputes. Into that vacuum has stepped a plethora of even harder-line gun-rights groups and social media influencers: louder, more brazen and pushing at the boundaries of a second-amendment free-for-all.
The Guardian repeatedly asked the Herrera campaign whether the candidate would explain his policy stance in an interview, but received no reply. We followed up with a list of detailed questions about his past comments and current positions, including his reductivist view of a child as a “cum trophy”, but that also went unanswered.
He did agree to talk to the New York Times recently, swatting away criticism of the base language he uses on the videos and in social media posts by presenting it as a “comedy performance”.
Then there’s the company that Herrera keeps. He has been endorsed by Kyle Rittenhouse, the gun rights activist who, then 17, shot dead two men and injured another amid 2020 street protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin. (He was later acquitted of homicide.)
Days after the Kenosha incident, Herrera had made another of his “jokes” on video – this time about the death of Rittenhouse’s victims.
“Good luck, kid. You minted some good commies,” he said, adding that he was not encouraging anybody to go “get themselves into some shit … it’s not worth it.”
The duo have now campaigned together and fired a machine gun in unison out of a helicopter.
But sometimes, even some of his followers recoil from the “edgy” humour. One of the remarks that has drawn the strongest condemnation came on the Unsubscribe podcast, when he said he often thought about “putting a gun in my mouth, so I’m basically an honorary veteran”.
In 2023, the latest year for which records are available, 4,690 US military veterans died by suicide using a gun. In 2025, more than 28,000 people in the wider US population died by firearm suicide.
Another disturbing “joke” he has made relate to the Nazis and the Holocaust. In a 2022 video viewed 2.3m times, he calls the MP 40, the submachine gun used by the Germans in the second world war, “the original ghetto blaster”. Later in the video, he and an associate goosestep to the sound of Ericka, the military marching song adopted by the Waffen SS.
The Nazi references were not the only evidence of Herrera’s flirtation with far-right historical imagery. The news outlet Jewish Insider uncovered private videos produced by a younger Herrera in North Carolina on behalf of the Fayetteville chapter of the Sons of Confederate Veterans.
The group has promoted the “Lost Cause” narrative which reframes the civil war as a struggle over states’ rights rather than slavery. Herrera described SCV as an “historical honor society dedicated to preserving confederate heritage”, without mentioning its longstanding links with white supremacist groups. His involvement with neo-Confederacy activity continued until at least 2019, the newspaper reported.
Such an unsettling back catalogue has provoked objections to his candidacy even from within Texas conservative circles. Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist based in Austin, challenged Herrera by saying there should be zero tolerance for making light about Nazi Germany. “I don’t think the Holocaust is something we should be joking about,” he said. “I don’t think we should be singing the song of the stormtroopers.”
Steinhauser told the Guardian that anything perceived as antisemitic was likely to play negatively with Texas Republicans and independent voters, both of whom tend to be strongly pro-Israel.
True to form, Herrera lashed back at Steinhauser, posting on social media: “When did conservatives become pearl clutching virtue signalers?”
Could this toxic screed prove to be Herrera’s political undoing?Nationally, the Democratic party has begun to wake up to the possibilities.
In August, the Democratic congressional campaign committee added Texas 23 to its target list, denoting a shift in strategy from previous assumptions that the district was irredeemably Republican.
Opinion polls have been few and far between, and those that have been conducted came from partisan sources. A survey back in March was carried out by the House Majority Pac sponsored by the Democratic party. It put Herrera’s Democratic rival, Katy Padilla Stout, two points up. A poll conducted from the other side of the aisle last month put Herrera ahead by six points. That came from the Remington research group, on behalf of the rightwing website Breitbart.
On the ground, his opponent Padilla Stout sees his most egregious outbursts as a turn-off for many voters, especially his depiction of children in the wake of the Uvalde massacre at Robb elementary school.
“So many children in Uvalde were affected by the shooting. When people hear the way he describes children, their jaws are on the floor,” she said.
And yet, Padilla Stout has a palatability problem. How do you talk about “creampies” and “cum trophies” without offending voters anew?
“As a mother myself, that’s a hard thing for me to put on thousands of doors.”
Texas 23 is a deeply rural and relatively sparsely populated district that has hunting and shooting in its DNA. Padilla Stout herself grew up within that culture.
“My dad bought a ranch shortly before I was born, it was part of his American dream,” she said. “And that aspect of gun culture, the hunting and ranching part, I’ve been part of it all my life. I have cousins who would get their first shotgun on their 12th birthday, that’s our family tradition.”
Given the prevalence of guns in the local way of life, she hasn’t made Herrera’s gun rights policy front and centre of her campaign. Voters, she said, rarely raise it.
Her first campaign ad focused on the cost of childcare and groceries, and the prolonged drag of the Iran war.
But she told the Guardian that she would continue to sound the alarm whenever she is able. “Herrera is a gun manufacturer who makes money off his gun absolutism. That’s his end goal. He wants to remove all boundaries on the second amendment, and dismantle public safety piece by piece.”

‘This is where I live now, the back of a truck’: a day in the life of a grandmother in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:00:46 UTC
20:00:46 KST

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.
The flat-bed truck is open to the hot summer air, its metal frame covered on two sides by draped tarpaulins, the rear by a pegged-up bedsheet. On the tin floor lies a squab mattress and pillow with a yellow frilled cover.
Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem balances a thin cushion at the truck bed’s metal edge to protect her knees as she crawls in and out. She lowers her foot to the plastic chair below, then drops to the ground, staggering slightly as she gets her balance. Mansoura is 76 years old. The truck is her home now. All around her, her family live in tents, the fabric ripped and fraying.
This is a day in the life of a grandmother living in Gaza.
Daybreak
 Last night, I stayed awake until 2am. I barely sleep during the night because of the mosquitoes and the heat. I fall asleep for a short while, I wake up early in the morning, pray to God, and wait to hear the call to dawn prayer. When I wake up, I call for my grandson to bring over the white plastic chair that I need to climb in and out of the truck.
This is where I live now: in the back of a pickup truck. This truck, we brought it with us when we were fleeing for our lives from Beit Lahia [a city in northern Gaza]. Its owners had abandoned it, so we took it with us, displaced from place to place – until we ended up here. When we finally arrived, there was no space for me anywhere else – the tents that we have are small, torn and overcrowded, they fall down on the children – so I was forced to live in the truck. I sleep in it to escape the sand, dirt and insects. That is the story of the truck.
After I wake up, I fold up the mattress and prop it with the pillows against the wall, then use a cloth to sweep the dirt and sand from the tarpaulin floor. I sit with my grandson, and we try to make the tiny gas stove work, to boil water for coffee. It’s an old stove – inherited from my own grandfather – and it’s hard to get it to light, as there isn’t enough gas, but eventually we get a flame. I boil water in a small pot and brew coffee for my sons and I – a few spoonfuls for each person. The coffee is filled with the taste of paraffin.
Midday
Mansoura’s son holds up the phone for a video call with one of her grandsons, who left Gaza and is now living overseas, and she chats to him for a while. For lunch, Mansoura takes a few basil leaves from a plant the family have grown in a tin can, and grinds them with garlic in her mortar and pestle. She adds a chopped tomato and eats it with a little bread.
 This is the salad I used to make at home – back then I would add rosemary, green thyme and mint. When I see vegetables growing, it reminds me of Beit Lahia, of our farming, crops and land.
Before the war, I lived like a queen. I had a beautiful life. I was a farmer. I planted and harvested my land. I had animal shelters where I raised livestock, chickens, rabbits and ducks. I lived a very beautiful life, but it has changed for me.
Now, we have no home, no source of income and no good food. Life in tents is terrible – actually unbearable. There are insects everywhere, mosquitoes, sand, dirt, garbage and torn tents. And the wind. In winter, it blows everything away. In summer, we die from the extreme heat. We do not even have enough space to build a proper bathroom – a person who showers in a tent comes out dirtier leaving the bathroom.
My feeling is that for people my age, death is more honorable than living this life. This isn’t life. We are not living. We are dead. Everything beautiful is gone. It has disappeared, and I have disappeared with it.
After eating, I wash the clothing for my family. Back home, we lived in a two-storey house, and had a washing machine – I used to run it on the long cycle, rinsing the clothes once, twice, even three times. Now, even though I am an elderly woman, I wash all the clothes by hand in a plastic bucket.
Afternoon
After lunch, Mansoura sits on the ground outside, gathers her grandchildren around her, and quizzes them about their old lives. Some are young and can barely remember a time before the war: they have spent nearly three years living in tents amid the rubble.
“Where did we live, Mohammed?” Mansoura asks.
“In northern Beit Lahia,” he answers.
“Where in the north?”
“Near 36th Street.”
“Tell them what Beit Lahia was like before the war.”
“Honestly, it was good, better than these days.”
“We will return there,” Mansoura says.
She draws her leather satchel toward her, looking through the pockets.
“Look at what I have in my bag. What is this?” Mansoura asks, dangling an object in front of her.
They answer: “The key of the house.”
 This is the most precious thing I own – the key to our house in the north. It is the key to the house that the occupation forces bulldozed. They flattened it: the house, the trees, the well, even a pen full of animals – they bulldozed it all. We couldn’t take anything with us, no money, no livestock.
I lived through wars before this. None was as bad as this one. During the 52-day war, we sheltered in schools, and we were OK – there wasn’t bombing like this, not the level of killing, and not the destruction of homes. But this war is extremely difficult. The destruction is enormous, the devastation is enormous – and all without any benefit. All of this is for nothing.
Life has become very different. Our family never knew hunger before, never knew displacement, bombardment, missiles, killing and destruction in this way or on this scale. The other thing I keep in this bag is a bullet – it was pulled from my son’s back. During the famine, he had nothing to eat and nothing to feed his seven children, so he went to get a bag of flour to feed his children from the aid stations, and they shot him. I keep this as a reminder of what happened – all for the sake of getting food.
Honestly, every day is the same for me now. I wake up, arrange the place around us and our sleeping area, clean it, eat, sit, and sleep.
The things that make me smile are when I wake up in the morning and find my children safe, when I hear that my grandchildren are well, and when I myself am OK, thank God … This is the greatest life for me and the greatest happiness for me.
At night, I call my grandson to bring the chair. Then I crawl back into the truck to sleep.

Consciousness may have evolved to solve a problem that pure intelligence couldn’t handle, fascinating new theory suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:00:18 UTC
20:00:18 KST

Consciousness may have evolved to help living things resolve competing needs when their survival is at stake, rather than simply emerging from greater intelligence. This theoretical account was published in Frontiers in Neuroscience.
How did conscious experience emerge from the chemistry of life? Existing theories examine how brains broadcast information, integrate signals, and generate predictions. But explaining these mechanisms leaves an evolutionary question: what problem did consciousness help organisms solve?
Jeff Stibel, a cognitive scientist and author who serves as a trustee of the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County and Tufts University, proposes that cognition and consciousness arose from different evolutionary pressures. Cognition helped organisms navigate uncertainty, while the regulatory processes underlying consciousness helped them preserve themselves and manage competing demands.
“This paper was deeply personal. It grew out of years of conversations with my late mentor, Dan Dennett, who pushed me to formalize some of my thoughts on the evolutionary differences between cognition and consciousness,” explained Stibel. “When Dan passed, I felt an obligation to revisit our discussions, and it became even more pressing given the advances we have seen across AI. What pulled me in was a growing suspicion that we have been asking the wrong question: treating consciousness as the top rung of intelligence, when it looks more like a separate adaptation with its own evolutionary job. The timing felt urgent as AI grows more capable, alongside a widespread assumption that a clever enough machine will simply ‘wake up’ or has already awoken. That narrative is everywhere, and I think it rests on the same confusion.”
Stibel draws together existing research in cell biology, evolutionary theory, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. He traces a possible progression from cells protecting their boundaries to organisms coordinating multiple needs under conditions of uncertainty, limited resources, and potentially irreversible consequences.
The author outlines six predictions to make the framework testable. These concern whether conscious engagement increases with competing demands; whether different needs must become comparable; whether attention, bodily state, memory, and readiness to act change together; whether consciousness diminishes when this coordination is disrupted or less necessary; how these capacities differ across species; and whether artificial systems require genuine self-maintenance pressures.
Suggested experiments would vary conflict or risk while holding sensory input constant, disrupt coordination while preserving simpler processing, or compare artificial systems with different self-maintenance requirements. The paper also identifies potentially disconfirming findings, including consciousness persisting despite disrupted settlement capacity.
The central argument describes three levels of regulation. “Proto-control” protects an organism’s integrity, such as by preserving a cell’s membrane and limiting destructive processes; the paper explicitly does not describe this as conscious. “Meta-control” manages conflicts among separate regulatory processes. “Settlement control” makes competing needs comparable and coordinates them into a shared course of action. For example, a hungry animal encountering food near a possible predator must weigh feeding against danger. A decision to retreat would involve coordinated changes in attention, bodily readiness, movement, and learning. Stibel identifies consciousness with this coordinated state in a system whose continued existence depends on its own regulation.
“Intelligence and consciousness are not the same thing, and they did not evolve for the same reason. Intelligence is outward facing: it is for modeling the world, predicting, planning, solving problems. Consciousness evolved for something more internal: holding a fragile organism together when survival is on the line. The analogy I use in the paper is cannibalism. Intelligence helped early life forage efficiently, but without a self to protect, the most efficient meal was often the nearest neighbor, or the organism itself. The earliest precursors of consciousness helped define biological boundaries, which likely protected early cellular life from eating itself.”
Applied to artificial intelligence, the argument is that greater capability alone would not produce consciousness: a system would also need to maintain itself and resolve competing demands with genuine consequences for its continued existence.
“The upshot for AI is blunt. Scaling today’s models makes them better predictors, not systems with anything of their own at stake. LLMs have no boundaries and no self to protect, and humans provide everything they need,” Stibel told PsyPost. “In that respect, the problem isn’t that they are too simple or fall short of AGI. They are too coddled. Without real skin in the game, no amount of capability will magically cross over into consciousness.”
The paper does not restrict consciousness to biological organisms. However, an artificial system would need more than programmed self-preservation, such that its continued operation would have to depend on conditions that it maintains itself.
Stibel emphasized the implications: “The most important takeaway is that biology and evolution reframe the AI debate. The fear that we will accidentally scale our way into a suffering machine, and the engineering hype that digital minds are just around the corner, both rest on conflating intelligence with consciousness. If those are genuinely separate things, then consciousness is not something that sneaks up on us through sheer capability. It is a specific kind of organization we would have to deliberately build, and I would argue, one we have good reason not to. Getting that distinction right is how we choose our ethics rather than stumble into them.”
Testing this account presents a fundamental challenge: researchers may be able to examine whether a system has the proposed capacities for self-maintenance and coordination, but they cannot directly observe whether it has subjective experience.
“The biggest unanswered question is measurement,” Stibel said. “It is impossible to observe consciousness in anyone other than yourself, so the paper proposes testing the necessary precursors instead. At the heart of the test is whether a system genuinely works to maintain its own existence under constraint, rather than just reacting to threats it was built to detect. Turning that into a real experiment, in both biological and artificial systems, is the hard road ahead.”
Stibel also identified an unresolved ethical question: “There is also a deeper question the paper raises but doesn’t settle. If we ever did build a system with genuine stakes in its own survival, we would have created something that can be harmed, a moral patient whose interests may not align with ours. That is a line worth understanding well before we approach it, not after.”
The paper, “From chemistry to cognition: the adaptive origins of consciousness under constraint,” was authored by Jeff Stibel.

China hawks grumble over Trump’s lavish welcome planned for Xi state visit
Chorus of disapproval rises ahead of the Chinese leader’s arrival, even as others say the welcome is the show, not the deal
4-MIN READ4-MIN
5
 Listen
Hours before President Xi Jinping’s aircraft lands at Joint Base Andrews, Washington is preparing for a scene that seemed unthinkable in recent years: his American counterpart waiting on the tarmac for the leader of a country that much of the US national security establishment regards as its foremost strategic adversary.
While the Donald Trump administration is betting on warmth, deals and stability with Beijing, recent public surveys show that American anxiety over China has eased from its 2024 peak.
But the China hawks who helped shape the debate have spent the week warning that the ceremony risks obscuring a more familiar reality: Beijing remains a rival, and the issues that have defined that rivalry have not gone away.
They are making that case from outside the room. Since Trump returned to the White House, the chorus has lost resonance inside the building and with the public. The US president has disputed their arguments himself while calling Xi a “great gentleman”.
