Venezuela: Three months after the two earthquakes, a human rights-centred response remains absent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

On 24 June 2026, two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 in magnitude struck northern Venezuela, causing one of the country’s most serious disasters in recent decades. According to official figures, 6,509 people were killed and 60,785 affected homes were assessed, of which 11,001 were classified as high risk.
“Three months after these events, there remains a debt to those affected that must be addressed by placing their human rights and dignity at the centre of the recovery,” said Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
“Three months after these events, there remains a debt to those affected that must be addressed by placing their human rights and dignity at the centre of the recovery.”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
The earthquakes struck a population already facing a complex humanitarian emergency, serious difficulties in accessing economic and social rights, including the rights to health, food, housing and work, as well as a policy of systematic and widespread repression that has pushed at least 25% of Venezuela’s population to flee the country since 2015 in search of international protection.
Amnesty International interviewed 21 people directly affected in Caracas and La Guaira between 23 July and 14 August 2026. Those interviewed said that the Venezuelan authorities’ response was delayed and poorly coordinated. Family members and neighbours removed rubble with their bare hands or improvised tools while requesting heavy machinery, specialized personnel and search dogs. They also reported that, although there was a large deployment of police, military and intelligence personnel, their activities focused on surveillance and territorial control rather than directly participating in rescue operations or efforts to locate missing people.
Lack of information and conflicting figures
Public information provided by the Venezuelan authorities has been marked by opacity and a lack of transparency. To date, no official figures on missing people have been published, on the grounds that the authorities wish to avoid speculation. The only official estimate was provided by the governor of La Guaira state, who put the number at 1,579 missing people. In the absence of official data, independent citizen initiatives have recorded more than 41,000 reports of missing people. Despite these valuable efforts, errors and duplicate names have been identified in these records, making official figures essential.
There are also significant discrepancies in the recorded number of deaths. The governor of La Guaira state said the death toll was estimated at 7,265 people, while the national government’s most recent update, on 24 August, reported a total of 6,509 deaths resulting from the disaster.
In addition, the available data are not disaggregated by sex, age, location or other essential characteristics, making it impossible to identify the differentiated impacts of the earthquakes and design appropriate responses for children, older people, women, people with disabilities and other groups that may require specific protection and assistance measures.
Families forced to search on their own
During interviews conducted by Amnesty International, people reported very limited institutional support and a lack of information about the mechanisms available to them to find out the whereabouts of their relatives or what measures the authorities had taken.
Families have undertaken searches on their own, visiting public institutions, morgues, hospitals and collapsed buildings; putting up posters with photographs of their loved ones in strategic places such as hospitals and temporary shelters; sharing information on social media; and, together with civil society organizations, creating databases and digital platforms in an attempt to locate those who remain missing.
“My children [grandchildren aged 13 and 14] are still missing. I have a lot of faith that the children were taken to another shelter, to another state, that they are alive. At no point have they said they are going to provide help to search for them — no, never.”.
Person interviewed by Amnesty International.
The uncertainty of not knowing whether their loved ones are alive, whether their bodies have been recovered, or whether they will be able to bury them according to their customs and beliefs has caused profound anguish.
Handling of bodies and remains of people who died
Thousands of people who died have still not been identified and continue to be processed in improvised morgues, without clear protocols and without their families and loved ones knowing which authorities they should approach to search for and recover their bodies and/or remains.
People interviewed who had searched for relatives at Los Silos, an area within the port of La Guaira designated as a temporary morgue, described unclear procedures and the absence of centralized information on search, recovery and identification efforts, as well as on the tools available when genetic testing or other identification methods are required.
Some said they had to review numerous photographs of bodies on a digital tablet, many of them unrecognizable, and that in some cases they attempted to identify bodies and remains directly inside bags. These accounts raise serious concerns about the dignity of the procedures and the support provided to families.
One woman who was waiting for the results of a DNA test said:
“They told me I had to keep waiting because there are so many dead, and that I should remember the Vargas tragedy [the 1999 mudslides], where there are still families looking for missing people. Imagine how I feel.”
Other people said they visited Los Silos and various institutions several times a week in the hope of obtaining information.
The lack of psychological support during these processes was also highlighted. Some people said they had received the cremated remains of relatives, which caused them to question whether the identification had been carried out correctly.
“I don’t trust it, because sometimes I think they could cremate all those dead people together and mix up the ashes. Sometimes I think that.”.
Person interviewed by Amnesty International.
Material losses and lack of durable solutions
According to official figures, as of 5 July, 17,345 people had lost their homes. Some stayed with relatives or people close to them, others went to temporary shelters established by the government, while others chose to remain near their homes in tents they set up themselves.
“They can’t just tell you: they’re going to call you so you can go over there, to Matusalén [meaning somewhere very far away], and what about your land here? What’s going to happen to your land here? Who’s going to look after it? Who’s going to keep an eye on it? If you’re not here looking after what belongs to you, let’s be clear, they’re not going to resolve anything for us.””.
Person interviewed by Amnesty International.
The authorities implemented a damage assessment system using red labels (entry restricted), yellow labels (limited use) and green labels (fully habitable) on the façades of homes. People interviewed who had been affected said they had been included in official censuses and registered, among other mechanisms, through the Sistema Patria, an official digital platform used to administer and distribute social programmes. However, they did not have sufficient clarity about the purpose and scope of the process, the criteria used for allocating housing, or the timelines for providing permanent housing solutions.
“My house is marked yellow, but my house is high risk because two walls collapsed and all the columns gave way, and the floor lifted up. I mean, there’s an uneven level in the floor. […] I can’t go into that house with two adults and two children when it’s like that.”
Person interviewed by Amnesty International.
The lack of certainty about whether housing solutions are temporary or permanent is compounded by the loss of sources of income. Those interviewed said the destruction of workplaces and the decline in tourism had limited the recovery capacity of many families.
“Every week they promise us they’re going to give us [construction] materials, that they’re going to sort things out, and they don’t sort anything out. This is really getting out of control now, because people are tired and overwhelmed by so many promises.”.
Person interviewed by Amnesty International.
Discretionary access for civil society organizations to temporary shelters
The state response included the establishment of camps and temporary shelters in schools, sports facilities and other public spaces, but the operation of these facilities has not been standardized, leaving people in uncertainty because there are no specific protocols governing how they operate and no clear information about when they will close.
Civil society organizations also told Amnesty International that there was no single mechanism for gaining access to shelters to provide humanitarian assistance. Authorization varied depending on the shelter and each organization’s relationship with the authorities, delaying assistance in some locations. They also reported a lack of protocols for assisting people in vulnerable situations, including children, as well as an uncoordinated distribution of aid, with services and assistance varying disproportionately from one temporary shelter to another.
The anti-NGO law obstructs the civil society response
The work of civil society organizations has been restricted since the publication of the Law on Oversight, Regulation, Operation and Financing of Non-Governmental Organizations and Non-Profit Social Organizations (the anti-NGO law) and the recent publication of two circulars by the Ministry of Interior and Justice. By imposing legal and financial obstacles on organizations, these measures have delayed or even prevented them from providing assistance.
In addition, donors and international cooperation agencies often require organizations to have the registration established under the law in order to access funding. One representative of a non-governmental organization said: “Donors, funders and even banks ask for the registration. For any procedure, they ask you for the certificate. There is a huge administrative bureaucracy; all institutions and funders, instead of making things more flexible, impose more requirements and administrative obstacles, even though we are in an emergency context.”
Conclusions and recommendations
“Although earthquakes are an unavoidable tragedy, the human rights violations that result from them are preventable. The Venezuelan authorities must guarantee the rights of all those affected,” said Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
Although earthquakes are an unavoidable tragedy, the human rights violations that result from them are preventable. The Venezuelan authorities must guarantee the rights of all those affected.”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
Amnesty International calls on the Venezuelan authorities to guarantee transparency and ensure that all people affected by the earthquakes, as well as organizations working to provide humanitarian assistance, have access to information. The authorities must publish up-to-date information on the timelines, criteria and types of support provided to victims, as well as how people can access that support. This information must be provided in a format that is accessible to everyone.The authorities must also provide detailed information on people who have died as a result of the earthquakes, people who remain missing, and the measures being taken to inform families. All information must be disaggregated by gender, age and other relevant factors.
The authorities must also create a single registry of victims that is accessible to the public and guarantees access to housing and government support without discrimination.
At the same time, the authorities must publish a reconstruction plan for affected homes and designate a specific authority to oversee its implementation; provide medical care, including psychological support, to those who need it, particularly relatives of missing and deceased people; immediately publish protocols governing temporary shelters and facilitate access for journalists and human rights organizations; and immediately repeal the anti-NGO law in order to enable community and social solidarity initiatives.

A Startup Wants to Power Data Centers With ‘Supercritical’ Carbon Dioxide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

A new company has a plan to make the dirty gas turbines powering data centers more efficient: liquid carbon dioxide.
American Supercritical came out of stealth Wednesday, announcing $8 million in funding. It wants to retrofit inefficient gas turbines that many data centers rely on for power with units that can generate more power, without adding more emissions (though the gas-fired turbines will continue to emit carbon pollution). The technology can also theoretically be used on a wide variety of energy sources at a time when power demand is skyrocketing.
“We want to start with gas turbines but eventually expand beyond that,” says cofounder Simon Shuham.
Most large gas-fired power plants in the United States use an array of heat engines in what’s known as a combined-cycle process: First, turbines generate electricity from burning compressed air and natural gas, then a separate engine uses the hot exhaust to make steam and create additional energy. But for a variety of reasons, data centers across the US have opted to power their operations with what are known as simple-cycle turbines, and exclude the steam component.
These turbines are much less efficient than combined-cycle plants. Usually, only about 35 percent of the energy from simple-cycle turbines is converted to electricity, while the rest escapes as exhaust. (In combined-cycle plants, that figure hovers closer to 60 to 65 percent.) That exhaust includes greenhouse gases, making plants that run on simple-cycle turbines a much worse choice for the environment than combined-cycle plants.
The size of some of these plants combined with their inefficiency is a recipe for climate disaster. A massive data-center power plant in Texas that Amazon is building with just simple-cycle turbines, for instance, is permitted to emit more than 33 million tons of greenhouse gases per year—more than the annual total of some small countries.
But all these small, inefficient turbines could be a great match for supercritical CO2 technology, American Supercritical’s founders say. Carbon dioxide becomes supercritical when it’s pressurized and held at a certain temperature. In this state, it gets the density of liquid but still behaves like a gas, meaning it can move energy more efficiently through much smaller amounts of equipment.
American Supercritical wants to attach its units to small gas turbines and help generate more energy. While the turbines themselves would still use gas, the supercritical CO2 unit can use the hot exhaust generated from those turbines to create additional electricity. Instead of using that heat to boil water and create steam, the heat is transferred directly by the pressurized CO2 to generate additional energy with no additional emissions.
“We’re essentially building miniature combined-cycle plants,” says Shuham.
Using supercritical CO2 also can eliminate or greatly reduce water use in the power generation process—something that’s drawn intense scrutiny when it comes to data centers. Importantly, the CO2 involved operates in a closed-loop system, meaning that it doesn’t have to be refilled. Cofounder Matthew Carlson, who researched supercritical CO2 for more than a decade, likens it to refrigeration systems that circulate CO2 to facilitate cooling.
The company plans to initially sell a 10-megawatt unit—relatively small by gas plant standards. By American Supercritical’s math, adding supercritical CO2 units could increase turbines’ efficiency by up to 50 percent without adding any more greenhouse gas emissions or water use.
But retrofitting all of the country’s inefficient gas turbines powering data centers with supercritical CO2 units won’t reduce emissions to zero. Natural gas production and use, even with efficient turbines, warms the planet. Data centers also represent a massive new source of pollution—right at a time when the world needs to be scaling back on its use.
Using supercritical CO2 for power has been studied for more than 50 years in US national labs. Over the past two decades, research has moved away from theory toward trying out practical applications, assisted by technological breakthroughs that help with the pressurization process. Doug Hofer, an adviser to American Supercritical who spent two decades at GE as a turbine engineer, says that one important innovation has been the development of more compact and more affordable heat exchangers—devices that help both heat and cool the CO2.
American Supercritical isn’t the only company trying to bring this technology to market, says Subith Vasu, a professor of engineering at the University of Central Florida, who runs a lab at the school’s Center for Advanced Turbomachinery and Energy Research. The companies still have hurdles to overcome to achieve commercial success.
“Whenever you are venturing into new technologies, you need to have all the associated components, the supply chain,” in place, he says. Technical challenges also abound, he adds, “and cost has been a huge issue.”
Hofer says that part of the delay has also simply been because larger companies are satisfied with the performance of traditional power plants and unwilling to invest in different technologies—and turbine makers are not interested in funding potential competitors. “It’s the innovator’s dilemma, right?” he says. “Getting this [technology] out there needs to have an outside influence.”
The $7 trillion set to be invested in data centers globally by 2030 has helped open up a whole new potential market, especially for an industry racing to get as much power on the grid as it possibly can to come out ahead in the AI race.
“There’s this incredible willingness to pay [for power], but they’re bottlenecked,” says Shuham. “The goal is to come in here, retrofit their existing systems, and give them the ability to build additional data centers—or get rid of some of the gas turbines.”
Earlier this year, China announced that operations started at the world’s first geothermal plant using supercritical CO2. Carlson says that in his career, he’s worked on supercritical CO2 applications in nuclear, geothermal, and solar energy. He and Shuham say that their units could be converted to work with small modular reactors, a technology that’s enjoyed strong support from the Trump administration. (The company says it has already signed an initial agreement with one company, though it didn’t name it). It can work with other sources of heat as well.
“We just need to get something hot, and then we can convert that into electricity,” says Carlson.

America Must Win Back Its Global Standing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

“From this day forward, a new vision will govern our land,” President Donald Trump declared in his inaugural address in January 2017. “From this moment on, it’s going to be America First.” An insular, populist nationalism, coupled with an antipathy toward globalist ideas and institutions, became the central theme and the clarion call of both his terms in the White House.
President Trump has spent considerable energy lambasting the United Nations, an institution the United States helped create 80 years ago and has shaped ever since. He has derided it as an “unelected, unaccountable, global bureaucracy,” and little more than “a talking shop.”
A majority of Americans no longer agree with their president. In a Sept. 2025 global poll commissioned by The Rockefeller Foundation, 61% of American respondents agreed that their country should cooperate with others to solve global challenges, even if doing so meant compromising on some national interests. Only 16% responded with a no. Such American support for international cooperation has only increased. When the same question was posed in the 2026 iteration of the poll, which surveyed more than 35,000 people across 34 countries, support in the U.S. rose by four percentage points to 65%, while the opposition fell by two percentage points to 14%.
American public support for multilateral cooperation in 2026 exceeds that of Western Europe, where it stands at 61%. Despite President Trump’s attacks on the UN, 62% of Americans say they trust the institution—eight percentage points more than last year—while only 30% claim to distrust it. Nearly half of American respondents, 46%, say they comfortable with the UN playing a leading role on the world stage. Only 21% say they are uncomfortable.
As global stability has eroded and peace has grown increasingly fragile, the desire for cooperation across border has increased among Americans. In the same poll, respondents were asked to choose three priorities from a list of 13 global issues: among American respondents, 40% ranked preventing wars and conflicts among their most pressing concerns.
The message to President Trump is clear. For most of the last 80 years, America has acted multilaterally, even during its unipolar moment. Americans do not want the U.S. to act unilaterally in an increasingly multipolar era. They want their country to practice the politics of consensus building rather than coercion.
A new call for international cooperation
I joined an initiative involving 100 former prime ministers and presidents from every continent that calls upon today’s leaders to build a stronger basis for cooperation in an increasingly fragmented and multipolar world. On Monday, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, many of us came together to endorse core principles that could provide the basis for a new global consensus on solving shared problems and helping those in need.
As the poll commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation found, more than half of American respondents, 53%, would support their president publicly endorsing these principles of cooperation. This finding suggests that America is not a nation committed to an “America first and America only” ideology, but a nation with a strong sense of the enduring values that bind it to the wider world.
Yet as American support for cooperation with the rest of the world rises, the inclination across the rest of the world to cooperate with America hangs in the balance. For decades, people everywhere have looked to America for hope and inspiration. That faith is now being questioned.
America’s appeal as global leader, the same poll found, has diminished. Only 39% of the respondents worldwide are comfortable with the U.S. playing a leading role on the world stage. And 34% of the respondents across the globe regard the U.S. as a major threat to their own countries. On that grim metric, Russia scored even higher, at higher 42%. China, surprisingly, fared better at 30%.
When respondents to the 2026 poll were asked which countries they would be comfortable seeing take a leading role in world affairs, America ranked in the bottom half of the table. Canada outpolled America, with 60% of the respondents globally comfortable with it playing such a role, the highest vote recorded for any country.
Several middle powers were viewed more favorably by respondents as potential global leaders: Japan (58%), Australia (55%), the United Kingdom (54%), Germany, Spain, and Italy (all 53%), France (51%) and South Korea (42%).
While none of these countries comes remotely close to matching American economic and military power, America’s soft power has certainly suffered in recent years. It is estimated that 900 million people want to live somewhere other than their own country.
Surveys asking people which country they would prefer to live in have consistently put America in the lead. According to Gallup data, 24% of respondents in 2009 named America as their preferred new home. By 2025, that preference had shrunk to a mere 15%.
Renewing American leadership
America can still regain its soft power. Americans have not lost their optimism or their sense of belief in a better future. In the 2026 poll, 55% of American respondents professed that, during a crisis, their own community would pull together. An even more decisive majority, 64%, believe that, as Americans they share a responsibility to help others, even in countries they don’t know. And 76% of American respondents believe it is possible to build a better future for the next generation.
Americans need to convey these convictions more clearly and widely. Under pressure from an affordability crisis at home and military overreach abroad, Americans may not any longer be prepared to “bear any burden or pay any price.”
But the values that underpin America are still embraced by a majority of its people. This suggests that America still has what it takes to resume the global leadership that is needed more than ever in our turbulent world.

More than 30 trains are delayed amid Russian attacks — where the biggest delays are

2026-09-23

More than 30 trains are delayed amid Russian attacks — where the biggest delays are
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv’s railway stations were not damaged, but more than 30 trains are running behind schedule. The biggest delays are affecting services from the central regions, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk region.
Railway stations in Kyiv were not damaged by the Russian attack, but there are train delays, with the largest delays affecting trains from central Ukraine, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk region. This was reported on September 23 by JSC "Ukrzaliznytsia," UNN writes.
Details
"The enemy launched a massive attack on Kyiv. Our monitoring center closely tracked the situation, which made it possible to avoid stopping passenger train services. At the Central Railway Station and Darnytsia Station, passengers boarded and disembarked via underground passageways, as предусмотрено for the yellow level of air-raid threat when targets are detected near railway stations," the statement said.
Which trains are delayed
The capital's railway stations have not sustained damage as a result of the attack. There are train delays. The trains most behind schedule are those running from central Ukraine, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk region
According to the Ukrzaliznytsia train delay-tracking service, more than 30 trains are running behind schedule. The longest delays—more than 9 hours—affect the Kryvyi Rih–Chernivtsi and Kryvyi Rih–Rakhiv trains.
The Kyiv City Express trains, as reported, are operating on the full loop with delays of between 10 and 30 minutes.

Masterpiece of Kyiv modernism: Railway Market destroyed in Russian attack on Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Masterpiece of Kyiv modernism: Railway Market destroyed in Russian attack on Kyiv
A fire broke out in the former Railway Market building, a masterpiece of Kyiv modernist architecture near the Central Railway Station, during Russia's large-scale drone attack on Kyiv on the morning of 23 September.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)
Details: Footage being shared by local Telegram channels shows the building engulfed by a huge fire.
The former Railway Market at 1 Mokra Street in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district is an example of 20th-century Kyiv modernism. It was built in 1973 to a design by modernist architects Alla Anishchenko and Nataliia Сhmutina. The building's distinctive rounded shape is formed by concrete elements with radial cables supporting the roof. The premises cover an area of 3,807 sq m, and the building has two floors, a basement and a storage area. The market was designed to accommodate 140 retail units.
In the late 1980s, the building housed the Okean shop, while in the 1990s it was occupied by the Kyiv Universal Exchange. Later, a Velyka Kyshenia supermarket was there for many years before it closed in 2021. That same year, there were reports of plans to demolish the building for redevelopment, but architects both in and beyond Ukraine raised concerns due to the uniqueness of the site, and following a public outcry, the plans were dropped.
The consequences of the attack, including any casualties and the extent of the damage to the building, are being confirmed.
Background: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko has reported that a drone struck a nine-storey non-residential building at third-floor level in the Solomianskyi district. In the Holosiivskyi district, a drone crashed onto the roof of a non-residential building, while another crashed in the grounds of a transport infrastructure facility. Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) said no damage was caused to the Central Railway Station building itself.

Israeli minister promotes settlement tours to West Bank as world leaders warn against annexation

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:59:55 UTC
19:59:55 KST

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s far-right Religious Zionism Party has launched tours of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, as international leaders renew warnings that settlement expansion and displacement are destroying prospects for peace.
In a Hebrew-language post on X, Smotrich invited Israelis to join the tours during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.
“Come, see the settlement revolution with your own eyes and feel the security it provides to the State of Israel,” he wrote.
Smotrich shared a link to a party-run website promoting the tours, listing routes through settlements and outposts built on land seized from Palestinians. He invited Israelis to visit 160 illegal outposts and 104 illegal settlements that he said had been established under the current government.
The initiative turns settlement expansion into a cause for celebration, even as world leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York forcefully reiterate their condemnation of illegal Israeli settlements and renew warnings that they are destroying prospects for Palestinian statehood.
Warnings of ‘ethnic cleansing’ and ‘annexation’
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Tuesday that Israeli violence, displacement and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank were “bulldozing the path to peace and raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing”.
“We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes,” he told the General Assembly.
Guterres said the devastating situation in the occupied Palestinian territories must not be overlooked amid the broader turmoil engulfing the Middle East.
European Council President Antonio Costa echoed those concerns at a high-level meeting on the two-state solution and a comprehensive peace plan for Gaza on the sidelines of the gathering.
“In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, the two-state solution is being jeopardised on a daily basis,” Costa said on Tuesday.
“We see the images and hear the testimonies of what is happening in the West Bank daily – settler violence, impunity, displacement of whole communities, and de facto annexation. These settlements are illegal under international law.”
Trade measures by Western allies
The settlement drive is also facing concrete pushback from some of Israel’s Western allies, with Britain, Canada and France moving beyond condemnation towards targeted trade measures against illegal settlements.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned on the sidelines of the General Assembly that Israel’s endorsement of the illegal E1 settlement plan east of occupied East Jerusalem posed “a direct threat to peace”.
Carney said Canada and its allies would, “with reluctance”, implement restrictions targeting goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements, describing the move as “a pragmatic, practical action” towards “a durable peace for Israelis and Palestinians”.
The announcement follows coordinated action earlier this month by Canada and 11 European countries, including Britain and France, to introduce targeted trade measures against products originating from illegal settlements.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham similarly vowed on Tuesday not to stand by as “horrific suffering” grows and the prospect of a two-state solution “comes under attack” in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Addressing the General Assembly, Burnham said Britain’s recent sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements recognised that Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful.
The October 7 attack on Israel “does not justify the Israeli government's actions in Gaza or the West Bank”, he said, adding that “far too many people have died, including so many children”.
Western sanctions have also targeted Smotrich personally. France banned him from entering the country in July, as part of measures coordinated with Britain, Canada, Australia, Norway and New Zealand over escalating settlement activity and violence in the occupied West Bank.
France also imposed entry bans on four leaders of illegal settler organisations and 21 violent Israeli settlers.
Announcing the measures at the time, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Smotrich actively promoted annexation of the occupied West Bank, illegal new settlements, the re-colonisation of Gaza and the economic collapse of the Palestinian Authority.
Retaliation over sanctions
Israel has responded to Britain’s sanctions by ordering the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said. Sources familiar with the matter said consulate diplomats were given 30 days before losing their accreditation, while British diplomats in Ramallah were told to leave within seven days.
Smotrich also lashed out at Britain over its planned ban on trade with illegal settlements, demanding the immediate expulsion of the British ambassador.
“Expel the British ambassador tonight! We will not be a trampled doormat of an antisemitic government. The British Mandate in the Land of Israel is over,” he wrote on X on September 8.
Smotrich and fellow far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also demanded sanctions against Britain and recognition of Argentine sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.
Expansion on occupied land
Bezalel Smotrich, a leading advocate of annexing the occupied West Bank, has championed the settlement expansion at the centre of those international warnings.
Israel has accelerated the expansion of existing illegal settlements and the establishment of new ones across the territory, which it has occupied since 1967.
Around 750,000 Israeli settlers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 illegal settlement outposts across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.
Israeli settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law, but Israel has continued expanding them despite international criticism.
The occupied West Bank has seen escalating Israeli raids and arrests since October 2023, alongside increasing illegal settler attacks, movement restrictions and closures of entrances to Palestinian towns and villages.

Moldova to extend Gazprom subsidiary's status as gas supplier to Transnistria to May 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:59:11 EEST
19:59:11 KST

Moldova's Energy Ministry has asked national energy regulator ANRE to extend the authority of JSC Moldovagaz, which is 63% controlled by Russia's Gazprom, as the natural gas supplier to the breakaway Transnistria region until April 30, 2027, Energy Minister Dorin Junghietu said.
"For the first part of the winter, Moldovagaz was initially designated or proposed for designation as the entity responsible for supplying gas to the left bank [of the Dniester River], and we have recently submitted to ANRE a proposal to extend Moldovagaz's obligation to supply gas to the left bank until the end of the heating season, namely until April 30," Junghietu said in parliament during consideration of a government proposal to declare a state of emergency in the energy sector starting September 26, Moldpres reported.
"Under this obligation, Moldovagaz is also responsible for creating the reserves and contracting the volumes amounting to 15% [of annual consumption]-the so-called storage obligation for the left bank. As far as we know, Moldovagaz is working on this matter," Junghietu added.
In the course of the debate, Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said Moldova is holding negotiations on this with Moldovagaz.
"This gas [for Transnistria] is paid for by the region's partners, and now that the winter season is approaching, under Moldova's legislation, we must ensure that Moldovagaz creates the necessary gas reserves, including for the region on the left bank of the Dniester. The law that applies to us also applies to them. We are in discussions with Moldovagaz, and Moldovagaz, in turn, is in discussions with its main shareholder," Tofan said.
In August 2025, ANRE tasked Moldovagaz with ensuring gas supplies to Transnistria after it stripped the company of its license to supply gas to Moldova proper on the right bank of the Dniester. Moldovagaz was also designated as the company responsible for forming and maintaining natural gas reserves for consumers in Transnistria. The company's current status as gas supplier to Transnistria expires at the end of this year.
Hungary's MET Gas and Energy Marketing AG, with the financial participation of intermediary companies, including ones registered in the United Arab Emirates, has been supplying gas to Transnistria since February 2025 through Moldovagaz, and then through Tiraspoltransgaz. The authorities of the unrecognized Transnistria republic said earlier that gas was being supplied to the region with financial support from Russia.
At the beginning of September, ANRE raised the target for gas reserves for the heating season for Transnistria by 150% to 136 million cubic meters from 53.7 mcm. This reserve is supposed to be created by November 1, 2026.
Annual gas consumption in Transnistria totals about 1 billion cubic meters.

Ministry rules out gray-list risk after FATF review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:56:46 UTC
19:56:46 KST

Türkiye faces no risk of returning to the Financial Action Task Force’s (FATF) gray list, the Treasury and Finance Ministry said on Sept. 23, citing the watchdog’s latest assessment.
FATF’s fifth-round mutual evaluation rated Türkiye compliant or largely compliant with 38 of its 40 recommendations. The remaining two were rated partially compliant.
In a separate assessment of practical effectiveness, Türkiye received substantial ratings in three of 11 areas and moderate ratings in the other eight.
The ministry said the findings confirmed that Türkiye had no strategic deficiencies in combating money laundering, terrorist financing and the financing of weapons of mass destruction.
It said legislative changes, institutional reforms and improvements in implementation had strengthened the country’s capacity to tackle financial crime.
FATF noted progress in financial intelligence and international cooperation, while calling for stronger money laundering investigations and prosecutions in high-risk areas and better recovery of criminal assets abroad.
The watchdog placed Türkiye in enhanced follow-up, a review process separate from gray-list monitoring, and set out a three-year roadmap for further action.
Türkiye was removed from the gray list in June 2024 after completing an action plan to address strategic shortcomings.
The ministry said work on issues identified in the report would continue under national strategies covering money laundering, terrorist financing and asset confiscation for 2026-2030, and proliferation financing for 2025-2029.

When climate mitigation becomes 'political': The Guardian uncovers IPCC links to Saudi oil industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:53:26 UTC
19:53:26 KST

When climate mitigation becomes politicised: The Guardian uncovers IPCC links to Saudi oil industry
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Eoghan Gilmartin, an award-winning investigative journalist and part of The Guardian team whose investigation examined links between IPCC authors and Saudi Arabia’s oil industry, including Saudi Aramco. Their findings take us to the intersection of climate science, political and economic interests, and institutional credibility, and into the politically consequential terrain of climate mitigation: how societies decide to respond to climate change.
The investigation identified 20 authors whose affiliations raised what Gilmartin describes as significant conflict-of-interest concerns, including 11 with links to Saudi Aramco or Saudi state institutions. This raises a broader question about the production of authoritative climate knowledge: what happens when researchers helping to assess the pathways for mitigating climate change also have ties to actors with substantial economic interests in the choices being assessed?
For Gilmartin, the deeper issue is one of transparency and institutional legitimacy, rather than evidence of illegality or scientific misconduct. The IPCC derives much of its authority from its reputation for independence. Even perceived conflicts of interest can therefore become consequential when researchers assess technologies and pathways that intersect with the economic interests of their employers or funders.
That tension becomes particularly significant in the debate over carbon capture and carbon dioxide removal. Gilmartin argues that the central dispute is not whether these technologies have a role in climate mitigation, but how large that role should be. His analysis places this debate within a broader struggle over the pace and character of decarbonization: whether carbon-management technologies complement rapid reductions in fossil-fuel use, or risk becoming a rationale for postponing them.
The investigation therefore points to a larger question of climate governance: who helps define the technological pathways presented as viable, necessary or desirable. And how can institutions safeguard scientific credibility when those pathways carry enormous geopolitical and economic consequences?

Butenko: we are not proposing to shorten all classes to 35 minutes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:53:23 EEST
19:53:23 KST

Minister of Education and Science Andriy Butenko has explained what recommendations on adjusting lesson durations in connection with prolonged air raid alerts mean.
"Since yesterday, a fragment from a broadcast on one of the television channels regarding the possibility of shortening classes has been circulating on social media. But it is important to understand the context of the conversation with journalists in which these words were spoken. We are not proposing to shorten the duration of all classes to 35 minutes. We are talking about how to organize learning when children spend hours in shelters, do not sleep due to nighttime shelling, and come to school exhausted," Butenko wrote on Facebook.
He noted that today Ukrainian schools operate in very different security conditions due to air raid alerts, and the education system cannot ignore the physical and psycho-emotional state of children.
"At the same time, we must do everything to ensure that children continue to receive a quality education. That is why, at the request of teachers, we, together with educators, parent organizations, school principals, and heads of education departments, have developed methodological recommendations that give schools the opportunity to more flexibly organize learning during prolonged and repeated air raid alerts," he added.
According to him, flexible lesson duration means that if children study in a shelter for a long time, the teacher can adapt the class, in particular shorten its duration, taking into account the age and psycho-emotional state of the students, while it is important to adapt the educational material accordingly so that students achieve the results provided by the educational program.
"Schedule adjustment. If students missed classes due to a prolonged air raid alert, in elementary school you can change their sequence so that after the all-clear signal, the necessary time can be devoted to subjects that require greater concentration and direct work with the teacher. In basic and senior school, this is also possible, but requires advance processing by the management of the institution of various scenarios for schedule adjustment," the minister wrote.
Butenko emphasized that these recommendations are not an order, but merely a tool for educators.
"Separately, I want to remind you that the Sanitary Regulations define the maximum duration of a continuous class: 35 minutes for the first grade, 40 minutes for grades 2-4, and 45 minutes for grades 5-11(12). This does not mean that every lesson under any circumstances must necessarily last exactly that long. We recommend that school principals provide for various scenarios of organizing education in advance in case of prolonged alerts and remain in constant contact with the regions to help in this process," the head of the department stated.
He also recalled that the law on general secondary education provides for the possibility for an institution to flexibly organize the educational process, in particular to adjust the duration of classes.
"I trust our teachers and school principals. It is they who see the condition of children every day, know the capabilities of their institutions, and understand how to organize learning under specific circumstances. The ministry's task is to provide them with clear recommendations, provide the necessary flexibility, and, of course, help in this process. We cannot predict how long the next air raid alert will last. But we can prepare in advance for various scenarios to preserve the most important thing in each of them: the safety of children, their health, and the opportunity to continue learning," the minister wrote.

Ukrainian COMFY retailer launches marketplace, targets 300 partners by late 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:52:57 EEST
19:52:57 KST

Home appliance and electronics retailer COMFY is transforming its business model and launching a marketplace, a nationwide online platform offering home goods from partner sellers, with 500,000 products from 300 sellers expected by the end of 2027, the company's press service said.
"The launch of the marketplace is our strategic step in response to global changes in retail. Today, competition based solely on price is losing its meaning, so we are creating an ecosystem that combines assortment, a proven level of service and a high level of trust in the brand. COMFY has always set trends in the Ukrainian home appliance and electronics market, and the launch of this platform confirms our commitment to maintaining absolute leadership. We have created new business processes and modernized our infrastructure to expand the assortment and increase logistics reliability," COMFY founder and key beneficiary Stanislav Ronis was quoted as saying in the press release.
According to him, the COMFY marketplace service will be fundamentally different from what is currently available on the market. "It is not only about the speed of receiving a product, but also the quality of delivery, as well as professional pre-sale and after-sales service. In addition, we are interested in being convenient and easy to understand for sellers, listening to their expectations and needs," Ronis said.
With the launch of the marketplace, COMFY is offering a wider selection of products in one place: the company's website https://comfy.ua/ and mobile app now feature offers from partner sellers alongside the company's own products. Customers can see who is selling a product, read reviews and choose a convenient delivery method.
At the first stage, the marketplace will develop within product categories familiar to customers, with the assortment subsequently expanding through adjacent categories. By the end of 2027, the platform will offer 500,000 products from 300 sellers. The expansion of the assortment will contribute to growth in traffic and the number of purchases on the platform. Orders will be delivered under a dropshipping model: directly from the seller to the customer, without storing products in the company's warehouses. This will shorten the order's journey to the customer.
The company notes that the product assortments of electronics retailers currently overlap to a significant extent, while shoppers can instantly compare prices online; under these conditions, price competition is losing its effectiveness. In the coming years, platforms that not only offer a broad assortment but also stand out through high-quality personalized service and a high level of customer trust will have an advantage in the market.
COMFY's management team decided to transform the business model at the end of 2025 following a strategic market analysis that confirmed the natural growth of online sales. The company also took into account changes in customer behavior offline: more than 70% of customers make their choice before visiting a store and expect speed, convenience and a personalized approach.
In 2026-2027, COMFY will continue scaling up the marketplace, including expanding its IT infrastructure for new product categories, developing capabilities for partner sellers and improving the convenience of online shopping.
As of September 2026, the COMFY chain has 115 stores in 56 cities across Ukraine, eight of them in Dnipro.
According to the company, revenue in 2025 amounted to UAH 55.8 billion, up 17% from 2024.
According to YouControl, Comfy Trade LLC is owned by Comfy Holdings Limited (100%, Cyprus), with Stanislav Ronis and Svitlana Hutsul as the ultimate beneficiaries.

Ukrainian FPV Drone Kills Russian Artillery Regiment Commander Who Defected in 2014

Ukrainian FPV Drone Kills Russian Artillery Regiment Commander Who Defected in 2014
A Ukrainian FPV drone strike killed Colonel Oleksandr Isaiev, commander of Russia’s 8th Artillery Regiment and a former Ukrainian officer who switched sides during Russia’s attempted annexation of Crimea in 2014.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s “Book of Executioners of the Ukrainian People” project, Isaiev was killed in Ukraine’s Kherson region on September 19. The project is maintained by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence and prosecutors.
Isaiev commanded Russia’s 8th Artillery Regiment, military unit 87714, which operated on the Prymorskyi tactical axis as part of Russia’s Dnepr grouping of forces.
The Ukrainian project said Isaiev was struck by an FPV drone. Militarnyi published an image alongside its report showing Isaiev and a Ukrainian Bulava drone.
Isaiev was born in Mykolaiv, Ukraine, on June 20, 1975, and began serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces in 1992. He graduated from the Odesa Institute of Ground Forces in 1996 and Ukraine’s National Defense University in 2011.
By 2014, Isaiev was serving as chief of staff and first deputy commander of the 406th Separate Coastal Artillery Brigade within the Ukrainian Navy’s coastal defense forces.
During Russia’s occupation of Crimea that year, Isaiev switched sides and subsequently entered Russian military service. He was appointed chief of staff and deputy commander of the 8th Artillery Regiment of Russia’s 22nd Army Corps, which was then subordinate to the Black Sea Fleet.
Isaiev was discharged into the reserve in 2015 but returned to Russian military service in October 2022, taking up his previous position in the regiment and participating in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
In September 2024, he was promoted to colonel and appointed commander of the 8th Artillery Regiment, a position he held until the September 19 drone strike.
Former Belgorod mayor Konstantin Polezhayev was also recently reported killed while serving in Russia’s war against Ukraine. He had joined the Russian military after being convicted in a multimillion-ruble bribery case and sentenced to five years in a maximum-security penal colony.

Likud rejects Otzma Yehudit's Ben-Gvir's push for Defense Ministry, Justice Ministry for Gotliv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:51:33 UTC
19:51:33 KST

Likud officials pushed back on Wednesday against Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir's demand to receive the Defense Ministry in the next government and hand the Justice Ministry to MK Tally Gotliv, Maariv learned on Wednesday.
Likud was displeased with Ben-Gvir's demands, and has made it clear that the party does not intend to relinquish either portfolio in future coalition negotiations.
Shortly after he presented his demands, a message was conveyed to him that, as far as Likud is concerned, the Defense and Justice ministries are two of the party's core portfolios and it therefore has no intention of giving them up in coalition negotiations.
Likud officials stressed that they regard the Defense and Justice ministries as portfolios that belong within the party and that the demand to hand both to Otzma Yehudit is not viewed as realistic ahead of possible negotiations following the election.
Alongside the dispute over the allocation of ministries, Likud officials also voiced concern about the diplomatic consequences of such statements. According to party officials, presenting Ben-Gvir as a candidate for defense minister could prompt sharp reactions from neighboring Arab countries, particularly Egypt and Jordan, and further strain relations with them.
Ben-Gvir demands change to IDF rules of engagement, code of ethics
The message came after the press conference held on Tuesday night by Ben-Gvir and Gotliv, during which they presented the demands and plans they intend to advance in the next government.
Ben-Gvir announced that Otzma Yehudit would demand the Defense Ministry for itself, while he wants the Justice Ministry for Gotliv.
Alongside his demand for the Defense Ministry, Ben-Gvir presented a series of measures concerning the IDF and its operational policies. Among other things, the plan includes changing the rules of engagement, providing broader backing for IDF soldiers, raising their salaries, and providing free land to combat soldiers.
Ben-Gvir also stated he’d push to change the IDF's ethical code, which he called "Asa Kasher's progressive ethical code," and alter the screening process for elite units. Under the plan he presented, units including Unit 8200 would be opened more broadly to applicants from across the population.
Gotliv seeks dismissal of attorney-general
Gotliv, for her part, presented the measures she wants to implement if appointed justice minister. At the top of the list, she placed the immediate dismissal of the attorney-general upon the formation of the next government.
The plan also includes changing the process for appointing Supreme Court justices. Under Gotliv's proposal, candidates for the Supreme Court would undergo a hearing before the Knesset Constitution, Law and Justice Committee, and their appointment would require approval by a two-thirds majority.
Gotliv is also seeking changes to the powers of the High Court of Justice, including restoring standing requirements and enshrining the principle that "not everything is justiciable," alongside an explicit definition of matters that would not be subject to judicial review.
The plan also calls for abolishing the course used to screen judicial candidates, which Gotliv describes as a tool for filtering judges, as well as increasing punishments for criminal organizations and terrorists to strengthen deterrence, she said.
Another provision concerns investigative policy. Gotliv wants to abolish the procedure requiring prior approval from the State Attorney's Office before criminal investigations can be opened into offenses including incitement, sedition, and calls for disobedience.
The demands presented by the two have placed the question of how portfolios would be allocated in a future government on the agenda while the election campaign is still underway. Likud, for its part, moved quickly to make clear to Ben-Gvir that, at least on the Defense and Justice ministries, it has no intention of giving them up.

Russia Launches Morning Drone Attack on Kyiv, Killing Two and Injuring 22
Editor’s note: This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.
A Russian drone attack on Kyiv on the morning of September 23 killed at least one person and injured seven others, with strikes and falling debris reported across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
UPD: The death toll from the Russian attack on Kyiv has risen to two, Klitschko reported. One man died in hospital from his injuries, while another person was killed in the attack. A total of 22 Kyiv residents were injured, with 16 of them currently receiving treatment in city hospitals.
According to Klitschko, one of the injured, who had been hospitalized in serious condition, later died in hospital. Four people remained hospitalized following the attack.
The drone attack was still ongoing at the time of Klitschko’s latest update, with the mayor urging residents to remain in safe locations.
In Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district, a Russian drone fell onto the roof of a non-residential building. Klitschko later clarified that the site was a four-story business center, with emergency services dispatched to the scene.
Monitoring channels reported a strike in the area of Kyiv’s Central Railway Station during the attack. Ukraine’s state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia later clarified that the station itself had not been damaged.
The latest attack also targeted fuel infrastructure in the capital. On September 23, Russian drones also struck two gas stations in different districts of Kyiv.
In the Holosiivskyi district, a Russian drone was initially reported to have struck a gas station. Local media later identified the facility as an Ukrnafta gas station.
In Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, another strike hit transport infrastructure, with preliminary reports indicating that a fire broke out on the roof of a gas station. Local Telegram channels reported that the facility was a UPG gas station on Kharkivske Highway.
The latest strikes followed another daytime Russian attack on Kyiv on September 22, when Russian forces deployed jet-powered Shahed drones. One of the drones directly struck fuel storage tanks in the capital’s northern Obolonskyi district, according to Klitschko.
That attack injured eight people across the city. Three were hospitalized, while five others received medical assistance at the scene or were treated on an outpatient basis.

Trump's Board of Peace to unveil $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan

Donald Trump's Board of Peace to unveil $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members on Wednesday, Axios reported.
The 66-project proposal includes estimated spending for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, the report added, citing a copy of the plan.
The White House and US Department of State did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The plan estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade, the Axios report added.
It also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects.
Trump's administration told Congress in late July it is sending more than $206 million for a proposed Gaza peacekeeping force, the first significant funding for the stalled US plan to rebuild the devastated enclave.
Trump claims he set up a Board of Peace to oversee an ambitious plan to end Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
But since the announcement of an agreement in late July, the effort has stalled, and Israel continuing to kill Palestinians on a daily basis.
The report said the Board of Peace and the Palestinian government have not secured the entire $2.45 billion but are confident that, once political hurdles are cleared, donor countries will step up.

AI leaders to brief UN Security Council on artificial intelligence capabilities, safeguards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:51:23 UTC
19:51:23 KST

Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face will brief the UN Security Council on Wednesday amid warnings increasingly powerful AI technologies could soon improve themselves, slip beyond human control and threaten international security.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue are due to brief the 15-member council during the annual General Assembly gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
Altman plans to urge world leaders to adopt benchmarks for measuring AI capabilities and assessing the safeguards companies put in place as they develop the technology, an OpenAI executive told reporters on Tuesday.
Council members, including leading AI rivals the United States and China, are also set to speak. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot will chair the meeting.
A European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the main objective of the meeting was to shine a light on the practical risks of AI losing control in ways that affect international security and the security of individual states.
"These are issues that fall squarely within the Security Council's mandate," the diplomat said. "The key question is whether we could one day face a situation where algorithms interacting with each other trigger a war. That is really at the heart of the issue."
Trump rejects stifling growth of AI
Ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, the US and China have discussed setting up a notification system for common goals and common threats that would cover AI-related incidents that rise to a national security level.
Trump told world leaders at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that he "rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control" AI, describing the technology as amazing, but noted that the US would be careful.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution."
"We're going to encourage it, not rein it in. We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice," he said.
Guterres warns of AI advancement risks
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned that rapidly advancing artificial intelligence poses risks that cannot be ignored, putting him at odds with Trump.
Guterres has long pushed for global governance of AI and in 2023 created a 39-member advisory body for one year, with members including tech company executives, government officials and academics from countries such as the US, Russia, and Japan.
The 193-member UN General Assembly then created the Independent International Scientific Panel last year. Yoshua Bengio, a Canadian considered one of the "Godfathers of AI" and co-chair of the panel, will also brief the Security Council.
The Security Council met for the first time on the risks of AI in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a "runaway horse" and the United States warned against its use to censor or repress people. Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken chaired a Security Council meeting on AI in 2024.

Ukrainian Drone Forces Target 38 Energy Sites in Mid-September, Bringing Total to 412

Ukrainian Drone Forces Target 38 Energy Sites in Mid-September, Bringing Total to 412
Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) have targeted 412 energy infrastructure sites in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories and inside Russia since launching the “Crimean Switch Off” operation in July, SBS Commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi reported on September 22.
According to Brovdi, Ukrainian drone units carried out the strikes between July 6 and September 22, targeting energy infrastructure supporting Russian operations across temporarily occupied territories and Russia. The campaign comes in response to continued Russian strikes on Ukraine, including attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During the second ten-day period of September alone, USF units successfully targeted another 38 energy facilities. These included 10 sites in temporarily occupied Crimea, nine in the occupied part of Donetsk region, 13 in the occupied part of Luhansk region, four inside Russia, and one each in the Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Among the facilities targeted were several major electrical substations, including the 220-kV Krasnodonska substation near Prokhladne in the Luhansk region and the 220-kV Amvrosiivka substation in the Donetsk region. Other reported targets included 110-kV substations near Kypuche, Selidove, and Bilovodsk.
Inside Russia, Ukrainian drone units targeted the 110-kV Bolshaya Chern and Znamenskaya substations in the Oryol region, as well as other energy infrastructure.
The operation has also focused on gas infrastructure in occupied Crimea. Brovdi reported strikes against gas distribution stations at Orlivka, Bakhchysarai, Bilohirsk, Kyr-Bailar, Kholmivka, Hornostaivka, Klepynine, and Islam-Terek, with the Kholmivka facility targeted more than once.
Other reported targets included the Kreidyanka gas distribution station in Russia, the Rodakove gas distribution station in the occupied Luhansk region, and the Tasunove compressor station in Crimea.
Multiple SBS formations are involved in the operation, including the 414th “Madyar’s Birds,” 412th “Nemesis,” 9th, 20th “K-2,” and 429th “Achilles” Separate Unmanned Systems Brigades, as well as the 413th “Raid” Brigade, 427th “Rarog” Brigade, the USF’s 1st Separate Center, and the Phoenix unit of Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service.
The campaign is part of broader SBS operations targeting Russian infrastructure. On September 22, Brovdi also reported that Ukrainian forces had disabled 300 vessels belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Azov and Black seas over an 11-week period.
The reported strikes were carried out as part of Operation “MoLoChKa,” another SBS campaign that has been underway since July 6.

US Democrats to introduce bill sanctioning individuals involved in Israel's E1 settlement project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:51:05 UTC
19:51:05 KST

A group of US Senate Democrats will introduce legislation on Wednesday to sanction individuals or groups that facilitate Israel's "E1 project," a widely condemned West Bank settlement plan cutting across land the Palestinians seek for a state, according to a copy of the legislation seen by Reuters.
The introduction of the bill is the latest sign of growing friction between Democrats in Congress and the Israeli government over its handling of the West Bank, with many in the party - and a few Republicans - calling for curbs on US military aid to Israel over its conduct of the war in Gaza.
US Democratic lawmakers have also recently urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to rein in violence by West Bank settlers and mass arrests of Palestinians by Israeli security forces in the area.
The measure's lead sponsors are Chris Coons of Delaware, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Ruben Gallego of Arizona.
"As Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behavior is unacceptable and that it remains committed to freedom, security, prosperity and self-determination for all Israelis and Palestinians," Coons said in a statement.
Democrats control minority of Senate, could win majority in midterms
The bill has at least 10 co-sponsors, all Democrats.
Democrats currently control only 47 seats in the 100-member Senate, but polls show they could win majorities in November 3 midterm elections from US President Donald Trump's Republicans, who have aligned themselves closely with Netanyahu.
The bill would impose sanctions on foreign companies, individuals, or other entities that the Treasury Department determines to have been responsible for or complicit in the construction of any Israeli settlements or related structures in the E1 area of the West Bank, including by submitting a bid for E1 tenders.
It also would sanction those who attempt to organize, direct, finance, or facilitate the transfer of Israeli civilians into settlements in the E1 area.
Approval of the E1 project, which would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from east Jerusalem, was announced in August 2025 by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Two-state solution could be undermined by E1 project
The two-state solution to the decades-old Israeli-Palestinian conflict envisages a Palestinian state in east Jerusalem, the West Bank, and Gaza, existing side by side with Israel.
Western capitals and campaign groups have opposed the E1 settlement project due to concerns that it could undermine a future peace deal with the Palestinians and diminish the chance for the two-state solution.
Most of the international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law.
Israel disputes this, citing historical and biblical ties to the area and saying the settlements provide strategic depth and security.
Congress's lower chamber, the US House of Representatives, is currently not in session, so even in the unlikely chance of the bill's passage in the Senate, the House would not be expected to take it up before the midterms.

19:50:43 KST

LONDON, September 23. /TASS/. Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four in the previous day, according to preliminary shipping data, Reuters reported, citing shiptracker Kpler.
All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait.
Before the US-Iran conflict started on February 28, around 125 large commercial vessels passed through the strait every day, including bulk carriers, container ships, crude and gas tankers, carrying roughly one fifth of the world’s daily oil and liquefied natural gas supplies.
Meanwhile, 22 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a trade route between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, on Tuesday, the agency added. Fourteen vessels headed towards the Red Sea and eight towards the Gulf of Aden. They included five Panamax tankers, six Supramax vessels, four Aframax tankers, one Suezmax tanker, and one very large crude carrier (VLCC).
The number compared with an average of around 26 ships using the strait in the past 10 days.

jenny holzer’s truisms and the power of the public screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:50:42 UTC
19:50:42 KST

When Jenny Holzer put Truisms on a Times Square billboard
In 1982, sentences appeared between advertisements on a giant electronic billboard in Times Square. PRIVATE PROPERTY CREATED CRIME. TORTURE IS BARBARIC. ABUSE OF POWER COMES AS NO SUPRISE. They were not selling anything, offering directions, or announcing a new product. Jenny Holzer had placed her Truisms inside the Spectacolor board, turning one of New York’s most conspicuous commercial surfaces into a vehicle for ambiguous, confrontational statements.
The gesture was sharp because Holzer used the visual language used for advertising — the scale, movement and glow of the billboard remaining the same, but instead of selling a product, it delivered short, unsettling statements. For a few seconds, a space designed for advertising became a place to encounter language.
More than forty years later, Holzer’s Wrong Answers at the Serralves Museum of Contemporary Art in Porto revisits some of the same ideas in a very different media landscape. Screens are no longer unusual or concentrated in a few places. They are part of buildings, streets, public transport, and the phones we carry every day. In 1982, Holzer was finding a way to put critical language on the commercial screen. Today, the challenge is making people stop and read it. Holzer has spent her career testing what happens when words are taken out of books and put into the world around us. They appear on walls, buildings, stone, lightboxes, and screens, changing the way we encounter and read them.
Holzer’s move toward the electronic screen was preceded by years of experimentation with how language could inhabit the city. Beginning in 1977, she pasted Truisms across New York on sheets of paper. The statements were anonymous, direct and deliberately difficult to classify. Some sounded like political slogans, others like conventional wisdom, threats, advertisements or fragments of philosophical argument. On a city wall, the words did not arrive with the institutional framing of a museum. They were encountered while walking, waiting, shopping or just passing through.
Holzer soon began testing what happened when the material changed. Her Living series transferred language onto bronze plaques, giving subjective observations the visual authority of civic markers. The text remained, but its status shifted. Paper suggested the temporary and unofficial; bronze suggested permanence, history and institutional weight.
The Spectacolor board took that experiment into the architecture of mass communication. The system Holzer used consisted of thousands of incandescent bulbs arranged as a large matrix, capable of displaying simple animated images and text. Through the public art project Messages to the Public (1982-1990), artists were given access to a surface otherwise dedicated to advertising. Holzer’s intervention lasted only seconds within a much longer commercial sequence. The work appeared where an advertisement was expected to appear. Passersby looking up at Times Square encountered something that initially behaved like an advertisement but refused to resolve into one. The billboard became a space for reading.
The conditions that made the Spectacolor intervention so effective have changed. In 1982, a giant electronic billboard was unusual enough to command attention. Today, Times Square is surrounded by screens, while the individual viewer carries another one in their pocket. Advertising has moved from broadcast messages addressed to everyone toward systems that target individuals through data, algorithms and personalized feeds. The commercial screen is part of the atmosphere. That changes the possibilities for artistic intervention.
Holzer’s Wrong Answers in Porto, installed across Serralves, brings together paper works, stone inscriptions, LED installations and newer pieces responding to contemporary political communication. The works create different conditions for reading, moving between the permanence of stone and the instability of electronic text.
In READY FOR YOU (2023–25), contemporary political language becomes particularly difficult to separate from the media systems that circulate it. The work incorporates material connected to Donald Trump alongside AI-generated transformations, reflecting an information environment in which political statements are endlessly reproduced, altered and accelerated. Here, the problem is no longer that critical language cannot access the screen, but that the screen is already full.
The Truisms appeared on the Spectacolor billboard for only a few seconds before the next commercial message took over. That brevity was part of their character. You could catch a sentence, think about it, and then it was gone. The situation is very different now. Screens no longer need to fight for attention because they are already woven into almost every part of daily life. There is always another image, headline, notification or message waiting behind the one in front of us. This is also why Holzer’s use of different materials remains important.
At Serralves, the words move between paper, stone, paint and LED. A text printed on a sheet of paper has a different presence from one carved into stone; an LED message can appear and disappear before you have had time to take it in. The exhibition makes these differences tangible. You walk closer to some works and pass others at a distance. Some stay with you; others are gone almost as soon as you have read them.
Holzer has been doing this for decades, changing not only the words but the places and materials through which they reach us. The setting is never quite neutral. A poster on a city wall, a sentence on a bronze plaque, or a message glowing across a screen each carries a different kind of weight. In 1982, the unexpected thing was finding Holzer’s words on a billboard. Today, the unexpected thing may be finding enough quiet to read them.

Estonia, Canada convene first Canada-NB8 ministerial meeting
