Estonia, Canada convene first Canada-NB8 ministerial meeting
Estonia and Canada convened the first Canada-Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) ministerial meeting in New York Tuesday, bringing together foreign ministers from eight countries.
The ministers, in New York for the UN General Assembly, reaffirmed support for Ukraine, opposition to changing borders by force, and coordination on Baltic Sea, North Atlantic and Arctic security.
Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) and his Canadian counterpart Anita Anand convened the meeting with the foreign ministers of Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway and Sweden on Tuesday .
During the meeting, the Nordic-Baltic countries and Canada reaffirmed their commitment to the rules-based international order, international law and the UN Charter.
They said they stand united against any attempt to change borders by force and will continue close coordination in the context of the UN, OSCE and NATO and with the EU, to uphold these principles and ensure accountability.
The ministers reaffirmed that EU-Canada relations support shared goals on trade diversification, supply chains and strategic partnerships, and highlighted Canada's role in European security, including through its agreement with the EU to participate in the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument.
Together, Canada and the NB8 reaffirmed their common interests in the Euro-Atlantic region. Ministers stressed that the Baltic Sea, the North Atlantic and the Arctic are interconnected elements of allied security, noting the importance of responding to Russian threats to critical infrastructure, including energy, and hybrid activities across these regions.
The ministers reaffirmed their unwavering support for Ukraine for as long as it takes and steadfast support for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. They committed to continued coordination to ensure their efforts remain effective, complementary and responsive to Ukraine's evolving needs, and emphasized the importance of restoring a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine. They reiterated Ukraine's call for Russia to agree to a full and immediate ceasefire.
Ministers also underscored the need to sustain international pressure on Russia to cease its aggression, with particular attention to repeated strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure. Canada welcomed the participation of senior NB8 delegations at the September 28–29 Pathways to Peace conference in Toronto on returning Ukrainian children, detained civilians and prisoners of war.
Tonight in New York, Canada's Foreign Minister @AnitaAnandMP and I convened the first Canada–Nordic-Baltic Eight #NB8 ministerial meeting.
From the Baltic Sea to the North Atlantic and the Arctic, our security is connected. Russia's hybrid activities and threats to critical… pic.twitter.com/GUTUaAnYSv
The attendees also welcomed Estonia's plans to host the next Ukraine Recovery Conference in late January next year, and underscored their commitment to supporting Ukraine's recovery, reconstruction and long-term resilience.
They identified concrete opportunities to deepen practical cooperation on defense industrial cooperation, maritime security, critical infrastructure protection and economic security, and discussed strengthening collective security and readiness, including efforts to counter hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation.
The leaders agreed to remain in close contact, regularly convene in the Canada-NB8 format, and continue advancing shared security, defense and resilience priorities under Norway's forthcoming NB8 chairmanship.

19:49:15 KST

The reality behind Trump’s misleading UN address
TEHRAN — Donald Trump’s address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly was a cascade of verifiable falsehoods, internal logical collapses, and explicit threats of destruction.
Speaking from the podium of an institution founded to prevent aggressive war, the American president presented world leaders with a binary ultimatum regarding Iran: accept unilateral submission or face total physical erasure.
Ten minutes into the speech, the Iranian diplomatic delegation stood up and walked out of the hall. They left behind a single junior representative sitting stone-faced in an empty row.
The Cuban delegation exited shortly after when Trump branded their government a failed state.
The walkout was a deliberate refusal to validate an argument grounded in coercion rather than international law.
Outside the UN complex near Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza, protesters clashed with New York police while chanting against U.S. military aggression, carrying placards denouncing Trump, including one that read, “TRUMP is a WAR CRIMINAL.”
The nuclear 'obliteration' lie and the asymmetric reality
Trump’s primary justification for the nearly seven-month-old war against Iran relies on a claim he has repeated since June 2025.
"Operation Midnight Hammer," he insisted, "obliterated" Iran's nuclear program "beneath mountains of rubble."
That statement collapses under the weight of Washington’s own timeline.
Leaked Defense Intelligence Agency assessments and International Atomic Energy Agency claims following the June 2025 strikes confirmed that hardened facilities such as Fordow suffered structural damage, not total destruction.
By February 2026, Trump himself cited resumed Iranian uranium enrichment as his explicit justification to launch the current campaign of aggression.
A program permanently erased in 2025 cannot serve as the rationale for launching a massive military campaign in 2026.
His assertions regarding conventional military damage follow the same pattern.
Trump claimed that the war launched on February 20206 sank "all 159 ships" of "Iran's navy" while "erasing" its air force, radar networks, air defenses, and missile production.
CENTCOM claimed destroying roughly 17 surface ships in the war's initial weeks. But conventional surface warships have never formed the core of Iranian maritime strategy.
For 30 years, Tehran designed its defense around asymmetric survival.
The doctrine relies on the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy, operating mobile shore-based anti-ship missile batteries, fast attack craft, and extensive naval mining capabilities embedded along mountainous terrain, now combined with the effective strength of the IRGC Aerospace Force equipped with various types of state-of-the-art missiles and drones.
Degrading conventional surface ships does not mean the Iranian navy was destroyed.
As for Iran’s missile prowess, months of missile attacks on U.S. bases across the region have demonstrated that its missile forces remain an effective and operational component of its military power.
Hormuz escorts and the munitions shortage contradiction
If Iran's naval capabilities were truly resting on the seabed, Washington would not be forced to deploy naval escorts to protect commercial energy shipments.
Trump boasted that the U.S. Navy has escorted over one billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, moving groups of "up to 37 ships" every day and night.
The claim refutes his own argument. A state whose maritime defenses have been erased does not have the ability to move global energy markets and does not require daily naval convoys to pass through a strategic choke point.
Trump’s claims regarding military logistics proved equally contradictory.
He attacked critics who highlighted U.S. ammunition shortages, calling them "cowards and traitors" and claiming America possesses "more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using."
He then announced that 18 massive new munition plants are currently under construction across the United States.
Both statements cannot be true. A nation possessing inexhaustible stockpiles does not undertake an emergency industrial expansion in the middle of a war.
Reports from the Pentagon’s Inspector General and defense analysts outside the Pentagon confirm that seven months of intense missile strikes against Iranian targets, alongside ongoing arms transfers to Israel and Ukraine, have severely depleted critical stocks of precision-guided munitions and air-defense interceptors, including Tomahawk cruise missiles and PAC-3 air-defense interceptors.
The U.S. military has been forced to expend multi-million-dollar interceptors against low-cost drones and conventional missiles.
The construction of 18 new facilities is an admission of industrial exhaustion under a sustained war of attrition.
'Strategic desperation' of 'a deranged sociopath'
The central foreign policy statement of the address supposedly offered Iran a choice between capitulation and destruction.
"Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic," Trump asked, promising to drive the nation "into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations."
Delivered before the United Nations, this language directly violates Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which strictly prohibits threats or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.
Legal analysts have noted that explicitly threatening the total destruction of nation meets the threshold of genocidal intent defined under the Rome Statute and the UN Genocide Convention.
Trump added a bizarre domestic calculation to this threat, predicting that Tehran would sign a deal "right after the election" because Iranian leaders were "waiting to see how I do in the midterm election."
He then corrected himself mid-sentence, noting that he is not running in the midterms.
The slip revealed a profound misreading of Iranian defense strategy. Iranian national security policy is not calibrated around American congressional election cycles.
Iran and the Resistance Front operate on a long-term structural defense against the hegemony of the U.S. and Israel and their proxies, regardless of which American political party holds majorities in Washington.
Reactions to the speech were swift and scathing.
In Tehran, Iran’s General Staff and Central Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters dismissed Trump’s remarks as “a tool for domestic propaganda,” arguing that repeated threats reflected U.S. “strategic deadlock” and military exhaustion rather than strength.
They said the rhetoric showed “strategic desperation” and warned that Iran’s armed forces were prepared to respond with “even harsher, more devastating, and unpredictable blows.”
Media commentator Brett Erickson called Trump "a global embarrassment to the United States," adding that "taking 30 minutes at the UN General Assembly to spew hatred, nonsense, and propaganda" was "single-handedly dismantling American credibility."
Independent American journalist Glenn Greenwald highlighted the shifting pretexts of American interventionism, pointing out how administration narratives shifted from liberation to open aggression once initial arguments dissolved.
Political analyst Andy Ostroy responded bluntly: "Only a deranged sociopath would make a comment like this."
Imperial plunder in Caracas, Greenland, and Gaza
Trump abandoned diplomatic euphemism when describing U.S. military interventions elsewhere in the world.
Discussing the U.S. military operation in Caracas that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and the deaths of more than 100 Venezuelans and Cubans, Trump cited the deal covering 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, summarizing his doctrine in five shameless words: “To the victor belong the spoils.”
That statement constitutes an explicit admission of state piracy. Pillage and the expropriation of sovereign economic assets from subjugated nations are explicit war crimes under the Geneva Conventions.
Combined with his announcement of an agreement granting the U.S. permanent security control and two major military bases in Greenland, the Venezuela declaration exposes American strategy as an unvarnished effort to seize global energy and territorial assets.
Trump applied the same transactional framing to Palestine, claiming he had "ended the war in Gaza" through a 20-point plan and an international "Board of Peace" chaired by himself.
The claim ignores the reality on the ground. Since the so-called ceasefire and implementation of Trump’s plan began in October 2025, more than 1,394 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, while the Strip continues to face widespread destruction, severe shortages and acute humanitarian needs.
Trump’s "Board of Peace" includes no Palestinian representation, functioning instead as a colonial management mechanism designed to bypass Palestinian self-determination and replace statehood with foreign administration funded by Arab states in the Persian Gulf.
Collapsing domestic consensus and global rejection
Trump’s attempt to project absolute global dominance comes at a moment when domestic support for his foreign policy is rapidly eroding.
A CNN poll released on the day of his speech revealed that 71 percent of Americans disapprove of his handling of foreign affairs, a record high across both of his terms. Only 26 percent of Americans approve of his handling of the war against Iran.
78 percent believe he is not doing enough to end the conflict, while 76 percent conclude that the human and financial costs of the war, which has already exceeded $45 billion in direct Pentagon spending and over $132 billion in broader economic damage, are not worth it.
Republican approval for his Iran policy dropped from 73 percent in March to sixty percent in September.
Trump arrived at the United Nations demanding complete global isolation for Iran and asserting total victory across multiple war zones.
The facts on the ground tell a different story. The war in the Persian Gulf remains active, U.S. military stockpiles are straining under attrition, global energy markets are disrupted, and domestic public opinion has turned decisively against Trump’s war on Iran.

Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth's speech at the UK Space Power Conference
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:47:54 BST
19:47:54 KST

Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth's speech at the UK Space Power Conference
Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth delivered the opening keynote of the UK Space Power Conference, setting out how the UK will defend its interests in space.
Well, good morning, everyone. I think I am in control of the PowerPoint. There we go. The Minister has just said to me it’s boiling up there so I’m glad I wore my woollen Spitfire suit.
It’s really good to see so many distinguished guests, colleagues, allies and friends here and welcome to the UK Space Power Conference here in what is a relatively unexpected sunny London, which is great. It’s so good to see lots of familiar faces in the audience – I’m slightly worried that there’s a sea of light blue at the back there to hold me to account on what I’m about to say.
But I’m particularly glad to see so many new faces and to meet so many new characters from across the space enterprise, scientists, academics, industry experts. We’ve got some leaders in finance and of course, there is a good group here from across government. So thank you all for supporting the conference. I really do from a personal perspective, I appreciate that.
I stood here just a few months ago alongside many of my fellow international air and space chiefs at what was the Global Air and Space Chiefs Conference. And then I outlined how the RAF is now formally on a journey to becoming Europe’s first sixth generation air force with the Global Combat Air Programme and now our new Collaborative Combat Air programme, the Storm Fighter, operating alongside F-35, Typhoons and a range of many other autonomous systems. But these capabilities will never fulfil their potential without space. And that’s why these conferences and this discussion over the next two days are so very important.
From my perspective, I don’t think I can get to a sixth-generation air force if I still have a fourth-generation space force. And that is a topic that I’m hoping we can cover over discussions in the coming two days. Space is obviously a prerequisite for modern air power. Every element of a sixth-generation air force depends intimately on space, the networks, the targeting, the navigation, the command and control.
Space is no longer just simply supporting air power from the sidelines. It is completely embedded within it. It is essential. It’s actually part of the DNA and you don’t have to scratch too far to see that. And space is no less relevant to the other domains. The effective use of space is critical to the ability of our new integrated force to understand, to communicate, to move and to fight. And as we learn critical lessons from ongoing conflicts in places like Ukraine and the Middle East, it is clear that a pivot to uncrewed systems is required at pace.
And of course, if we’re going to do this, an uncrewed force is broadly a space-dependent force, once again reinforcing the importance of this vital domain to defence. We often refer to space as the ultimate high ground, through which the integrated force gains a decisive operational edge, enabling it to act with greater speed, better precision, and overall better effectiveness. It is an advantage we must maintain, and if possible, deny to our adversaries.
Space services are not just the invisible thread between our ships at sea, our soldiers on the land and our aircraft in the skies. They now completely underpin our whole approach to strategic deterrence, command and control, and decision advantage. And more broadly, across the fabric of our society, space underpins our modern way of life.
Just coming here, being linked to space told me, if I don’t hurry up, I’m going to be late. And the Air and Space Commander was panicking, thinking he was going to have to do this keynote. It’s been six years since I was appointed as the first director of space for the MOD, as Anu mentioned. Space was an important topic then, but I would argue now it is a critical matter which must be better understood and better championed across the whole of government, specifically if we are serious about our approach to modern deterrence. It is our responsibility to make sure that everyone in defence knows that the integrated force will not succeed without space. Space must become embedded in how defence generates and operates force.
To reflect this, the Royal Air Force’s headquarters at RAF High Wycombe transitioned to become Air and Space Command just a few weeks ago. I’m sure some of you saw that announcement. This is more than just a simple name change. We are demonstrating that space is no longer just a supporting function. Space is now seen as a warfighting domain in its own right and with equal importance to the other domains.
It is a contested, congested and competitive environment where our operational edge and strategic advantage can be won but can also be very quickly and easily lost. Space can no longer be delayed, no longer deferred, or delegated. It must now be delivered and that has been my big message into our own department on this topic.
But importantly it cannot be delivered via national means only and we know in UK we cannot do this alone and I’m delighted that we are joined today by so many international colleagues from around the globe. Our greatest strength is our coalition of space partners spanning the world, an alliance that is envied and feared in equal measure by our potential adversaries, with all members bringing different capabilities from unique geography to unique on-orbit assets, making our collective security greater than the sum of the space parts.
In the UK, NATO is of course our most critical alliance. And whilst we are building sovereign space capabilities, these will always be part of a NATO force, always part of our strategic deterrence approach. NATO led the way by recognising space as a domain in 2019. And two years later, NATO expanded the scope of our collective defence policy, making it clear that attacks to, from, or within space present a clear threat to the alliance and could possibly trigger an Article 5. This was a major statement of intent. In short, an attack on one of us in space is an attack on all of us, just as it is in the other, more traditional domains.
And whilst UK strategy is NATO first, we are not only NATO. Earlier this April, I went to Colorado to meet with my counterparts from 10 other nations, from the USA in the West to New Zealand in the East for the Principals Board of the Combined Space Operations Initiative, or CSpO. There we agreed to redouble our efforts to deliver capabilities in support of combined space operations, creating a web of global space power, generating and delivering mutually supportive capabilities that no adversary can match. Again, a fundamental approach to our collective deterrence posture.
And central to this is Multinational Force Operation Olympic Defender. This is now our primary international operational framework within which we deliver responsible, combined space operations, and these are happening on a very routine basis at this very moment.
Last September, we delivered the first ever UK-US space operation under the banner of OOD. We completed a Rendezvous Proximity Operation in geostationary orbit, moving one of our SKYNET satellites close to a satellite operated by US Space Command. 35,776 kilometres from Earth’s surface, to be precise. These satellites were traveling at 11,000 kilometres per hour. That’s 3 kilometres per second. So, a collision would most definitely be catastrophic, creating substantial, long-standing debris in an orbit that is congested, full of critical assets.
That is why operations like this must only ever be delivered with the utmost of care, with the utmost of precision, communication, expertise and most importantly, collaboration and agreement. When another nation manoeuvres their satellite close to ours without collaboration, that is unacceptable. It is dangerous and it is unprofessional. It is no different than flying an aircraft to within 50 feet of my aircraft without coordination.
Unfortunately, we are now seeing more and more irresponsible and provocative actions from our adversaries in flagrant disregard of the norms for responsible behaviour by space-faring nations. In May of this year, we tracked a series of unusual and significant manoeuvres by 5 Russian military satellites, moving to within rapid reach of two finished commercial satellites. These manoeuvres were uncommon and dangerous, raising serious questions about Russia’s intent in space. And the next month, in June, it was confirmed that a Russian satellite constellation had caused disruptions to GPS signals across the breadth of Europe, Greenland and Canada over at least 75 days since 2019.
We all know and we all rely on GPS. It’s an excellent system operated by our colleagues in the US Space Force. It is used by billions of people and industries around the world and of course it’s used by many global military forces. Major disruption to GPS would cost the UK economy to the tune of £1.4 billion of impact every day. Sat-Nav systems would fail, congestion on the roads would create havoc. Our emergency services would take much, much longer to reach those in need.
So make no mistake, the satellite services you may have taken for granted now face unprecedented threats. And losing these services, be it the Sat-Nav that keeps ups moving, the timing signals for financial transactions, the Earth observation that allows us to monitor the weather or the effects of climate change. All of this would make every sector sitting in this room less efficient, less prosperous and less secure.
Our adversaries know this. They are developing sophisticated space systems and they have both the capability and the intent to use them. Last year, and most of you will know this handsome chap, last year, the commander of UK Space Command, Tedders (ret. Major General Paul Tedman) here today. He’s not. He knew I was putting this picture up. So our previous commander of UK Space Command denied that Russia is attempting to jam UK military satellites with ground-based systems every week. At the same time, Germany’s defence minister said that Russia had been shadowing their military satellites. Alongside grey zone activity across all domains, space is a region of growing strategic competition. Space has become a warfighting domain, whether we like that or not. And the UK, as well as its partners and allies, must be prepared for this.
Fortunately, this is now recognised across government here in the UK. And in June of last year, we had the Strategic Defence Review, it outlined that space remains a critical national infrastructure sector. Space underpins 20% of the UK’s GDP. In real money, that’s almost £500 billion. But it is also a site of growing competition. The SDR set out the MOD’s requirement to invest in space control decision advantage, reconnaissance, navigation, and timing signals. And if the SDR set out what we in defence would call the ends, this year’s defence investment plan set out our means.
And I just heard the Minister for Space talk about the DIP. £9 billion of new space capability already earmarked for 2030 to 2035. And from this year to 2030, £2.3 billion for satellite communications, £880 million for space-based ISR and space control, and a further £440 million for novel space technology. And now we have a new UK Space Strategy issued just this month. A strategy that outlines how the UK government will act as one regards space, making our nation a competitive space power, assertive in protecting our interests and driving our own economic growth. To protect the nation and also to help it prosper is MOD’s aim.
Space has never been more important for our nation’s defence and security, for our prosperity and our daily lives. And our adversaries are not waiting until we’re ready for them. We must now get on with delivery of space capability and operational effect at pace. At the heart of the UK space arsenal and a major offer to our global alliance is Skynet and many of you in this room will know of our Skynet programme and the capability that offers. It’s the backbone of UK’s sovereign global comms capability and provides command and control for our entire integrated force.
And I’m grateful that the Defence Investment Plan allocated an additional £50 million to extend the life of our in-service SKYNET 5 satellites. And these will be joined next year with the launch of our new SKYNET 6 series, SKYNET 6A. While our demand for SATCOM only increases, and as threats in space grow more serious, SKYNET will be supplemented with allied and commercial SATCOM services. These will provide additional capacity, coverage, and resilience, with resilience being the keyword. Using both SKYNET and commercial SATCOM, UK armed forces will be able to make and communicate decisions quickly around the world. And this is an incredibly important keystone of our quest for decision superiority in today’s modern warfare.
And the decision-making of our integrated force will be further improved by space-based intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. Through our ISTARI programme, we’re delivering a constellation of satellites to provide a multi-sensor, multi-spectral capability to observe activity on the Earth, day or night, heat wave or snowstorm. One of these satellites, the Tyche, is now in space. Over the next two years, three more will be launched: Titania with in-space missions, Juno with SSTL, and Oberon with Airbus Defence Space.
ISTARI will feed our nascent digital targeting web, which in itself has been allocated £1.8 billion under the DIP, an initiative which will truly make our armed forces a single integrated force, connecting sensors, deciders, and effectors driving speed and how we decide to degrade or destroy an identified target in any domain underpinned by world leading AI and software. Our integrated force also relies on these services, so we must monitor them.
We deliver this through world leading sensors, both military and commercial, on the ground and in space. and many of you will recognise these pictures, including RAF Fylingdales, the UK’s primary military space sensor, and the only three-faced and foreign-operated radar in the US space surveillance network. Alongside Fylingdales, we will have our new deep space advanced radar capability, the DARC, a trilateral programme with sites in Australia, the UK, and the USA, enabling us to detect, identify, and trap objects in the deepest of orbits.
But Fylingdales and DARC aren’t simply radars. They too are part of the integrated battle management architecture, forming part of defence’s pervasive multi-domain sensor network. NOCTIS 2, the first sovereign UK sensor for our National Space Ops Centre, or the NSPOC, declared fully operational capability this year. This high-precision optical sensor system, developed in partnership with Spaceflux, is now observing the vital satellites we rely on for military ops around the world. NOCTIS 1 will be soon followed by NOCTIS 2, another advanced sensor which will achieve even higher rates of precision and fidelity.
And we are building the infrastructure for these sensors to be modular, changeable and transportable. So we can swap out and move them as strategic demand evolves. This way, our space domain awareness capabilities would be agile, integrated and ready to support the integrated force anywhere in the world. And unsurprisingly, we will establish more advanced sensors to enhance our SDA using cutting edge technology.
This includes neuromorphic sensors which will help search for unexpected activity around our own satellites. Neuromorphic technology will allow us to monitor large volumes of space with drastically reduced power consumption, latency and data bandwidth, allowing us to detect events in orbit whilst increasing both our global sensor footprint and our observation capability.
However, it isn’t all about the sovereign sensors and what we’re building within the military. Commercial data procured from our industry partners will always be part of the hybrid, flexible and resilient SDA effort. This year, many of us will have avidly and I’m sure excitedly kept on top of the groundbreaking Artemis II mission. The first crewed Artemis flight and the first lunar flyby since 1972. Our team in the NSPOC using data from Spaceflux tracked this historic mission, demonstrating easily just how we can monitor significant events in orbit using the sensors and the data from our space industry partners.
The value of commercial data for our space domain awareness is shown day in and day out by the Joint Commercial Ops Initiative, the JCO. The JCO programme now encompasses over 20 nations with the JCO UK team and UK Space Command leading the Meridian region between the Americas to our west and the Pacific to our east. JCO teams worldwide are providing unclassified information on activity in orbit, strengthening integration with the commercial sector and integrating public information into military operations. But this SDA will be of limited value unless we can convert it into effective decision making. And so this year, our BOREALIS command, control and data processing system developed by CJI as part of a five-year, £65 million contract reached initial operating capability six months ahead of schedule. I don’t often get to say that.
This system used by No.1 Space Ops Squadron in the NSPOC is providing timely, quality information to government and military commanders, allowing us to make effective decisions and provide operational understanding of the space domain to the whole of the integrated force. Through all of these capabilities, space is now the connective tissue of that integrated force and we must protect these vital capabilities from the threats we see growing every day. This month’s new UK Space Strategy outlined the UK’s Control of Space requirement.
Through a whole of government approach, the UK will safeguard allied space interests, we will gain and maintain our freedom to operate in space, and we will deny our adversaries that same freedom.
But we are not doing this for its own sake. We’re doing this to enable our own freedom of action and for that of NATO and for our overall security. We’re protecting the command and control of our integrated force by defending global strategic communications and the systems that generate our decision advantage and combat edge. To help our nation fulfill the control of space requirement, UK defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare.
This can be described as actions and effects conducted within space to achieve military objectives, electronic warfare and capabilities to counter anti-satellite weapons. Alongside other supporting operations, these capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.
To deliver these capabilities, I am incredibly proud today to announce that we are forming No. 3 Space Effects Squadron, UK defence’s first dedicated squadron to deliver operations in support of the UK’s Control of Space mission. No. 3 SES will disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity to defend UK space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force.
The squadron will be staffed by specialist personnel from across defence and will support offensive and defensive space operations, safeguarding the critical space services which are so incredibly precious to us.
But with all of this said, let’s be very clear, and this is particularly important for this audience. No one wants a war in space. We are positioning to deter this. The UK will always operate responsibly in ways that promote stability and avoid escalation.
Alongside our colleagues across government, we aim to promote norms, rules and responsible behaviours in space so that space is preserved as a safe, secure and sustainable domain for prosperity, research and exploration. Our approach to control of space will always be transparent and rooted in international collaboration and norms.
We will never escalate military activity in space, but we must respond responsibly to a rapidly changing environment in which threats to our critical space systems are growing every single day.
UK Space Command and its associated Space Squadrons operating under the newly established HQ Air and Space Command will deliver space power to protect this nation. We already have No. 1 Space Ops Squadron working as part of the NSPOC and No. 2 Space Warning Squadron delivering the operational activity that we all know so well from our RAF Fylingdales. Our new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will deliver precise, integrated effects to safeguard our national interests in space. And we are planning more. Numbers 4, 5 and 6 Squadrons, including a Space Tactics and Training Squadron, and squadrons which will deliver the deep space advanced radar capability. And a Space Defence function working as part of the newly established Integrated Air, Space and Missile Defence Operations Centre.
The Strategic Defence Review gave us the ends. We’ve discussed that here. The Defence Investment Plan gave us the means, and I’ve talked to some of those numbers. Together though, I think we are all the ways.
And it is time for us to harness our resources. It is time to get moving. It’s time to act. and it’s time to deliver more meaningfully with our space capabilities.
To work with all of you to turn our approved budget lines into real, tangible capability so that we can monitor space, make effective decisions, deter our adversaries, and if necessary, prevail in this vital yet increasingly contested domain.
Thank you very much indeed and thanks again for supporting us.

Risks of creating biological weapons with AI help are real — Brazilian BWC official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:47:27 UTC
19:47:27 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Risks of creating biological weapons using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are real, Frederico Meyer, chairman of the Working Group on Strengthening the Convention on the Prohibition of Biological and Toxin Weapons (BWC), said on Wednesday.
According to Meyer, who also serves as permanent representative of Brazil to the Conference on Disarmament (CD), US technology company Anthropic recently announced that it had "detected and prevented several attempts by artificial intelligence to create biological weapons."
"This case illustrates how the combination of artificial intelligence and biotechnology can lower barriers to accessing and applying biological knowledge. At the same time, it boldly demonstrates the dual nature of these technologies," Meyer noted in his opening speech at a seminar on the national implementation of the Convention on the Prohibition of Biological and Toxin Weapons.
According to him, "this is exactly why the BWC must address these tasks in order to maintain and support the achievements of scientific and technical institutions, while ensuring the preservation of capabilities that would not facilitate actions prohibited by the Convention."
"This also highlights the urgency of our work and the importance of achieving positive results at the Working Group’s final session in December," Meyer concluded.

Italy's Colosseum closes after worker dies in accident
ROME, Sept 23 - Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli ordered the one-day closure of the Colosseum on Wednesday as a mark of respect after a worker was killed overnight in an accident.
Andrea Moretti, a 22-year-old technician, died after falling several metres while installing a new lighting system inside the ancient Roman arena.
Built 2,000 years ago, the Colosseum was the biggest amphitheatre in the Roman Empire, used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts. It is Italy's most visited tourist attraction.
"The news of the tragic death of Andrea Moretti, a skilled worker who died overnight ... has deeply shocked and saddened us," Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said.
Culture Minister Giuli also ordered the suspension of all construction and maintenance work at the Colosseum until further notice.
Initially, only a partial closure of the monument was announced, but this drew protests from Italy's biggest union, the CGIL.
"Humanity comes before tourists," said Natale di Cola, the CGIL's Rome chief, adding that the union was calling on Giuli to explain all the circumstances surrounding Moretti's accident.
The incident comes less than a year after the death of a Romanian worker who was trapped for hours under the rubble of a partially collapsed medieval tower near the Colosseum last November. REUTERS

This App Makes Your Laptop Screen Look Like Paper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Tech is so sterile now—everything lives on the same shiny screens. It's nice, then, when you find an application that exists mostly just to add a little grit to these devices.
That's how I'm interpreting Paperman, which makes everything on your computer screen look like it’s printed on paper. The application, from Finnish developers DoublOne, does this by adding a textural overlay onto everything you see on the screen. I'm typing this on my MacBook, but everything on my screen looks like it's on premium stationery.
Fans of old video games know about CRT filters, which emulate the look of old convex displays. Paperman is like that, but it mimics paper instead of a retro television. Just open the application, choose which kind of paper you want, and your entire display gets overlaid with a pleasing texture.
The goal is to help you focus on your work and to make the screen more pleasing to look at. The developers have collected a bunch of academic research, collected on a page on Paperman’s website, that points to studies showing that matte surfaces and paper texture help with visual fatigue. Can a virtual matte or paper layer on your screen help in the same way?
Zoé Kilperti, half of the two-person DoublOne studio behind the application, admits she isn't sure. “A lot of that research looks at why reading on physical paper feels so restful,” she tells WIRED. “Its texture breaks up harsh light and softens sharp edges. Modern displays are the opposite: an intensely uniform, razor-sharp grid of backlight.” Paperman's filter is built to break up that uniformity.
The app offers a variety of textures, from Classic Matte to Sunbaked Parchment. I'm partial to Whisper Weave, the recommended texture. You can toggle how much intensity there is to the effect, and I recommend that you do.
I find this application works best when I'm reading, writing, or otherwise working with text. But you should know that everything on the screen is textured, including images, videos, and even some games. You can set Paperman to not apply the texture when certain applications are open, which is useful if you're doing something like graphic design work or browsing photos.
If you use multiple screens, you can also toggle Paperman to apply the texture effect to the content of one display and not the other. There are also customizable keyboard shortcuts, meaning you can toggle the effect on and off on the fly. You're always going to want to have some method of turning the effect off, so it's good there are so many options.
I've been using Paperman intermittently for a few weeks. I really do like what the texture adds to both reading and writing. Is that texture helping me focus or reducing my eye strain? It's hard to say.
Kilperti, for her part, isn't claiming there's any scientific evidence that Paperman reduces eye strain or increases focus, calling the application “a design hypothesis rather than something backed by science.” Users have been reaching out, though, saying the application has helped them. “The feedback has been lovely, and it's been really rewarding to see how much it helps people get through their workdays,” she said.
You can try this out yourself. The application costs $12 for macOS and Windows, with occasional sales and discounts. On Windows there's a free version that lets you use it for one hour every day, or you can pay $12 for the full version. There's no free trial for macOS, but you can get Paperman as part of the Setapp subscription bundle of indie apps.

US, Iran hold 1st talks in months with both desperate to end war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

The first U.S.-Iran shuttle talks in months raised hopes Wednesday for progress toward ending the Middle East war, though neither side reported a change in position.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
"Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran, merely mediators. Let's see what happens with that," U.S. President Donald Trump said. "They've been mediated for a while, but I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It's what we're hearing from everybody."
Earlier, Trump had told the U.N. General Assembly in a speech that he had to decide whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate" the country. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian was due to address the gathering Wednesday.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had engaged with the United States through a Qatari mediator in New York and conveyed conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression."
Some Iranian state media had earlier reported that Araghchi and Witkoff had met, but Iranian officials clarified to Reuters that this was not face-to-face. Araqchi met the prime minister of Qatar, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has been one of the main mediators at previous talks.
The diplomatic opening helped keep oil prices near two-week lows, with Brent crude now holding just below the $100-a-barrel threshold it had shot through this month, after Houthi fighters in Yemen launched a major offensive and fired into Saudi Arabia.
The war, launched by Trump in February alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury," has lasted nearly seven months, killing thousands of people, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region – first to Lebanon and more recently to Yemen.
Trump repeated previous assertions that the war could end around the time of November's U.S. midterm elections, though he has not explained why.
Since diplomacy broke off in July, the sides have repeatedly exchanged fire, although Trump has held back from a full-blown resumption of strikes after receiving advice from his military commanders that munitions were running low.
An interim agreement reached in June and signed by Trump and Pezeshkian would have given Iran its main demands: lifting financial sanctions and unfreezing assets in return for talks on limiting its nuclear program.
But that deal unraveled within weeks over shipping rules in the Strait of Hormuz, conduit for a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas before the war. Iran wants to exert greater control of the strait and collect fees from ships that use it, which Washington rejects.
Despite near-daily attacks on tankers, traffic through the strait has gradually increased in recent weeks. Oil producers have paid shipping companies fees worth as much as a quarter of a cargo's value to switch off transponders, navigate the route and transfer crude to other vessels beyond the strait.
Exports from the United Arab Emirates have already recovered to prewar levels, and Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of Gulf oil for both this month and next, to be delivered beyond the strait off the coast of Oman, a big increase from August.
Even so, disruption continues to squeeze global energy markets. About a third of Gulf oil is estimated to be missing from global supplies. Shortages have particularly hit refined products such as diesel, causing inflation, pushing up interest rates and hurting Trump's Republicans ahead of the elections.
The risk of further disruption has increased since the Iran-backed Houthis advanced in Yemen this month, threatening traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, an alternative export route used by Saudi Arabia.
Washington, for its part, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, deepening Iran's economic crisis. Iranian officials say they are willing to endure the blockade to achieve their goals, and will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until it is lifted.

Powerful El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths, scientists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:44:52 UTC
19:44:52 KST

Powerful El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths, scientists say
Heaviest toll expected in poorer countries, already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, report says.
More than 450,000 people are projected to die from additional heat due to the unusually strong El Nino event over the next six months, according to a research report.
The projection, published on Wednesday by the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, runs to February 2027 and compares estimates of heat-related deaths that could be attributed to El Nino with the level expected in a typical year.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3El Nino: A phenomenon supercharged by climate change
- list 2 of 3US records hottest summer in 132 years
- list 3 of 3El Nino reaches super status: Where will it bring rain, drought and heat?
Researchers estimate that global land temperatures could climb by about 1.2 degrees Celsius (2.1 degrees Fahrenheit), with extremely hot days 44 percent more frequent than in an average year.
Developing nations and Africa’s Sahel region are expected to be hit disproportionately hard.
The report projected about 66,800 additional deaths across the Sahel, with Nigeria having the highest projected toll of any single country at 31,400, ahead of Indonesia at 19,300 and Sudan at 17,600.
Elsewhere, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia are forecast to see a combined 19,400 extra deaths, with 15,800 projected in India and 13,300 in Brazil.
‘Much more dangerous’
Michael Greenstone, cofounder of the lab and co-author of the study, said the findings show heat poses the greatest threat where temperatures are already high and incomes relatively low.
“If you’re already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous,” he said.
Richer places tend to have better access to air conditioning, steady water supplies and health services, he added.
Greenstone said the heat risk was likely to outlast the El Nino itself, with repercussions stretching into next summer.
Abhiyant Tiwari, who specialises in heat at NRDC India, told The Associated Press news agency that the projections should spur action.
Funding and delivery remain weak points, he said, even in India, which has sound plans on paper.
“The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths,” he said.
This year’s El Nino began developing in June and is expected to be one of the strongest ever. Experts say the natural weather pattern, which occurs cyclically, is being “supercharged” by climate change.
In early September, the United Nations’ weather agency reported a 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027. But researchers say its dangers could linger into mid-2027.

Africa must get permanent seats on Security Council – UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

Africa must get permanent seats on Security Council – UN chief
Africa’s continued lack of permanent representation on the United Nations Security Council is unjust and must be addressed, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has said.
Speaking at the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly debate in New York on Tuesday, Guterres called for reform of the 15-member body to better reflect the modern global order. Africa remains the only continent without a permanent seat on the council despite accounting for more than a quarter of UN member states and every third child born.
“We must reform the security council ... A 21st UN security council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible. This must change,” the UN chief said.
UN Security Council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible — Antonio Guterres
‘Security Council was designed in the aftermath of WWII, but the world has fundamentally changed since then’ https://t.co/L8S7U38rY5pic.twitter.com/wlNk3cB5sw
The Security Council has five permanent members – Russia, China, the US, the UK and France – which hold veto powers, as well as ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. African countries – the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia – currently only participate through the latter category.
Earlier this month, Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama renewed calls for permanent African representation on the Security Council, arguing that the continent’s continued exclusion undermines the legitimacy of the UN’s most powerful body.
“It is no longer acceptable for Africa to be excluded from permanent seats on the United Nations Security Council,” the leader said.
Other African leaders have made similar demands. In July, representatives of several countries renewed calls for the continent to be granted permanent representation on the Security Council, arguing that its current structure no longer reflects global realities. The African Union’s shared position calls for at least two permanent seats with the same privileges as existing members, including veto powers.
Calls for reform have also received support from Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously backed expanding the Security Council to include greater African representation.
In August, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov noted that greater representation for the continent would help correct a historical injustice, arguing that any future expansion should primarily benefit African countries rather than Western states, which he said are already overrepresented.

Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:41:41 UTC
19:41:41 KST

Iran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz in surprise talks held in New York under the mediation of Qatar between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Trump said the three-hour talks held in a room at the UN headquarters had gone very well and been very productive. He suggested further talks were possible imminently, which led to the price of a barrel of Brent crude to fall to below $100 (£75) for the first time in two weeks. Witkoff said the talks had been “encouraging, constructive and successful”.
In his speech to the UN general assembly, Trump said he had a decision to make very soon on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” or help turn it into one of the great countries of the Middle East, the kind of bombastic threat Trump often deploys during talks with Iran.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the talks had occurred, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz – a key waterway for transporting oil – that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. Latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day, but estimates of the US navy are much higher.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by the uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis’ (the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries) of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran or indeed with the Houthis as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular war that the Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.
The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday after arriving in New York on a flight from Tehran as talks were under way.
Pezeshkian is an advocate of negotiations with the US but has not played a direct role in the talks. He has said the memorandum of understanding (MoU), agreed with the US on 17 June, remained the starting point.
Implementation of the MoU fell apart after the two sides accused one another of breaching its terms by trying to take control of the strait. Iran said the MoU clearly left Iran in control of the strait for an interim period before a long-term agreement on its management was reached, including the possibility of Oman and Iran charging fees for navigational services.
Pezeshkian is expected to condemn western double standards over what he regards as an illegal US assault on Iran that has left schoolchildren dead and infrastructure ravaged. Europe’s preparedness to call out Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, and its reticence in criticising the attack on Iran, or Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in Gaza, has been a constant theme of Pezeshkian’s remarks.
Many of the most powerful speeches on Tuesday at the UN general assembly came from European and Arab politicians who decried the inability of the west to enforce peace. In his farewell speech to the UN, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, criticised the attempt to overthrow the Iranian government by the US and Israel, arguing: “Every time a few states, sometimes even in the name of international order, have tried to replace the people in order to change a regime or a system, they have plunged those states into even greater chaos.”
He also said that the west had not imposed a peace in Gaza. “Some boast of a supposed peace. But this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second. Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!”
Macron landed himself in hot water with Israel when he suggested Hamas was not present in the West Bank, as opposed to Gaza.
Netanyahu’s office responded, using the biblical name for the West Bank: “Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria.”
Jordan’s King Abdullah II attacked the Israeli government for “moving the goalposts”, for continuing attacks and the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza, and for refusing to withdraw from the war-torn Palestinian territory. This has forced the Palestinian population in Gaza into barely one-third of the territory, he said.
Observers must no longer treat Israeli policies as “temporary military measures” or a “consequence of war”, he said.
“Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza,” he added.

AI leaders to brief UN amid warnings the technology could slip beyond human control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:41:35 UTC
19:41:35 KST

AI leaders to brief UN amid warnings the technology could slip beyond human control
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 23 - Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face will brief the UN Security Council on Wednesday amid warnings increasingly powerful AI technologies could soon improve themselves, slip beyond human control and threaten international security.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue are due to brief the 15-member council during the annual General Assembly gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
Altman plans to urge world leaders to adopt benchmarks for measuring AI capabilities and assessing the safeguards companies put in place as they develop the technology, an OpenAI executive told reporters on Tuesday.
Council members, including leading AI rivals the United States and China, are also set to speak. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot will chair the meeting.
A European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the main objective of the meeting was to shine a light on the practical risks of AI losing control in ways that affect international security and the security of individual states.
"These are issues that fall squarely within the Security Council's mandate," the diplomat said. "The key question is whether we could one day face a situation where algorithms interacting with each other trigger a war. That is really at the heart of the issue."
Ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, the US and China have discussed setting up a notification system for common goals and common threats that would cover AI-related incidents that rise to a national security level.
TRUMP WANTS TO ENCOURAGE AI, NOT REIN IT IN
Trump told world leaders at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that he "rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control" AI, describing the technology as amazing, but noted that the US would be careful.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution."
"We're going to encourage it, not rein it in. We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice," he said.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned that rapidly advancing artificial intelligence poses risks that cannot be ignored, putting him at odds with Trump.
Guterres has long pushed for global governance of AI and in 2023 created a 39-member advisory body for one year, with members including tech company executives, government officials and academics from countries such as the US, Russia and Japan.
The 193-member UN General Assembly then created the Independent International Scientific Panel last year. Yoshua Bengio, a Canadian considered one of the "Godfathers of AI" and co-chair of the panel, will also brief the Security Council.
The Security Council met for the first time on the risks of AI in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a "runaway horse" and the United States warned against its use to censor or repress people. Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken chaired a Security Council meeting on AI in 2024. REUTERS

Road safety institute weighing up zero tolerance for drivers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:39:54 UTC
19:39:54 KST

Road safety institute weighing up zero alcohol limit for drivers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch Road Safety Research Institute has released a new study on reducing the drug and alcohol limit for drivers to zero, finding it would probably decrease road accidents but would increase pressure on the police.
SWOV looked at the policy in eight countries with limits lower than the Netherlands, which is of blood alcohol level of 0.05% or 0.02% for those who have been driving for less than 5 years.
The risk of accidents is already elevated at the 0.05% level, the report says. Other countries, including Norway and Sweden, set the level at 0.02% for all drivers.
“An absolute zero limit is considered to be a simple and unambiguous standard that leaves less room for interpretation of what is still permissible and what is not,” the report says, and would improve road safety.
However, lowering the limit will lead to more work for police but also testing facilities. It can be difficult, especially with cannabis, to properly detect the levels, especially with saliva tests.
“Particularly for THC and cocaine, concentrations or metabolites can remain detectable long after the immediate effects have disappeared,” the institute wrote, which would create legal problems for criminal prosecutions.

Tunisia-Libya trade choked at Ras Jedir border crossing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:39:18 UTC
19:39:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Tunisia-Libya trade is being strangled by massive delays at Ras Jedir border crossing
Difficulties faced by Tunisian traders and workers at border crossings with Libya, particular at Ras Jedir, have grown for months, with travelers to or from the Libyan border forced to wait for hours.
There are growing warnings about the ramifications following continued economic strangulation of border areas.
Recently, Mustafa Abdelkabir, head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights, said Tunisian workers and traders face what he described as "humiliating" difficulties because they are held for days at Libyan border crossings.
He called on the Tunisian authorities to intervene to permanently resolve the crisis at the border-crossing and protect citizens' rights from violations.
For residents of southern Tunisia, the Ras Jedir border crossing is not merely a border gateway. It is part of a wider economic system based on trade, services, transport, accommodation, restaurants and the exchange of goods.
Small traders rely on daily movement between the two sides, while Tunisian companies, particularly in the food, industrial materials and construction sectors, are linked to the Libyan market, one of the most important Arab destinations for Tunisian exports.
Congestion
Mustafa Abdelkabir, head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights and an expert on Libyan affairs, said the problems were no longer limited to periods when the crossing is closed or to security disturbances—they also include lengthy crossing procedures, disputes over goods and customs documents, changes to procedures on the Libyan side, as well as congestion caused by the heavy movement of travellers and traders.
Abdelkabir told The New Arab that the organisation intervenes daily to resolve problems involving the detention of Tunisian traders and workers, who remain stranded at border crossings for periods of up to four days.
In September 2026, Tunisian President Kais Saied stressed during a phone call with Libyan Presidential Council President Mohamed al-Menfi the need to intensify consultations to remove obstacles to the free movement of people and goods at border crossings.
This reflects the continued importance of the border-crossing issue in Tunisian-Libyan relations.
Unofficial local estimates suggest that more than 20,000 families in southern Tunisia are directly or indirectly connected to cross-border trade, whether through transporting or selling goods or providing related services.
The same estimates indicate that the city of Ben Guerdane alone relies heavily on commercial activity with Libya, with the sector providing a livelihood for thousands of young people amid limited industrial activity and high unemployment.
Unemployment in some southern governorates exceeds 20%, compared with a national rate of around 15%, according to official reports.
This means any disruption to commercial activity quickly affects social and economic conditions.
Workers in cross-border trade resemble day labourers, relying on daily trips to bring in goods, either by vehicle or on foot from Libyan areas bordering Tunisia.
Economic and social stranglehold
Civil society activist in the border city of Ben Guerdane, Atef Chouat, points to another aspect of the crisis, saying the area, which has relied for decades on thriving trade between Tunisia and its southern neighbour Libya, has suffered an economic and social stranglehold for more than two years.
This has caused the region to come to a complete standstill and left hundreds of families without their only source of income.
Chouat told The New Arab that problems at the border crossings and difficulties in the movement of people and goods threaten to trigger waves of irregular migration from the area, given the lack of any other employment prospects for residents of Ben Guerdane and other border cities.
In March 2026, traffic at Ras Jedir returned to normal after disruptions lasting several hours following protests by many Ben Guerdane residents.
The protests came after Tunisian traders were detained by the Libyan side and amid what protesters described as mistreatment of traders.
The incident showed at the time that any tension on the Libyan side can quickly spread to the Tunisian border area and affect the movement of people and trade.
Official figures indicate that formal trade relations between Tunisia and Libya remain significant, even though movement at the crossings is affected by factors extending beyond formal trade.
Data from the Tunisian Export Promotion Centre show that trade between Tunisia and Libya reached about 2.892 billion Tunisian dinars in 2025, an 11% increase compared with 2024.
This included 2.469 billion Tunisian dinars in Tunisian exports to Libya (US dollar = 2.95 Tunisian dinars).
Mechanical and electrical industries accounted for the largest share of exports at 37.2%, followed by various industries at 35.5%, then agriculture and food industries at 27.3%.
In April 2025, the joint Tunisian-Libyan customs technical committee discussed addressing issues related to certificates of origin and reviewing a list of some foreign goods excluded from transit from Tunisia to Libya.
It also discussed activating the joint customs outlet mechanism at Ras Jedir.
The two sides also agreed to adopt a real-time communication mechanism to combat smuggling and customs crimes and to use a handover and receipt document for import, export and transit operations.
To reopen opportunities for Tunisian workers in a more organised manner, Tunisia and Libya signed a memorandum of understanding in April 2026 on vocational training, employment, and worker exchange.
The memorandum provides for an electronic link between the two countries to speed up responses to Libyan institutions' needs for workers.
Libya will identify its needs in terms of specialisations, while Tunisia will provide a database of job seekers, with workers recruited without work visas under the mechanism announced by the two sides.
The agreement also covers workers' rights and social protection and will remain in force for five years, renewable.
According to recently published official data, there is no unified statistic that can be used to determine the current number of Tunisians working in Libya, particularly given the presence of unregistered workers or those working periodically.
The World Bank had previously indicated in an assessment that the number of Tunisians working in Libya was around 100,000 before the escalation of the Libyan crisis.

Ancient wall found under Paris hotel could confirm origins of city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:39:03 UTC
19:39:03 KST

An ancient wall discovered beneath a Paris hotel could confirm the city's origins: "Major breakthrough"
An ancient wall discovered beneath Paris was described as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday by France's culture ministry, with the archaeological find possibly confirming the location of the city's original settlement.
A roughly 65-foot wall dating from the Gallo-Roman period was discovered in Paris this summer beneath a hotel on the Ile de la Cite, a stone's throw from Notre Dame Cathedral in the heart of the City of Light.
The stone-and-wood find is thought to be a fragment of the ramparts of Lutetia -- the ancient name for Paris -- built by the Gallic Parisii tribe which lived along the river Seine in the Iron Age.
The Ile de la Cite has traditionally been regarded as the center of Lutetia, but a rival theory, backed by archaeological research, contends that it was in Nanterre, a suburb to the west.
"We may be looking at one of the most important remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia," Culture Minister Catherine Pegard said in a statement from her ministry which was sent to AFP.
"Scientific caution still requires that we verify its function and its chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable at this stage," she added.
Lutetia was first mentioned in book seven of Roman leader Julius Caesar's "Gallic Wars" series, where it was said to be on an island in the river Seine — a vague description that has given rise to many theories about its location.
The wall, uncovered in the course of excavations beneath the Hotel-Dieu, also bears traces of fire, which may correspond to Caesar's account that the Gauls set fire to their town before the Battle of Lutetia against the Romans.
Through carbon dating technology, the charred evidence is estimated to date from 10-200 B.C., the ministry said in its statement -- a timeframe that includes the Battle of Lutetia in 52 B.C.
The Ile de la Cite, home to Notre Dame cathedral, is the largest island in the river Seine in the Paris region and became the center of the Roman settlement of Lutetia.
Notre Dame itself has yielded numerous archaeological finds. In June, officials announced the discovery of multiple artifacts, including a fourth-century coin and mysterious inscriptions.
In 2022, several tombs and a sarcophagus likely dating from the 14th century were uncovered by archaeologists at the cathedral.
The news of the ancient wall comes less than a year after a massive prehistoric stone wall was found in the sea off the coast of France near the Île de Sein.

SmartLabels QR Code Organizing System Review (2026): AI Made Sense of My Junk Drawer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:39:00 UTC
19:39:00 KST

A key ingredient to feeling organized is having a space that’s organized. That logic also helps explain the ubiquity of the junk drawer. It’s simply not realistic to have a dedicated spot for every item you own, so assigning a single destination where you can house all the leftover stuff makes sense. That is, until you can’t find your utility scissors or flashlight or stamps or favorite highlighter or double-sided tape when you need any of those things.
Regular organizing conventions won’t help you keep track of everything in your junk drawer—or any other storage area, for that matter. For example, nicely labeling your boxes is great, but if you lose track of where you put them, you’re toast. Also, that box labeled “kitchen stuff?” You definitely don’t know every item that’s inside. The clever SmartLabels system, which uses a QR code sticker for the outside of a bin, box, drawer, or other location and a companion app to keep a digital inventory of its contents, could help with each of these organizational pitfalls.
The system is simple to use, but its value in functioning as an up-to-date digital inventory of your belongings depends heavily on how often you update the app. The app won’t know, for instance, if you absentmindedly stow away your double-sided tape with your wrapping paper instead of putting it back in the junk drawer where it is cataloged. You’ll also need to remember to add new items to the app as you add them to a bin in question. But if you’re a gold-star user of SmartLabels, they do stand to help you keep track of your treasures.
Photographic Memory
Each package of SmartLabels includes 48 unique QR-code stickers (four sheets of 12 codes each). After you download the free SmartLabels app (compatible with iOS and Android), fire it up and select the QR code sticker you want to use for the bin in question. The app will prompt you to take a photo of the QR code, then it’ll ask you to photograph the contents that you’re going to store. Every item must be clearly visible, so you can’t simply dump random products in a box and snap a photo. If the camera can’t see an item, the app won’t be able to catalog it. The app is free, but you can opt for a premium subscription ($15 per year) that offers exportable PDFs and spreadsheets of your SmartLabel inventory, among a few other benefits. Businesses might be interested in this capability, but the average home organizer doesn’t need it.

International Criminal Court convicts Central African militia leader
THE HAGUE, Sept 23 - Judges at the International Criminal Court on Wednesday convicted a former Seleka militia leader from the Central African Republic of crimes against humanity including torture.
Prosecutors accused Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of running a prison where suspected supporters of then-President Francois Bozize were beaten and tortured. He denied all charges.
Presiding judge Miatta Maria Samba said that Said and others oversaw beatings and torture of prisoners as part of a plan to target perceived Bozize supporters in the capital Bangui.
He was found guilty on four counts of crimes against humanity including persecution and torture. The judges dismissed several war crimes charges, finding that at the time the alleged crimes were committed the armed conflict had already ended.
Said, dressed in jeans and a blue sweatshirt, gave no reaction as the verdict was read out.
A separate hearing will determine his sentence.
The predominantly Muslim rebels known as Seleka, or "alliance" in the Sango language, seized power in 2013 as part of the Central African Republic's long-running civil war, ousting Bozize. Their rule gave rise to opposing "anti-Balaka" Christian-dominated militias.
The ICC has been investigating the violence in the Central African Republic since 2014. It has convicted two "anti-Balaka" leaders, but Said is the first Seleka member to be convicted. REUTERS

What is Rome's Colosseum?
The ancient Colosseum is the world's largest amphitheater.
It was built in the first century under the Roman Empire. It was used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts.
It is one of Rome's most iconic sites and gets up to 20,000 visitors a day at peak times.

AI generated
MENLO PARK – Meta Platforms is expected to unveil new smart glasses at its annual Connect conference on Sept 23, including a pair without cameras, amid growing privacy concerns about AI devices that can be used to record people without their consent.
The social media giant is the early leader in the race to put AI devices in the hands of customers, with sales of the smart glasses it co-developed with EssilorLuxottica surging in 2025 to more than 7 million.
That has given Meta a dominant share of a market where it mainly faces competition from Chinese companies such as RayNeo and Xiaomi.
But the devices’ growing popularity has sparked concern globally about their ability to covertly record people, with several UK restaurants, pubs and theaters restricting their use.
The glasses have also drawn lawsuits, including a proposed class action in California alleging Meta misled users about privacy protections and that human annotators training its AI viewed and labelled footage of people’s private moments, including changing clothes, after the recordings were uploaded to its servers.

The potential Phoenix launch comes days after Snap unveiled new partnerships and software details about its US$2,195 (S$2,804) Specs augmented-reality glasses that launch later in 2026.
Some analysts are, however, doubtful that removing cameras alone could allay the privacy concerns about AI devices that can still record audio. Losing the camera may also blunt demand as capturing photos and video ranks among the devices’ most popular features.
“Microphones and audio collection could trigger similar concerns, although likely to a lesser degree,” said Linda Sui, founder of Smart Analytics Global, a market research firm.
“More importantly, removing the camera from glasses that also lack a heads-up display will create a product differentiation challenge. Consumers may ask why they need smart glasses rather than Bluetooth earbuds if the primary experience is limited to voice interaction, microphones and speakers.” REUTERS
