Denmark plans to raise the fine for repeated violations of residency requirements to 100,000 DKK, Housing Minister Jacob Mark of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, told Jyllands-Posten.
The current maximum fine for a second violation is 20,000 DKK, meaning the proposed penalty would be five times higher.
“Cheating on the residency requirement is destructive to smaller towns and small island communities,” Mark said.
“When a citizen buys a house, but chooses not to live there, the consequence is that lovely towns in beautiful surroundings turn into ghost towns, the local grocery store closes, and community life and neighborhood spirit die,” he said.
Owners of homes intended for year-round use must ensure that the property is inhabited for at least 180 days a year. If they do not live there themselves, they can rent it out for permanent residence.
Under current rules, a first violation can lead to a fine of up to 10,000 DKK, rising to 20,000 DKK for a second offense.
Municipalities set the detailed rules for different types of housing. Holiday homes are generally exempt, while some properties can be designated as flexbolig, allowing a year-round home to be used as a holiday home.
Several island municipalities, including Samsø, Ærø, Fanø, Bornholm, Læsø and Langeland, have previously called for stronger monitoring powers. They want to be able to check water and electricity use weekly when they suspect violations, rather than monthly.
Mark said he has invited the island municipalities and Landdistrikternes Fællesråd, an organization representing rural areas in Denmark, to discuss possible additional measures.
Bus and light rail tickets in Aarhus will cost 15 DKK from 2027 under a new municipal budget agreement approved Thursday evening.
Aarhus Municipality will allocate 35 million DKK a year from 2027 to lower ticket prices, TV 2 Østjylland reported.
A consultancy firm had estimated that introducing 15 DKK tickets across the municipality could cost 122 million DKK, although the figure was uncertain.
Mayor Anders Winnerskjold of Socialdemokratiet, Denmark’s Social Democratic Party, argued that the actual cost would be lower, and the City Council agreed.
The budget agreement also notes that the national government plans to introduce free public transport for people under 22. Aarhus expects that measure to cover part of the cost of the cheaper local tickets.
Since March, residents have already been able to buy 15 DKK tickets on three bus routes as part of a trial.
The municipality has said the trial is intended to show how cheaper fares affect passenger numbers and what changes may be needed if more people choose public transport.
The experience will also be used in planning for a permanent price reduction and for making sure buses and the light rail can handle more passengers.
Frie Grønne leader Sikandar Siddique has been removed from Copenhagen City Council after authorities ruled that he does not meet the requirement of living in the municipality.
The City Council approved the decision Thursday, following a long dispute over Siddique’s residence.
Siddique has called the case a “miscarriage of justice” by “the system” and said it had been influenced by Zionists, meaning supporters of the Jewish national movement and political ideology. Several parties rejected those claims during Thursday’s meeting.
“I believe that it is quite damaging when an election is called into question by Sikandar Siddique’s statements, but also so-called experts,” Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, said before the decision was approved.
Before the November 2025 municipal election, Siddique registered a move from Herlev to Copenhagen so he could run in the capital.
Copenhagen Municipality later cancelled his residence registration, citing, among other things, an unusually low electricity bill and a lack of documentation showing purchases near his registered Copenhagen address.
Siddique appealed, but the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization upheld the municipality’s decision on September 8.
His seat will now go to Frie Grønne’s first alternate, Asham Agha Nadeem, meaning the party keeps its mandate.
Frie Grønne received nearly 7,000 votes in the election, including more than 3,000 personal votes for Siddique. Nadeem received 612 personal votes.
Denmark’s oldest living person, Kirsten Schwalbe, has entered the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people, TV Midtvest reported Thursday.
Schwalbe turned 112 in March. She was born in Salling in 1914, a few months before the outbreak of World War I, and grew up with nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938 and had three children. Today, she lives in her own home in Struer.
Schwalbe has previously said that genetics may partly explain her long life. Four of her nine siblings also lived past the age of 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also said that mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Europe’s oldest living person is British woman Ethel Caterham, who is 117 and is also the world’s oldest living person.
Schwalbe is not yet among the world’s 20 oldest living people, according to TV Midtvest.
Meanwhile, a man in Costa Rica, Jose Flores, claims to be 119 years old. His age has not yet been confirmed, and specialists are reviewing documents to determine his date of birth.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.
Queen Mary and Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization Christina Egelund will present the Teaching Prize 2026 to teachers from seven higher education institutions.
The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.
The awards will be presented at the Opera in Copenhagen.
“For this year’s seven prize recipients, good teaching is about awakening the students’ curiosity and creating engagement,” Egelund, from the Moderates, said.
She added that the recipients had also created learning environments where students felt comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.
The seven recipients come from different areas of higher education.
Assistant Professor Amalie Trangbæk teaches political science at Aarhus University. Assistant Lecturer Brian Jørgensen teaches communication design at Design School Kolding, while Associate Professor Bjarne Schmidt teaches mathematics, physics and engineering didactics at the University of Southern Denmark.
The other recipients are Associate Professor Lars Plauborg Pedersen from Syddansk Erhvervsakademi, Associate Professor René Kirk Johansen from the maritime and polytechnic education center Martec, Associate Professor Gry Segoli from Københavns Professionshøjskole and Associate Professor Lene Krogstrup Jakobsen from UC SYD in Esbjerg.
Educational institutions nominate candidates for the prize each year. Relevant groups of rectors then assess the nominations and decide which candidates are put forward to the Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization.
Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
Politiken described the agreement signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump as a “diplomatic masterpiece.”
Politiken said the deal protects Greenland’s territorial integrity, but also described it as a high-risk agreement whose details remain open to interpretation.
Kristeligt Dagblad called it a “historic agreement on the security of the Kingdom of Denmark’s Arctic area” and said the Danish government could be satisfied with the result.
Other newspapers focused more strongly on the risks.
Ekstra Bladet described the agreement as a costly victory. It raised concerns that the U.S. could use Greenland for activities unrelated to NATO, including establishing its “Golden Dome” missile defense system there.
“We are paying a high, but unavoidable price,” Ekstra Bladet wrote. “We can well call it a victory, as long as we remember how dearly it was bought.”
Information described the agreement as a victory for the Kingdom of Denmark but also as a “submission to a tyrannical superior power.”
Despite its positive assessment of the agreement, Berlingske also warned that uncertainty remains because Trump is president.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office said the agreement would strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We do not surrender sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I will never do that as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told DR and Danish broadcaster TV 2.
More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.

Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.

Most Danes want the government to temporarily cut taxes on gasoline and diesel as fuel prices reach unusually high levels, a Voxmeter poll for the Danish news agency Ritzau shows.
In September, diesel reached a record 19.19 DKK per liter at gas stations.
The poll found that 53.8 percent supported temporary tax cuts, while 33.3 percent opposed them. Another 12.9 percent did not know.
Torben Kudsk, policy chief at FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ organization, said rising prices were creating serious problems for motorists.
“Fuel is historically expensive. As far as we can see, prices have not been higher in recent times,” Kudsk said.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats said the government was monitoring the situation.
“If energy prices continue to rise, and the situation develops further, we are of course ready to do more,” he wrote on Facebook. He did not describe possible measures.
The poll also asked what should guide decisions on fuel taxes. A total of 39.2 percent said reducing motorists’ costs should come first.
Another 27.2 percent said taxes should remain because of climate and environmental concerns, while 25.9 percent gave both issues equal weight. The remaining 7.7 percent did not know.
The price increases have been linked to wars and conflicts causing a global fuel shortage.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen traveled to New York on Sunday ahead of an expected security agreement involving Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The three governments expect to sign the agreement during the United Nations General Assembly in the coming week. It is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

He said he hoped the agreement would bring greater calm to Greenland.

US President Donald Trump described the agreement differently, saying it gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Denmark registered 502 suicides in 2025, the lowest annual number recorded from 2015 through 2025, according to the Centre for Suicide Research.
The total included 370 men and 132 women older than 15. It was 91 lower than in 2024.
Denmark’s suicide rate fell to 9.9 deaths per 100,000 people, an 18 percent decline from 2015. The rate dropped 30 percent among women and 12 percent among men.
Erik Christiansen, research head at the center, linked the decline partly to a national action plan introduced in 2024 and greater willingness to discuss suicide.
“At one time it was believed that it was dangerous to talk about suicide because it could inspire doing it. Today we know that this assumption is incorrect,” Christiansen said.
Doctors asking people directly about suicide risk can help them receive support earlier, he added.
Merete Nordentoft, a professor, chief physician and member of Denmark’s Council for Suicide Prevention, said help had become more accessible.
Suicide prevention clinics in Denmark’s five regions received additional funding to offer consultations to more people with suicidal thoughts or previous suicide attempts.
Livslinien, Denmark’s national suicide prevention helpline, received about 28,000 inquiries in 2025, up from fewer than 16,000 in 2019. Current funding allows it to answer about half of them.
Danish chef Jimmy Holm of Aarhus was among 12 finalists competing Sunday to be named the world’s best paella chef in Valencia, Spain.
Mexican chef Froilán Mújica won the World Paella Day Cup 2026, according to a live blog from organizer Visit València Foundation. Japanese chef Keisuke Mutsuura finished second.
Holm has worked at the Spanish restaurants El Bulli and El Celler de Can Roca. He also owned the tapas restaurant Los Socios in Aarhus.
He qualified for the final by winning the Nordic-Baltic semifinal in Denmark on June 11. That competition included chefs from Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
The Valencia final brought together chefs from Europe, Asia and North and South America. Seven judges assessed the dishes based on taste and presentation.
Each finalist prepared an individual version of paella and selected the type of rice to use. The competition was held in tents at Valencia’s harbor.
World Paella Day is held annually on September 20 to celebrate the dish and its origins in Valencia.
Paella is a traditional Spanish rice dish originating from Albufera, south of Valencia. Farmers originally cooked it over an open fire using local rice and available vegetables.
The dish takes its name from the large, flat pan used to prepare it. The pan allows the rice to form a thin, crisp layer.

Denmark’s plan to send foreign prisoners sentenced to deportation to a prison in Kosovo has been delayed again.
The 300 prison places are now expected to become available at the end of 2027 at the earliest and possibly not until the beginning of 2028, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen informed the parties behind the agreement Friday.
“I have been informed by the Danish Prison Agency that the construction of the prison in Kosovo is delayed, so the prison places can at the earliest be put into use at the end of 2027 and possibly not until the beginning of 2028,” Wammen said in a written statement to Ritzau.
Denmark reached a political agreement in 2021 to lease 300 prison places in Kosovo to reduce pressure on Danish prisons.
When the agreement with Kosovo was finalized, the first foreign nationals sentenced to deportation were expected to begin serving their sentences there in early 2023.
The latest delay means the prison could open about five years later than originally planned.
Wammen said the project remains an important priority for the government so “we can relieve pressure on the Danish prisons and get criminal foreign nationals sentenced to deportation out of the country.”
“It must happen as quickly as possible, and I naturally would have very much liked for us to have long since begun sending inmates there. Therefore, I am of course far from satisfied that the project is further delayed,” he said.
According to the Ministry of Justice, authorities in Kosovo have now emptied the prison of inmates.
An agreement with a contractor was signed in July, and the renovation work is expected to take about a year.
The project has previously been delayed by the approval process in Kosovo’s parliament, where opposition parties did not support international agreements.
Danish prisons have faced overcrowding for years, adding pressure to make the Kosovo prison places available.
The number of people injured in traffic accidents in Denmark increased in 2025, while the number of deaths fell slightly, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
Police recorded 2,832 people as injured or killed in traffic accidents during the year, an increase of 313 compared with 2024.
The number of traffic deaths fell from 145 in 2024 to 143 in 2025.
Denmark has now recorded fewer than 200 traffic deaths a year for 10 consecutive years. This is well below levels seen between 1965 and 1973, when more than 1,000 people were killed in traffic each year.
Of those recorded in 2025, 1,732 were seriously injured and 957 suffered minor injuries.
The number of injured road users increased across almost all forms of transport, with mopeds the exception.
Injuries among people riding electric bicycles increased from 173 in 2024 to 211 in 2025. Nearly three-quarters of those injured in this group were aged 45 or older.
The police figures do not show the full number of people injured on Danish roads because they only cover accidents reported to police.
Hospital emergency departments keep separate records of traffic injuries. In 2024, they registered 29,589 injured people, more than 1,000 above the previous year’s figure.
Denmark will bring forward and increase a military aid package for Ukraine to DKK 1.8 billion, days after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates and Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats announced the decision Friday after a meeting of the Danish Parliament’s Foreign Policy Committee.
Most of the money will go toward air defense systems produced in Ukraine. The support had been requested by Ukraine.
Løkke described the incident involving the Danish helicopter as a “severe Russian provocation.”
“If they think they can provoke us into being restrained with our support for Ukraine, then they are mistaken,” he said.
Ukraine has faced difficulties defending itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks because of shortages of suitable air defense missiles, including Patriot missiles produced by the United States.
The decision follows an incident Monday involving a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter and a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser in southern Denmark.
The Danish Defence said the helicopter was carrying out routine photographic surveillance of the Russian vessel when the frigate fired two flares toward it. One passed close to the helicopter.
According to Bruus, the Russian ship did not establish radio contact with the helicopter before firing the flares.
NATO has described the incident as an “irresponsible Russian act.”
“This fits into a pattern we are seeing around Europe, where Russia is escalating and constantly testing boundaries. It serves the purpose of shaking our unity and our support for Ukraine, and that must not work,” Løkke said.
Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador following the incident. Russia has said the Danish helicopter acted “provocatively.”
“If the Russians think that they can rattle us by doing this kind of thing, then our counter-response is that we will step up our support for Ukraine faster than we had intended,” Bruus said.
The captain of the Russian frigate has since received an award from Russia for his actions, according to the Danish report.
Denmark has been a major supporter of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. However, since December, Denmark has announced only one other major aid package in addition to Friday’s package.
The Danish Ukraine Fund, which has financed much of the country’s support, has almost run out of available money. Further support would therefore require politicians to find funding elsewhere.
So far, much of Denmark’s support has been financed through the government’s projected future fiscal surplus.

Denmark plans to raise the fine for repeated violations of residency requirements to 100,000 DKK, Housing Minister Jacob Mark of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, told Jyllands-Posten.
The current maximum fine for a second violation is 20,000 DKK, meaning the proposed penalty would be five times higher.
“Cheating on the residency requirement is destructive to smaller towns and small island communities,” Mark said.
“When a citizen buys a house, but chooses not to live there, the consequence is that lovely towns in beautiful surroundings turn into ghost towns, the local grocery store closes, and community life and neighborhood spirit die,” he said.
Owners of homes intended for year-round use must ensure that the property is inhabited for at least 180 days a year. If they do not live there themselves, they can rent it out for permanent residence.
Under current rules, a first violation can lead to a fine of up to 10,000 DKK, rising to 20,000 DKK for a second offense.
Municipalities set the detailed rules for different types of housing. Holiday homes are generally exempt, while some properties can be designated as flexbolig, allowing a year-round home to be used as a holiday home.
Several island municipalities, including Samsø, Ærø, Fanø, Bornholm, Læsø and Langeland, have previously called for stronger monitoring powers. They want to be able to check water and electricity use weekly when they suspect violations, rather than monthly.
Mark said he has invited the island municipalities and Landdistrikternes Fællesråd, an organization representing rural areas in Denmark, to discuss possible additional measures.
Bus and light rail tickets in Aarhus will cost 15 DKK from 2027 under a new municipal budget agreement approved Thursday evening.
Aarhus Municipality will allocate 35 million DKK a year from 2027 to lower ticket prices, TV 2 Østjylland reported.
A consultancy firm had estimated that introducing 15 DKK tickets across the municipality could cost 122 million DKK, although the figure was uncertain.
Mayor Anders Winnerskjold of Socialdemokratiet, Denmark’s Social Democratic Party, argued that the actual cost would be lower, and the City Council agreed.
The budget agreement also notes that the national government plans to introduce free public transport for people under 22. Aarhus expects that measure to cover part of the cost of the cheaper local tickets.
Since March, residents have already been able to buy 15 DKK tickets on three bus routes as part of a trial.
The municipality has said the trial is intended to show how cheaper fares affect passenger numbers and what changes may be needed if more people choose public transport.
The experience will also be used in planning for a permanent price reduction and for making sure buses and the light rail can handle more passengers.

Denmark’s oldest living person, Kirsten Schwalbe, has entered the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people, TV Midtvest reported Thursday.
Schwalbe turned 112 in March. She was born in Salling in 1914, a few months before the outbreak of World War I, and grew up with nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938 and had three children. Today, she lives in her own home in Struer.
Schwalbe has previously said that genetics may partly explain her long life. Four of her nine siblings also lived past the age of 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also said that mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Europe’s oldest living person is British woman Ethel Caterham, who is 117 and is also the world’s oldest living person.
Schwalbe is not yet among the world’s 20 oldest living people, according to TV Midtvest.
Meanwhile, a man in Costa Rica, Jose Flores, claims to be 119 years old. His age has not yet been confirmed, and specialists are reviewing documents to determine his date of birth.

Ethiopian Airlines suspends flights to three northern Tigray airports
The suspension comes after Tigrayan forces took control of Mekelle airport, days after the Tigray People’s Liberation Front announced an alliance with six other armed groups.
Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to three airports in northern Tigray amid an escalation of conflict by an armed group in the region.
In a post on Telegram, the airline said that due to the “current situation in the Tigray region”, flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire had been temporarily suspended from Wednesday.

“We sincerely apologise to our valued customers for any inconvenience caused by this suspension. We will inform you once flight operations resume,” the airline said.
Flightradar24, which tracks air traffic, also showed on Wednesday morning that the flight between Mekelle and the federal capital, Addis Ababa, had been cancelled.
The suspension comes after Tigrayan forces took control of the Mekelle airport from federal police overnight, according to local sources quoted by the Reuters and AFP news agencies.
An employee at Alula Aba Nega Airport in the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle, told AFP on Wednesday that while they were on their way to work, “our supervisor called the driver and told him that the airport had been taken over by Tigray forces”.
“Since there were no flights, he told us to return home,” the employee added, a development that was also confirmed to AFP by a foreign security source based in Ethiopia.
The suspension comes as tensions mount in the region. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) announced on Sunday that it had allied with six other armed groups across Ethiopia to overthrow Abiy’s government. Rights groups have accused the TPLF of forced recruitment campaigns this year as it prepares for renewed conflict.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined with the rise of Abiy’s premiership, triggering a devastating civil war from 2020 to 2022. The conflict killed about 600,000 people, according to estimates by the African Union, before the Pretoria Peace Agreement ended hostilities.
However, the region has not recovered, with about one million people still displaced and parts of the peace agreement unfulfilled. An uneasy calm held until late 2025, when clashes resumed, raising fears of a return to all-out war.
Compounding the crisis, Ethiopia also faces a myriad of other rebellions, including in its most populous regions of Oromia and Amhara.

Where to travel in Europe in 2027: Lonely Planet reveals its best destinations and experiences

The guide book publisher just announced its 2027 Best in Travel list, with spots like Šibenik in Croatia and the Swedish Riviera making the cut.
Lonely Planet has just unveiled its 2027 Best in Travel list – and 10 places and experiences in Europe made the cut.
Released annually ahead of the holiday booking season, the list has been curated by the guide book publisher’s community of travel experts based around the globe.
The list is split into two: 25 best places to visit, and 25 best experiences to book.
Places that made the cut this year range from Dunedin and the Waitaki, one of the “coolest and quirkiest” parts of New Zealand, to Fulidhoo in the Maldives, an affordable alternative to the standard resort islands.
On the experience front, Lonely Planet recommends wining and dining in Valle de Guadalupe, Mexico, before it hits the mainstream, and riding the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway in India.
For something a little closer to home, here’s everywhere in Europe that made the cut for 2027.
Lonely Planet’s best places in Europe for 2027
When it comes to the Veneto region of Italy, Venice dominates the conversation as people descend on the canal-crossed city for romantic breaks.
Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel list instead encourages tourists to explore the wider region, from the Dolomites and Lake Garda to other cities like Verona and Padua.
Another option in Southern Europe is Šibenik in Croatia, one of the country’s oldest cities, which Lonely Planet says boasts “impressive architecture, gastronomic delights and a colourful calendar of festivals throughout the year”.
Much like Venice, Spain has generated plenty of headlines this year in regards to overtourism.
That doesn’t mean you can’t visit the country responsibly, though – you just need to pick a destination that actually wants more tourism.
Like León in northern Spain, a medieval city on the French Way of the Camino de Santiago that draws in tourists looking to see its gorgeous Gothic architecture, and Antoni Gaudí’s Casa Botines.
Much has been said about the growing popularity of coolcations, and the coolest for 2027 is Skanör-Falsterbo, the twin towns found in Sweden’s Skåne province.
Known as the Swedish Riviera, visitors can slow down and soak in the coastal scenery and explore the area’s nature reserves.
Finally, Lonely Planet has also put the spotlight on Dessau in Germany, a city “synonymous with the Bauhaus movement” that packs a big cultural punch despite its small size.
The best experiences in Europe to book next year
For walkers, St Cuthbert’s Way from the Scottish Borders to Northumberland – a 100-kilometre historic pilgrimage – is an absolute must next year.
“Britain is blessed with so many breathtaking landscapes, stunning coastlines and remarkable history and heritage that it is fitting that a trail, which effortlessly combines all three, has received such a glowing endorsement by global travel experts,” Patricia Yates, CEO of VisitBritain / VisitEngland, said.
“With more than one in three international visitors enjoying countryside walks during trips to the North East, and as VisitEngland launches its major domestic coastal campaign, we can’t wait to welcome more people to explore St Cuthbert’s Way and the great tourism businesses along its route.”
If you’re more into road trips than long walks, another of the recommended experiences for 2027 is a trip along Route Napoléon in France.
Next year the route, which passes through spots like Grasse, Castellane and Sisteron, will celebrate its 95th anniversary.
If you’d rather take to the water, Lonely Planet suggests sailing the Aeolian Islands of Italy, “where rugged coastlines, crystal-clear waters and the authentic Italian lifestyle is waiting”.
Alternatively, you can dive into Greece’s Aegean Sea to discover centuries of maritime history.
Ireland’s Wild Atlantic Way takes in 2,600 kilometres of road, but for a shorter escape that’s “a strong contender for the most breathtaking place in the country”, Lonely Planet says you should be headed to Killary Fjord in Co Galway.

Russian forces lost an estimated 1,560 personnel over the previous 24 hours, along with 32 artillery systems and 1,426 operational-tactical UAVs, according to figures released by Ukraine’s General Staff on September 23.
The latest figures bring Russia’s total estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,522,440.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the same 24-hour period, Ukrainian forces destroyed three Russian tanks and 13 armored combat vehicles. Other reported losses included one multiple-launch rocket system (MLRS), two air defense systems, 380 vehicles and fuel tankers, three unmanned ground vehicles, and four pieces of special equipment.
According to the General Staff, Russia’s cumulative equipment losses since February 2022 have now reached an estimated 12,367 tanks, 25,387 armored combat vehicles, 50,216 artillery systems, 2,152 MLRS, 1,665 air defense systems, and 530,560 operational-tactical UAVs.
The overall tally also includes 442 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 5,111 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines. Russia is further estimated to have lost 152,553 vehicles and fuel tankers, 2,723 unmanned ground vehicles, and 4,737 pieces of special equipment.
The reported losses came amid intense fighting along the front line, with 247 combat engagements recorded over the same 24-hour period.
The update comes as Ukrainian forces continue targeting Russian military infrastructure beyond the battlefield. On September 22, Ukraine’s General Staff reported that its forces had struck a facility used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones in Russia’s Oryol region, damaging five launchers and multiple storage buildings.

The European Commission on Wednesday proposed lifting measures imposed on Hungary over rule-of-law concerns, potentially unlocking €4.2 billion ($4.7 billion) in cohesion funding and restoring full access to the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programs.
The proposal, which requires approval by the EU Council, follows an assessment by the commission of reforms and remedial measures notified by Hungary on Sept. 9, according to a statement.
The commission said Hungary had addressed previously identified shortcomings related to public procurement, anti-corruption safeguards, conflicts of interest, and the effectiveness of prosecutorial action.
"If adopted by the Council, the proposal would reinstate €4.2 billion in suspended cohesion policy commitments and restore access to Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe for students and researchers from universities maintained by Hungarian Public Interest Trusts," the statement said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Hungary had taken steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the EU's financial interests.
"I am glad that they will once again fully benefit from the opportunities our Union creates," she said.
The European Council in 2022 adopted measures against Hungary following a proposal aimed at protecting the EU budget from what EU institutions called "breaches of rule-of-law principles."
The measures included the suspension of 55% of budgetary commitments under three cohesion policy programs for the 2021-2027 period.
The EU Council also prohibited the commission from entering into new legal commitments with Hungarian public interest trusts and entities maintained by them for EU-funded programs implemented under direct or indirect management, including Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump in New York on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on September 22. The leaders held a brief 7-minute meeting with the press before continuing their discussions behind closed doors, which lasted 40 minutes.
Speaking at his personal press conference following the closed-door meeting, Zelenskyy commented on the outcome of the talks and outlined new defense and diplomatic initiatives aimed at securing long-term stability.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
His proposals included seeking US authorization for domestic air defense manufacturing, advocating for a mutual energy truce, leveraging American sanctions, and exploring direct trilateral peace talks involving Washington and Moscow.
Addressing air defense needs, Zelenskyy confirmed that military advisor Pavlo Palisa held preliminary discussions with American defense manufacturer Raytheon regarding the domestic production of Patriot air defense systems.
"As a security shield for Ukraine, in any way, we need licenses to begin the prepare production of Patriots," Zelenskyy said, noting that President Donald Trump is "positive with licenses."
While Raytheon expressed readiness to partner, the project relies on official US licensing, which could take a year to eighteen months to operationalize.
To address immediate interceptor shortages, Zelenskyy signed a contract with Germany for 600 Patriot missiles split into two packages. He appealed to the US for urgent missile transfers to protect civilians, stating, "I said very openly because it's deficit, I'm asking United States to help me now, to help our people now, to save our people now," offering to replenish American stockpiles by 2027.
On the diplomatic front, Zelenskyy voiced support for a mutual energy truce as an initial step toward de-escalation, confirming that the US side will convey Kyiv's proposal to Moscow.
"We spoke about how to end the war: we are ready for this. I am not sure that Russia is ready for this. We spoke about an energy truce. We are ready for it. Of course, we are ready to stop strikes on their oil refineries and energy system if they do not strike ours," Zelenskyy stated following his meeting with President Trump.
Clarifying the scope of the proposed energy truce, Zelenskyy emphasized that Washington did not ask Kyiv for any unilateral pause on strikes against Russian energy infrastructure. "We are speaking about an energy truce. If it concerns energy—it means all energy," Zelenskyy explained, noting that a complete arrangement must also cover water supply infrastructure and other critical municipal utilities.
However, the Ukrainian President expressed deep skepticism regarding Moscow's willingness to abide by any standstill, warning the US administration that Russian forces would likely violate the agreement.
"There will be attacks, and Putin will tell you that it happened because of Ukraine," Zelenskyy warned, citing recent Russian strikes as evidence of Moscow using fabricated pretexts to maintain its campaign of aerial bombardment.
Zelenskyy also reiterated his readiness for a direct trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin to end the war. "I'm ready anytime when all the sides will be ready," he stated.
Zelenskyy recently proposed a conditional energy de-escalation framework to Western partners, indicating that Kyiv is prepared to halt strikes on Russian refineries if international partners can secure and guarantee a complete end to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy, port, and logistics infrastructure.
In a statement, he emphasized that any mutual halt must be reliable, long-term, and enforceable rather than a brief operational pause. Expressing skepticism regarding Moscow’s willingness to abide by an agreement, Zelenskyy warned that Russia might seek temporary relief for its domestic fuel markets ahead of elections before resuming strikes.

Latvia Imposes National Sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman After EU Removal
Latvia’s Cabinet of Ministers directed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to prepare proposals, legal justification, and draft legislation to impose national sanctions against Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman following their removal from the European Union sanctions list.
The move came as EU member states reached a consensus to delist several influential Kremlin-linked Russian business figures and politically connected individuals. These individuals were initially sanctioned for belonging to Vladimir Putin’s inner circle and actively supporting or benefiting from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Despite opposition from Riga and concerns over weakening the sanctions regime, the decision to remove these individuals was finalized on September 22, following updated legal assessments and pressure from several member states.
Riga resisted the exclusion of politically connected figures until the end, remaining the sole EU member state to maintain opposition throughout the final stage of negotiations.
"By deciding to advocate for the further implementation of sanctions against these individuals, we achieved a result that is more beneficial for Latvia, Ukraine, and Europe in the long term," noted the Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs.
The Latvian Foreign Ministry received a mandate from the government to secure the strictest possible sanctions framework across the bloc. Following direct negotiations conducted by the Prime Minister with several European leaders, officials reached an agreement designed to protect the broader restriction regime against political pressure and frequent bargaining cycles.
"It was a choice not between a good and a bad decision, but between a bad and a much worse one–the opportunity to choose between changing the status of two individuals and the future of the entire sanctions regime, which affects about 3,000 individuals and organizations associated with Russian aggression. By deciding to advocate for the further implementation of sanctions against these individuals, we achieved a result that is more beneficial for Latvia, Ukraine, and Europe in the long term," noted the Prime Minister.
Under the agreed three-pronged approach, the 36-month extension provides long-term stability for the broader sanctions list. Simultaneously, the Cabinet directed the Foreign Ministry to draft legal grounds for national sanctions against Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman to prevent their assets from circulating in Latvia.
Lastly, Latvia’s representative will abstain from the decision-making procedure in the Council of the European Union while publicly maintaining political opposition to the removal of both individuals from the EU list.
Prime Minister Kuldbergs consulted with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the Prime Minister of Ukraine regarding Latvia’s decision. Ukrainian leadership thanked Latvia for its stance and noted the necessity of preserving the unified European Union sanctions framework.
In parallel bilateral discussions over the past 24 hours, including direct talks with French President Emmanuel Macron, Latvia advanced key defense objectives.
France agreed to initiate talks on Latvia joining its "Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative," with a French delegation scheduled to arrive in Riga to begin formal negotiations. President Macron also committed to strengthening France's military presence on NATO's eastern flank, with a focus on air defense capabilities.
Previously, EU envoys agreed to remove billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the Russian sanctions list while extending restrictions for around 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
The decision was reached after Latvia lifted its veto and abstained from the vote, following reports that France and Luxembourg had pushed for the exclusions.

EU must overcome &quot;sanctions fatigue&quot; and increase pressure on Russia, says European Commissioner
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:55:42 EEST
18:55:42 KST

EU must overcome "sanctions fatigue" and increase pressure on Russia, says European Commissioner
Kyiv • UNN
European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis called on the EU not to weaken its support for Ukraine and to increase economic pressure on Russia.
Europe must overcome its "sanctions fatigue" and intensify economic pressure on Moscow. EU Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis made this point in an interview with Euractiv after highly controversial French-led efforts secured the removal of two Russian oligarchs from the bloc’s blacklist, UNN reports.
Details
The governments of the bloc’s countries must "remain focused [and] not weaken or fall apart right now, because that is exactly what Russia is waiting for," the EU economy commissioner said in an interview with Euractiv on Tuesday, September 22.
"It is clear that there is a certain amount of fatigue [after] almost five years of war," added the experienced EU commissioner from Latvia.
"But from the very beginning, we committed to continuing to support Ukraine for as long as necessary, continuing to put pressure on Russia for as long as necessary, and it is important to stay the course," Dombrovskis emphasized.
His comments came after France succeeded on Tuesday evening, September 22, in removing Russian-Uzbek oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the EU sanctions list, prompting Luxembourg to seek the removal of Russian-Israeli billionaire Mikhail Fridman from the list. Both men had been under sanctions since 2022 because of their ties to Vladimir Putin’s war.
In a shocking move, Latvia blocked the proposed delisting late on Monday, September 21, but on Tuesday lifted its veto under pressure from Paris. Sanctions require the support of all 27 EU countries.
The turbulent events of Tuesday recalled an episode in July, when the EU’s latest sanctions package—the 21st since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine—was delayed for weeks by Greece, which demanded an exemption from the ban on supplying Russian liquefied natural gas, the publication notes.
What Dombrovskis proposes
Asked whether the EU sanctions regime should be changed so that it would not require unanimity—something previously proposed by Germany and Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission—Dombrovskis replied that this was "not possible immediately," as it would require changes to the EU treaties, which in turn would require the unanimous approval of all 27 capitals.
Instead, he said, Europe must find the political will to continue supporting Ukraine and intensify economic pressure on the Kremlin.
"There have been many peace initiatives," Dombrovskis said, referring to US efforts to end the war. "We have seen that Russia is not interested in any of these initiatives. It is interested only in continuing its aggression."
"In such a situation… the only way is to increase pressure on Russia," he added.
"It is clear that Putin and Russia will not stop on their own. They must be stopped," Dombrovskis emphasized.

Muslim bloc holds meeting on disputed Kashmir on sidelines of UN General Assembly in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:55:36 UTC
18:55:36 KST

The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation's (OIC) Contact Group on disputed Kashmir met on Tuesday on the sidelines of the ongoing UN General Assembly session in New York, reaffirming its support for the Kashmiri people's right to self-determination.
The foreign ministers and senior officials of the contact group's member states – Azerbaijan, Pakistan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Niger – attended the meeting, the OIC said in a statement.
OIC Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed reaffirmed the organisation's commitment to supporting the Kashmiri people's "inalienable" right to self-determination, as a foundation for a "just and lasting" peace in South Asia, in accordance with UN Security Council resolutions and the principles of international law.
In a joint statement, the group expressed "serious" concerns over the "continued detention and denial of bail" of prominent Kashmiri leaders, Yasin Malik, Asiya Andrabi, and Shabbir Shah, who has been diagnosed with cancer, according to Pakistan's foreign ministry.
‘Continuing’ restrictions
The group expressed solidarity with the government and people of Pakistan and indicated deep concern over military escalation in the South Asian region in May 2025, including the "unlawful and unwarranted" strikes carried out on multiple locations in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. They also stressed the need to exercise maximum restraint and avoid actions that would destabilise the region.
There was no reaction from India to the statement from the OIC on Kashmir.
The group welcomed the ceasefire between Pakistan and India following military escalation and expressed their appreciation for "the constructive efforts made by all countries to mediate and bring the two parties together to reach this agreement."
Pakistan's top diplomat Ishaq Dar highlighted the "continuing" restrictions on political and civic space in the disputed valley and "attempts to alter its demographic, political, and cultural character."
He said that Kashmir remains an internationally recognised dispute on the agenda of the UN Security Council and stressed that no domestic legislation, judicial verdict, electoral exercise, or demographic manipulation could substitute for the Kashmiri people's inalienable right to self-determination.
The disputed region has been a key bone of contention between Pakistan and India since 1947. The two nuclear rivals have fought three full-scale wars - two of them over Kashmir in 1948 and 1965 - in addition to the Kargil skirmish in 1999.

Russia downs nearly 200 Ukrainian drones over single region
Russian forces have downed nearly 200 Ukrainian drones over Kursk Region in 24 hours as a wave of cross-border attacks killed one civilian and injured three others, Governor Aleksandr Khinsthein has said. Homes, shops, and vehicles were also damaged across the Russian border region.
A total of 193 UAVs were intercepted between Tuesday and Wednesday, Khinshtein said in a statement on Wednesday. Ukrainian forces also shelled border areas 45 times and carried out 24 separate drone attacks using explosive devices, according to the governor.
A 49-year-old man was killed in a border village, while three other men were injured in incidents across the region, according to Khinshtein. The strikes also damaged homes, shops, and vehicles, with one car completely destroyed.
Kursk Region, which borders Ukraine, has faced a sharp increase in drone attacks in recent days. Russian forces downed 168 UAVs over the region during the previous 24-hour period and 169 between September 20 and 21, according to the governor.
The latest attacks come after a massive Ukrainian drone raid targeted Moscow and other Russian regions during last weekend’s parliamentary elections, killing three civilians and injuring dozens. More than 1,600 UAVs were repelled during the Sunday assault, including 450 on approaches to the Russian capital, according to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin. He described the attack as “unprecedented” and said it had been intended to disrupt the elections.
The worst damage was reported in Moscow Region, where a drone struck an apartment building, killing a 44-year-old woman and seriously injuring her husband, who later died in hospital. Their two children were also injured. An elderly man was killed when another drone hit and destroyed his home, while around 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-story apartment block after falling debris set its roof ablaze. Homes, warehouses, and other buildings were also damaged or set on fire across the region.
Russia has accused Ukraine of deliberately targeting civilians with long-range drones and undermining diplomatic efforts while publicly calling for renewed negotiations. Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week that the Ukrainian leadership is “talking about peace” while doing everything to prevent negotiations and an end to the conflict.

Former Daesh member gets 30 years in France over Syria execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:52:44 UTC
18:52:44 KST

A French court has sentenced former Daesh member Othman Garrido to 30 years in prison over his participation in the public execution of two Iranian prisoners in Syria in 2015.
The 32-year-old French citizen was convicted on Tuesday by a special terrorism court in Paris of murder committed as part of an organised group in connection with a terrorist enterprise.
The sentence includes a 20-year period during which he will not be eligible for parole.
The court also convicted him of belonging to a terrorist organisation for joining Daesh, but acquitted him of a separate murder charge alleging that he personally carried out the executions.
Court finds Garrido participated in execution
The two Iranian prisoners were publicly executed in Syria in September 2015 by two other French Daesh members, Yacine Rettoun and Oumar Diaw.
Investigators used photographs recovered from the phone of Garrido's wife, along with international cooperation and open-source material, to establish his participation in the execution, according to French media reports. Garrido was shown in photographs with the two executioners and the victims.
However, the court rejected the prosecution's claim that Garrido was himself one of the executioners. Prosecutors had sought a life sentence, arguing that his years with Daesh involved combat, propaganda and participation in public executions.
Garrido says he was shaped by radical environment
During the trial, Garrido said he had been raised in a deeply radicalised family and left for Syria with his parents and siblings at the age of 18.
He portrayed his involvement with Daesh as shaped by his upbringing and said he had undergone a process of ideological disengagement during six years in French detention. He described education, reading and psychological support as important parts of that process.
French prosecutors questioned the extent of that transformation, while the defence asked the court to take his conduct in detention into account when determining his sentence. The court ultimately imposed 30 years, below the life sentence sought by prosecutors.

Human Trafficking Raid Exposes Suspected Cyber Scam Operation in Papua New Guinea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

Reported by
Papua New Guinea police rescued 39 Indonesians believed to have been trafficked to work in a cyber scam compound, the first case of its kind uncovered in the Pacific island nation.
Four Chinese nationals were also detained in connection with the Tuesday raid in the country’s capital, Port Moresby, PNG police Commissioner David Manning told OCCRP.
“What we did find in there was 39 Indonesian citizens, 34 that were male and five females, all adults but they’ve been in very cramped, very cramped conditions,” Manning said.
Manning also said police seized a large number of documents and electronic devices from the property, a house in Port Moresby’s inner suburbs. He said the incident was the first case he was aware of involving the suspected trafficking of foreign nationals into the country to carry out online fraud.
He added that as far as he is aware Papua New Guinea was the final destination for the suspected trafficking victims.
“All indications are they were brought in specifically to run this scam from Papua New Guinea,” he said.
Senior Asia Advisor at the International Crisis Group, Richard Horsey, told OCCRP that the raid adds PNG to a growing list of smaller developing countries—including Timor-Leste, Madagascar and Sri Lanka—that are being newly infiltrated by global cybercrime and human trafficking groups responsible for hundreds of billions of dollars of fraud every year.
“The risk is that PNG will become a destination of choice [for scamming syndicates] because the state has limited capacity to fight against this. The amount of money that criminal syndicates can bring in is enormous compared to a small island state or Pacific state,” Horsey said.
Manning called the development a worrying trend, urging the public to remain vigilant against suspicious activity in their community.

OECD says growth 'resilient' in 2026 despite Middle East war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:49:00 UTC
18:49:00 KST

Growth 'resilient' despite Middle East war, OECD says
September 23, 2026
The OECD group of industrialized countries on Wednesday lifted its global growth forecast for 2026 despite the war in the Middle East.
It put the figure at 2.9%, an increase of 0.1 percentage points over June's estimates.
The 38-member Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) is a Paris-based forum for industrialized nations.
What did the OECD say about 2026 growth?
The OECD said growth remained "resilient" in 2026, and that "broader financial conditions remain supportive."
It added that the impact of the Middle East war was being softened by other factors.
"Sizeable oil inventories, additional supply from outside the Gulf economies and discretionary government support measures all helped to cushion the impact on the global economy," the group said.
It said investments in artificial intelligence could result in "stronger growth than projected," but warned that growth could still slow if investments do not pay off as expected.
Growth still threatened
However, global growth has dropped from last year's 3.4%, and the OECD has also dropped its 2027 forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3%.
Governments around the world have begun raising interest rates to cushion inflationary pressures sparked by rising oil and gas prices.
The OECD stressed that the outlook depends on whether a lasting resolution to the conflict is found, as continued fighting would likely lead to higher inflation.
The crisis has also led to an increase in government bond yields.
"Rising bond yields underline more than ever the need for enhanced efforts to contain and reallocate government spending, improve public-sector efficiency and strengthen revenues to ensure longer-term debt sustainability and maintain the ability of governments to react to significant shocks," the OECD said.
It said that other threats include weather-related risks like the El Nino pattern, which could cause supply bottlenecks and high food costs.

All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year,” the commission stated.The statement reiterated that EC, a constitutional body functioning under the strict mandate of Article 324 of the Constitution, statutory roles and established institutional conventions, operates as a multi-member constitutional body, "Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour,” it noted.The commission said all official orders, decisions and administrative directions issued by the Commission carry full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures under The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023."The Commission has recently successfully conducted major elections of Bihar, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Assam and West Bengal and election-related exercises during this period. This work involved wide-ranging administrative and operational machinery and many Commission approvals and instruction,” it was stated.On the commissioners’ alleged objection to centralisation of the electoral roll database or ERONet/ECINet, with restricted access to electoral registration officers (EROs) who are authorised under the Representation of the People Act to decide on addition of deletion of names in the electoral roll, the Commission said digital platforms such as ECINet operate under strict data security protocols to prevent unauthorised tampering, manipulation, etc.
"IT security checks and audit controls are standard cybersecurity measures implemented across national databases. United Kingdom announces action on disinformation and global AI standards
The United Kingdom will fight disinformation at home and abroad, and work to ensure global safety standards for artificial intelligence (AI), new Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday evening in his first address to the United Nations General Assembly.
Mr. Burnham said recent years have seen “an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment” in both the UK and many of its allies.
He told world leaders that “Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears”, including through the use of bots, fake websites and falsified news articles.
Election interference, AI threat
“They’ve amplified far right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 General Election,” he alleged. “We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events.”
False information shared online helped to spark riots following the fatal stabbing of three young girls at a dance class in the town of Southport in July 2024.
Mr. Burnham maintained that the Kremlin spends roughly $1.7 billion “on manipulating information”, noting that British companies and institutions have also suffered cyber-attacks.
“And we know that AI will multiply the threat,” he added.
Fighting disinformation, shoring up security
The Prime Minister said the UK will establish a new National Centre for Information Defence that will detect, attribute and disrupt information attacks while supporting and defending its democracy.
The UK will also use its experience to help other countries, having assisted Moldova with protecting elections against alleged Russian interference.
“As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues – some for the first time,” he said.
“So, we’re ready to share our understanding of how these actors work, and how we can respond – because this is vital for our collective security and resilience.”
UK-US partnership on AI
On artificial intelligence, Mr. Burnham described Frontier AI – the cutting edge of the technology – as “one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age”.
He announced that the UK is developing a new AI defence partnership with the United States to protect critical national infrastructure.
Support for global AI principles
He stressed that fundamental decisions on AI “are too important to be left to chance” and “must be taken by elected governments who serve working people.”
In this regard, the UK will bring the right people together to deliver on the potential of AI for good while also dealing with the risks.
“And we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness – and to ensure that AI development is safe,” he said.
The UN continues to uphold that the best way to address AI risks is to bring countries together to adopt shared principles and commitments on AI governance.

The Organization Fighting Ebola Has Never Been More Worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Ebola hasn’t gone away. In fact, the ongoing outbreak in Africa is among the most concerning epidemics the organization trying to tame it has ever seen.
“Other than Covid, which affected the whole world, this is the thing that has frightened me the most,” says Nicole Lurie, who has worked for Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations since 2017 and now serves as executive director for preparedness and response and the US director.
More than 7,000 people have contracted the Bundibugyo Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo since May, around half of whom have died, according to government data compiled by the World Health Organization.
“This is the most rapidly growing Ebola outbreak that we’ve seen. It’s probably on pace to be the worst the world has ever seen,” Lurie tells WIRED, “and it’s quite terrifying.”
While health officials were able to end the outbreak in Uganda through contact tracing, isolation, and clinical care, instability in the DRC means cases continue to climb. Millions of people have been displaced by ongoing violence, which has made contact tracing a “struggle,” according to Lurie. Matters have only been made harder by a distrust of outside humanitarian workers, which has made isolating and treating cases difficult. Locals have attacked Red Cross volunteers, destroyed medical equipment including ambulances, and delayed safe burial teams.
“I don’t think we’re going to be able to bring this to an end without a vaccine,” Lurie says.
Shortly after the first Bundibugyo cases were reported in May, nonprofit CEPI redirected $100 million of internal funding to develop a vaccine. That money helped fund scientists at the Serum Institute of India to manufacture doses of Oxford University’s ChAdOx1 BDBV vaccine at record speed. That and Moderna’s vaccine candidate, also supported by CEPI, have entered safety trials, with efficacy trials expected to start this month.
Though CEPI sees a vaccine as key to ending the epidemic, it’s likely that any trials, which require contact tracing, will still face challenges in the communities. "The thing that worries me is vaccine distrust and mistrust,” says vaccinology and immunology professor Teresa Lambe, who is the lead scientific investigator in the Oxford safety trials. “And even if we get vaccines that are fabulous, will they be used?”
She had been working on a hantavirus vaccine in May following the cruise ship outbreak when her phone lit up with a message from a former WHO employee about Ebola that made her swear out loud. She knew the instability in the DRC could make any Ebola outbreak escape control very rapidly, so she pivoted and kick-started her vaccine drive with philanthropic funding even before CEPI set up support.
"Covid was in some ways easier,” reflects Lambe, who says she hasn’t taken a day off since May. “We're not in a lockdown, we're not in a situation where people even know or care about what's going on in the DRC … You're not all pulling in the same direction because day-to-day life continues.”
Global responder organizations have been short of staff since the US withdrew from the World Health Organization and dismantled USAID at the start of President Donald Trump’s second term. His administration’s cuts to foreign aid have also left responders facing a shortage in basic medical equipment like masks, hand sanitizers, and testing gear.
The US State Department didn’t respond to a request for comment.
“CDC teams and partners are strengthening preparedness in the region by supporting surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory diagnostics, infection prevention and control, border health activities, community engagement, and other outbreak containment efforts in coordination with the governments of the DRC, Uganda, and other partners,” Emily Hillard, press secretary for the Department of Health and Human Services, writes in an email. She adds that in the US, the agency is helping provide “enhanced travel screening, clinical and public health guidance, laboratory readiness, and coordination with state and local health departments.”
While the US government committed $50 million to support CEPI’s work on countermeasures against the Bundibugyo outbreak in June, Lurie says that the group will run out of funds for its Ebola program by December unless it can raise more money. She adds that all governments need to play a role in supporting the work.
CEPI was set up in 2017 with funding from several governments and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation after the most widespread Ebola outbreak ever showed a need to stimulate and accelerate vaccine development for epidemics. By the time a vaccine had been developed and used to stem the 2014 to 2016 West Africa epidemic, more than 11,000 people had died. (This many months in, that outbreak had a little over 1,000 cases.)
Lurie was working in the Obama administration as assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the US Department of Health and Human Services during the West Africa Ebola epidemic. She recalls the “amazing amount of panic, and the phenomenal cost of what was required” to treat the 11 cases reported in the US. “I don’t think anybody really wants to go through that again.”
