Could we be about to see the end of northern English dialects? My experience – and the science – says aye | Zahaan Bharmal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:00:09 UTC
18:00:09 KST

At our wedding reception 15 years ago, my new father-in-law stood up, pint in hand, looked me squarely in the eye and welcomed me to the family – and to Yorkshire. He acknowledged my obvious defect – my London roots – before offering a note of comfort. “Don’t worry, Zahaan,” he said. “You’ll fit in here eventually. It’ll just take 50 years.” He added that if I’d been from Lancashire, there’d have been an extra zero on that 50.
Not long after the wedding, my wife and I relocated from our first place together in London to her beautiful home city of York. The quality of life and the glorious scenery on our doorstep have made the move more than worth it – but over the last decade and a half, it’s felt like the people of Yorkshire and I haven’t always spoken the same language.
My untrained southern ear quickly decided they all sounded like a cross between Sean Bean in Game of Thrones and former Spice Girl Mel B. It was, of course, a gross oversimplification – but for someone who had previously treated Watford as the edge of the known universe, it was the best I could do.
It wasn’t just how things sounded that caught me out – some words meant something else entirely up north. In the south, “kegs” are what you store beer in; in parts of Yorkshire, they are your trousers. When I was first offered “tea” up in Yorkshire, I imagined a hot drink, perhaps with a small plate of chocolate biscuits on the side. What actually arrived, of course, was a full evening meal. And that was after I’d had my “dinner” for lunch.
My own children now speak with a proper Yorkshire accent – and mercilessly tease me for my southern tones. I pronounce the green stuff on our lawn “gr-arse”. They say it as if the “a” is barely there. The same goes for “bath”: mine comes out “bar-th”, theirs stays clipped and short. They won’t let it go, repeating my words back to me and comically lengthening my vowels until the whole kitchen is laughing. Whenever I try to defend myself, they look at me as if I’m an amiable foreign exchange student who hasn’t grasped the basics.
That sense of not quite fitting in has never fully worn off. At school pick-ups, if I overhear another parent with a London accent, something switches on in me – a kind of homing beacon – and I find myself gravitating towards them. I feel as if I’ve bumped into a long lost friend. I’ll want to talk about the tube or the price of a two-bedroom flat in Hammersmith or the best curry house – anything London-related. And, perhaps for their benefit or mine, I’ve caught myself deliberately dialling up my own London accent, with more elongated vowels than I might normally use.
Over the years, I’ve never tried to change how I speak, and I certainly haven’t been trying to fake being a northerner. Yet, without me ever quite noticing, some things have changed. I recently offered someone directions to Tadcaster Road and, without thinking, completely forgot to pronounce the “arse” in the middle. And I’ve now started calling dinner “tea” – much to the amusement of my children. This kind of flexing is not uncommon: Andy Burnham, the “king of the north” himself, has been observed sounding more scouse in Liverpool and rather more Mancunian in Manchester.
So where do I belong? When I take the train between York and London, where along the 170-mile journey does “grass” become “gr-arse” and vice versa? On the way up, I still feel like a Londoner heading north. On the way down, oddly, I feel like a northerner heading away from home. In fact, it feels as if I’m not fully northern or southern any more.
Perhaps one of the reasons I struggle to know where I belong is because accents themselves are changing. Dialect boundaries are not fixed lines on a map. They behave much more like bubbles in a bath (pronounced “bath” or “bar-th”; your choice), distinct when left alone but merging and reshaping wherever they touch.
There are in fact some researchers – James Burridge and Tamsin Blaxter among them – who predict that this bubble behaviour may lead to many northern linguistic traits dissolving over time. The word “strut”, for instance, is steadily losing its rhyme with “foot” across parts of the north. And the old northern word for autumn, “backend” – now rarely used – will one day vanish altogether. Not every feature will budge: a 2024 study of the East Midlands, where the north and south bubbles touch, found the boundary between “gr-arse” and “grass” has stayed remarkably stable. While a 2020 study suggested that among city-dwellers in the north, local accents are softening into a more homogenous pan-northern accent. It seems that the same thing that’s happened to my accent and vocabulary is happening across the country. People move, marry, have children and absorb one another’s words and pronunciations.
As it happens, it’s predicted some of these changes could happen within the next 50 years – meaning my father-in-law’s joke may have been more prescient than either of us realised. Plenty of linguistic charm will be lost along the way, no doubt. But perhaps there is a small personal consolation. I may eventually fit in up here – not because I’ll ever talk like Ned Stark, but because there could be far less of a difference between the way people in the north and south speak. Mind you, my children will still find a way to take the mick out of how I say “bar-th”.
- 
  Zahaan Bharmal is the author of The Art of Physics and a senior director at Google, writing in a personal capacity

Brutalist cassette listening booth in Berlin's KaDeWe unlocks "music you can't find on Spotify"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:00:01 UTC
18:00:01 KST

Brutalist cassette listening booth in Berlin's KaDeWe unlocks "music you can't find on Spotify"
Design firm Yont Studio has used salvaged car seats and more than 140 cassette tapes to create an analogue sound installation inside Berlin department store KaDeWe.
Created in collaboration with Telekom Electronic Beats and local fashion brand Namilia, the installation is set on the second floor of the city's century-old department store, which was recently renovated by OMA.
The hybrid display stand and listening booth aims to take Berliners on a sonic ride down memory lane.
The collaboration was inspired by the 1977 Iggy Pop song The Passenger, which he recorded during his time in West Berlin with David Bowie, describing the sweet melancholy of watching the world pass by through a car window.
To evoke this same feeling, Yont Studio created a circle of second-hand black leather car seats, inviting shoppers to slow down and settle in with a pair of headphones, so they can listen to a selection of rare and second-hand cassettes.
"It comes almost from a place of nostalgia; the memory of listening to your favourite singer's cassette on a road trip as a kid," said Coşan Karadeniz, who founded Yont Studio together with Serdar Ayvaz. "Contrary to today's internet world, it's a slow and physical ritual."
The installation was designed to mark the launch of a collaborative fashion collection created by Namilia, run by Royal College of Art graduates Nan Li and Emilia Pfohl, music platform Telekom Electronic Beats and British indie rock band Wet Leg.
To display the pieces from the collection and hold the cassette players and tapes, Yont Studio created a quartet of bright-pink foam wedges, with integrated metal shelving and clothes rails.
The duo distressed the foam by hitting it with stones and burning it with flamethrowers and it was completed with metal rebar poking out of the polystyrene.
"It's really fun because it's an intuitive process," Ayvaz said. "It's quite manual, very Stone Age."
The aim was to evoke the brutalist concrete birthplaces of Berlin techno. At the same time, playful details like the glossy pink car paint and clothes hooks shaped like butt plugs bring moments of irreverence.
"Namilia's fashion attitude was quite a starting point for us – unapologetic, kinky, queer," Ayvaz explained.
"KaDeWe is a place with a really rich history; it's the first luxury department store in Berlin," he added. "And we were really happy to bring something very young, fresh, and in a way provocative."
Techno can also be found in the cassette collection itself, which includes sets by pioneering DJs like Sven Väth and Carl Cox, alongside little-known world music.
"There is a lot of music that I'm so sure you can't find on Spotify or anywhere else because it's just super niche or it was only recorded once," said the Telekom Electronic Beats team, who compiled the selection from second-hand shops and private collectors.
"There is a lot of music that was recorded from the radio, entire sets that someone just recorded. So you can basically only hear them here."
The listening booth is open until 27 September, with visitors encouraged to stay and listen for as long as they want.
"We encourage people to bring their cassettes and listen to whatever they want, or maybe exchange what they have there," Karadeniz said. "So it's kind of like a living organism."
Karadeniz and Ayvaz, two club kids who met while studying architecture at the Technical University Berlin, have found a niche in catering to the growing demand for well-designed music spaces.
The duo are known for creating playful brutalist DJ booths using their distinctive epoxy-foam combination, previously seen at this year's Milan design week and in a record store they designed in Berlin's Mitte district.
"We are getting more and more digitised, so people actually care more about sensual experiences," Ayvaz said. "Sound is one of the first things you notice when you're in a space. So I think people will care more and more about being physically in a place and experiencing that."
The photography is by Juan Camilo Roa for Telekom Electronic Beats.

UK to launch new military space squadron to protect satellites, defence ministry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:59:07 UTC
17:59:07 KST

Last year, the head of UK Space Command Major General Paul Tedman warned he was "really worried" by Russia attempting to jam British military satellites on a regular basis.
Britain announced on Wednesday that it will launch a new military space squadron charged with defending the country's satellites, in the latest move as various countries rush for military space capabilities.
The new Royal Air Force (RAF) squadron will protect critical satellites used in communications and to warn of incoming missile attacks, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said.
It described the unit, to be known as No III Space Effects Squadron, as the country's first dedicated to "disrupting, degrading, and denying enemy activity targeting British interests in space."
The MoD noted the UK launched two squadrons in 2023 that "watch and warn" of space threats while the new unit will "act against those threats, using advanced technology, including electronic warfare."
Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth will formally unveil the squadron on Wednesday at a two-day UK Space Power Conference starting in London, where Defence Secretary Wes Streeting will also warn Britain must "keep pace in the new space race."
The announcement comes just over a week after the United States confirmed for the first time that it has arms deployed in orbit above the Earth.
That prompted China to warn against turning outer space into a "battlefield" and Russia to caution it must be "free from any weapon" amid fears of an arms race in space.
The developments are being driven by rapid technological advancements but lack a comprehensive legal framework.
Last year, the head of UK Space Command Major General Paul Tedman warned he was "really worried" by Russia attempting to jam British military satellites on a regular basis.
He noted at the time that the UK was operating six dedicated military satellites for communications and surveillance, which were equipped with counter-jamming technology.

Israel's opposition bloc would secure 54 seats in the Knesset (parliament) compared with 50 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition if elections were held today, according to a poll released late Tuesday by Channel 12.
Neither bloc would reach the 61 seats required to form a government, while Arab parties would win 12 seats, according to the poll, done just weeks before Israel's Oct. 27 general elections.
The survey, done by the Sample research and consulting firm for Channel 12, included 2,498 respondents and had a margin of error of 4.4 percentage points.
Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party would emerge as the largest party with 23 seats, followed by Netanyahu's Likud with 20, according to the poll. Naftali Bennett's Together party would win 13 seats, while the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beiteinu would each secure nine.
Together, Yashar, Together, the Democrats and Yisrael Beiteinu would hold 54 seats, according to the results.
On Netanyahu's side, United Torah Judaism would win eight seats, Shas seven, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit six, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism five, and the Reservists-New Economic Party, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, four. Along with Likud's 20 seats, the bloc would have 50.
Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party would win four seats, while Arab parties would secure 12, including seven for the Joint List and five for the Ra'am party led by Mansour Abbas.
In a separate question on respondents’ preferred prime minister, Eisenkot got 41% compared with 38% for Netanyahu, according to the poll.
A total of 38 lists have registered to contest the upcoming Knesset elections, while polls indicate that 13 are expected to win parliamentary representation.
A government requires the support of at least 61 members of the 120-seat Knesset.
The elections will be held amid a fragmented political landscape, with Arab parties projected to hold a significant number of seats but with major Jewish parties having generally ruled out relying on Arab lawmakers to form an alternative government to Netanyahu's coalition.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since December 2022.
He is facing corruption charges, while the International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for him over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.

Not always 50/50: when one spouse may receive more property after divorce
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:57:20 EEST
17:57:20 KST

Not always 50/50: when one spouse may receive more property after divorce
Kyiv • UNN
A court may change the shares due to evasion of child support, concealment or damage to property. Debts alone or the child living with one of the parents do not guarantee this.
When dividing marital property after divorce, the basic rule is that the spouses’ shares are equal. At the same time, a court may depart from the 50/50 principle if it establishes circumstances of substantial importance. This was told to UNN by Alina Parkhuta, a family law attorney at "LOGIC Law Company" LLC.
According to her, a larger share may be awarded, in particular, if one of the spouses failed to provide for the family financially, evaded supporting the child, concealed, destroyed, or damaged marital property, or spent it to the detriment of the family’s interests.
"Equal shares remain the general rule; a departure from it is a consequence of circumstances established by the court. In such disputes, what is decisive is not the number of claims made against the former husband or wife, but whether they correspond to the grounds provided for in Article 70 of the Family Code of Ukraine and whether they can be confirmed by appropriate evidence," Parkhuta noted.
Alimony and division of property
One separate ground for departing from equal shares may be one parent’s evasion of child support.
As the attorney explained, in its ruling of February 24, 2025, in case No. 206/4992/21, the Supreme Court stated that such evasion does not depend on whether there is a notarized agreement on alimony payments, a court decision, or a court order.
"Evasion of child support does not depend on whether there is a notarized agreement on alimony payments, a court decision, or a court order. It may consist both in failing to comply with an already established alimony obligation and in actually failing to provide support for the child where the issue of alimony had not previously been formally regulated," Parkhuta commented.
At the same time, the mere existence of alimony arrears does not automatically mean that the spouses’ shares will be changed. The court assesses the circumstances in which the debt arose, the duration of the failure to perform the obligation, and the payer’s actual conduct.
"The existence of any arrears, in itself, does not yet mean that the shares will necessarily be changed. The court must establish the circumstances in which they arose, while the alimony payer has the right to prove that the delay or incomplete payment was caused by reasons beyond their control and that they took the necessary measures to fulfill the obligation," the attorney explained.
The Supreme Court separately drew attention to the consequences of evading family obligations and the possibility of departing from equal shares in its ruling of February 24, 2025, in case No. 206/4992/21.
When a child can affect the division of property
The law provides for another situation. The share of the spouse with whom the children live may be increased by a court decision if alimony is insufficient to ensure their physical and spiritual development and medical treatment.
At the same time, the mere fact that a child lives with their mother or father is not automatically grounds for receiving a larger share.
"The existence of a child and the fact that the child lives with their mother or father, in themselves, do not create a right to two-thirds of an apartment or to any other increased share. The Supreme Court consistently emphasizes this: if alimony is being paid and a party asks to increase their share specifically in the child’s interests, they must prove that such support is insufficient," Parkhuta noted.
Recent court practice also confirms this approach: in September 2026, a court refused to increase one parent’s share because the mere fact that two minor children lived with that parent was not sufficient grounds, and the insufficiency of the alimony payments was not confirmed by appropriate evidence.
According to the attorney, proving that alimony is insufficient requires confirming the child’s actual needs. This includes, in particular, medical prescriptions and expenses for treatment, examinations, and rehabilitation, as well as documents concerning the cost of education or other necessary services.
What happens if one of the spouses concealed property
The court may also take into account the actions of one of the spouses concerning marital property. Such circumstances include concealing it, transferring items to relatives in order to make division impossible, disposing of property without the other spouse’s consent contrary to the family’s interests, as well as destroying or damaging the property.
According to Parkhuta, several such circumstances may be assessed by the court in aggregate.
"In cases in this category, the outcome largely depends on how precisely the party has identified the basis for its claims. It is necessary to explain which specific part of Article 70 of the Family Code of Ukraine the party is relying on, which factual circumstances it considers grounds for deviating from equality, and what evidence confirms each of them," the lawyer emphasized.
Thus, before filing a claim for the division of property, it is worth clearly determining the legal basis of the claims and gathering evidence specifically to substantiate it. The general rule remains the division of jointly owned property in equal shares.
The issue of dividing property after divorce is particularly relevant for couples with a shared business, loans, or debt obligations — such circumstances most often become grounds for applying to the court with a request to deviate from the principle of equal shares.
An illustration of how complicated such situations can be was the story of blogger Anastasia Skalnytska, who publicly spoke about a conflict surrounding a shared business after her divorce.
According to her, her ex-husband left the business burdened with debt obligations, and some of the loans had been taken out in the names of her employees. Skalnytska also claims that the family largely lived on her income, while she additionally covered her husband's financial difficulties, including paying for the purchase of cars.

Brazil, Germany, India and Japan renew calls for Security Council reform
The foreign ministers of Brazil, Germany, India and Japan on Wednesday called for the reform of the UN Security Council (UNSC), saying it was more urgent than ever.
"Given the increasingly challenging geopolitical environment, UNSC reform is more necessary than ever before," the four foreign ministers said in a joint statement issued after the diplomats met on Tuesday.
The Security Council is a 15-member body with five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the UK and US — known as the P5 and 10 rotating members elected to two-year terms by the General Assembly.
Permanent members enjoy veto powers, which often means the body is kept from carrying out resolutions due to conflicts with the interests of one or more of them.
UNGA day 2: AI, Iran war, climate to dominate debate
Beyond speeches by the presidents of Syria, Iran and Ukraine, artificial intelligence (AI), the US-Israeli war in Iran and the still-pressing issue of climate change are set to dominate the agenda at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday.
On day 2 of this 81st UNGA session, tech industry leaders Sam Altman (OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic) and Clement Delangue (Hugging Face) will brief an emergency meeting of the 15-member UN Security Council. Their attendance comes as international concerns — raised from within the industry — prompt debate over slowing AI development before the new technology potentially spins out of control with unknown consequences.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday blasted calls to slow the technology as part of a "globalist scheme," brushing aside warnings that it could wipe out humanity within years if left unchecked.
After Trump used his General Assembly speech on Tuesday to threaten the annihilation of Iran and to drive its people "into hell," the Islamic Republic's President Masoud Pezeshkian will directly address world leaders for the first time since the start of the war against Iran in February.
The conflict in Iran has settled into a hot stalemate, directly impacting neighboring states militarily and the entire globe economically.
Iranian and US representatives have met on the sidelines of the General Assembly in New York, but, as has been the case for months, a peace deal remains elusive and the flow of oil through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz stunted.
Russia's more than four-and-a-half-year full-scale assault on Ukraine will also be the topic of diplomatic debate on Wednesday, with a Security Council session scheduled for the morning and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy set to address the General Assembly in the afternoon.
Lastly, climate urgency is on the slate, with outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blasting fossil fuel giants for treating the Earth's atmosphere like an "open sewer" for emissions.
He further chided "big oil" for its greed as the world grapples with armed conflict.
"Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits," he said, noting that at the same time just $34 billion (€29.8 billion) had been invested in helping developing countries adapt to a warming world.

UK's Andy Burnham: 'Britain is back'
In his debut as UK prime minister at the UNGA debate, Andy Burnham declared "Britain is back" 10 years after the country dealt with the turbulence caused by Brexit.
Burnham said the UK is "restoring our stability" and "building a more dynamic economy" while seeking trade and working together with other countries to tackle shared problems.
However, he said the UK needs to deal with forces of division and instability. He said this begins with Britain boosting its defense expenditures as a NATO member state and strengthening European capabilities.
Another issue Burnham addressed was disinformation being sowed online by Russia-aligned actors.
"Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fear," Burnham said. "They've used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organizations — including universities and the BBC. They've amplified far-right narratives."
The UK prime minister said there is evidence that Russia tried to interfere in the 2019 UK general election. He said the Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion ($1.7 billion, €1.5 billion) annually to sow disinformation.
As a solution, Burnham announced the National Centre for Information Defence to fight disinformation which hurts British interests.
Burnham also addressed the issue of AI, saying global standards are needed because "fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance." Burnham said the UK will work on convincing other countries regarding rules on AI transparency and access to AI models.
Japan's mission is to lead efforts towards world without nuclear weapons, Takaichi says
Japan's conservative Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said it her country's "mission" to lead efforts towards a "world without nuclear weapons."
She said this is because Japan is the "the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings during war." The US atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki during World War II in 1945 killed and maimed hundreds of thousands people, with the radiation causing illnesses in survivors in the years after.
Takaichi urged a stronger Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty regime. She also warned that North Korea's nuclear and missile programs along with other activities are a "serious threat to international peace and security."
In regards to technology, Takaichi said Japan intends to host an AI safety summit in the future.
The Japanese prime minister also called for a reform of the UN Security Council by expanding both the number of permanent and non-permanent members.

Here are some photos of leaders who spoke during this afternoon's session of the UNGA:
North Korea's vice foreign minister traveling to UNGA
North Korea's Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs Kim Son Gyong has departed from Pyongyang to attend the UN General Assembly debate in New York City, North Korean state media outlet KCNA reported.
It's unclear whether Kim will meet with officials from the Trump administration.
During his first term, Trump pushed for a deal where North Korea would give up its nuclear ambitions in exchange for sanctions relief.
Trump had met with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Singapore, Hanoi and the Korean Demilitarized Zone in 2018 and 2019 to discuss a possible deal, but ultimately a final agreement never materialized after talks broke down in Sweden in October 2019.
Zelenskyy meets Trump, says US and Ukraine want war to end before winter
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy characterized the meeting with Trump as "positive and productive."
"Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter. We discussed potential de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy," Zelenskyy said.
"I am grateful that in the meantime our teams keep working on launching Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine. This is what will help proect lives, should Russia spurn the negotiations and keep betting on ballistic missile terror against our people this winter and beyond," the Ukrainian leader added.
Zelenskyy said he also discussed a winter package of air defense for Ukraine with Trump, among other issues.
The negotiation process between Ukraine and Russia is still stalled, with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner visiting Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month to jumpstart the talks. It comes as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine will hit its 5-year anniversary in February 2027.
In comments to journalists after the 40-minute meeting, Zelenskyy said the two leaders discussed an energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy said "we are ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire" if Russia agrees to "not attack our energy system."
Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. He has, without evidence, blamed the Ukrainian attacks for raising the price of diesel fuel, as the US war with Iran disrupts energy shipments from the Strait of Hormuz.
Macron calls for open-source AI model not dependent on US, China
Towards the end of his wide-ranging address, French President Emmanuel Macron said there was a need for nations to develop their own artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities so as not to be beholden to the US and China.
"France is proud to have a competitive frontier model" he said, likely referring to Mistral AI.
Macron said likeminded nations such as India, Brazil, Singapore, African nations and the Gulf states should pool not only their financial resources but also their data processing capacity.
"I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers. Rather, we must come together to build an open-source frontier model, a cutting-edge model," he told the UN General Assembly.
"Our investment capabilities must be pooled to build a cutting-edge open-source AI model, which we will share. We should not depend on somebody else," he added.
Macron: 'Shame on all of us' of failing to do more for Gaza
French President Emmanuel Macron was addressing the General Assembly for the last time, as his term limit approaches and presidential elections beckon early next year.
He alluded to his previous visit to the event in New York, when a dozen countries including France announced plans to recognize Palestinian statehood.
"I understand that some of you are very cynical," Macron said, and some people would argue this recognition was only on paper and did not address the reality of the situation.
"But what is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza?" he asked. "Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. The scenes, the spectacle, it is shameful. Shame on all of us!"
Macron said that what was needed was respect for the "legitimate rights" of the Palestinian people, arguing that this was a "prerequisite for security" not just for Palestinians but also for Israel.
"But all those who claim that Israel's security requires the violation of the sovereignty of all of its neighboring states are making a very fateful error," Macron said. "They are weakening Israel's security, today, and going forward. They are threatening Israel's security, in fact."
What did Macron suggest regarding Ukraine?
Macron said that France and its allies would continue providing "unstinting support" to Kyiv, but he also floated a suggestion similar to those made by others involved either in the conflict or the efforts to broker a stop to the fighting.
He proposed a "double moratorium," saying that both Ukraine and Russia should commit to stop strikes on each others's energy infrastructure and on grain shipments in the Black Sea.
"Winter is coming," Macron said, explaining, "We'd like to express our support [for] a double moratorium. A moratorium on strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure, that's first. And a Black Sea moratorium which would allow us to release grain shipments."
In times of peace both Russia and Ukraine are prolific agricultural exporters, and use the Black Sea to ship their produce.
Part of supporting Ukraine, Macron said, was working to ensure that "useful negotiations" between the two sides start as quickly as possible. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was attending Tuesday's session; Russia's Vladimir Putin was not expected to travel to New York, or at least he has not done so since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump tells reporters US and Iranian officials met
A few hours after his speech at the assembly warning he was prepared to "annihilate" Iran if necessary, US President Donald Trump told reporters that American and Iranian officials had met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
"The had a very good meeting, a very productive meeting," Trump told reporters, saying it had lasted roughly three hours.
"They have another one scheduled in the very near future," he said.
Trump's speech, not unusually for the US president, contained mixed messages on Iran: a combination both of bombastic threats but also assertions that a "deal" to end the fighting was also a realistic prospect.
"I have a big decision to make,” Trump had said during his speech earlier. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Finland's Stubb: Choose cooperation, and competition, over conflict
Finland's President Alexander Stubb told the audience that the world faced a "choice between cooperation and conflict."
He said that a third "c" was natural and should not cause concern, provided the right balance was struck.
"Competition will always be there. Nations compete now harder than they did a generation ago. This doesn't worry me. What does, is that more and more of them now compete against the rules on which the international order rests," Stubb said.
Stubb said he wanted to defend those rules and the spirit of cooperation and multilateralism underpinning them.
"Small nations need it to survive, and large nations need it to be great," said Stubb, president of a country with a population only around the size of the US state of South Carolina or the Chinese city of Jinan.
Stubb said the rules were the best ways to ensure "that competition does not escalate into conflict, and that cooperation gains ground."
Stubb cited a quote, that itself seemed a riff on another Winston Churchill adage, that's sometimes attributed to former US Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott: "Multilateralism is hell and can be a real pain in the neck, but it is the best option for humanity as a whole."
The Finnish president said that "currently, however, we appear to be going the other way — more towards a non-cooperative and multi-polar world order."
Though he said he see it might be tempting, particularly for larger powers, he called it a fundamentally "short-sighted approach" that "will turn against us, whether you represent a great power, a middle power, or a small state like Finland."
Lithuania's President Nauseda urges assembly not to forget Ukraine
The first Baltic leader to speak, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, began by delineating his country's plans to help defusing mines in the Strait of Hormuz or helping bring about the Gaza peace plan — but he urged the assembly not to forget the longer-running conflict closest to his home.
"Ladies and gentleman, the one conflict that poses the greatest threat to the world order is Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine," Nauseda said, even 12 years after it began with the annexation of Crimea and the beginnings of a Russian-backed uprising in eastern Ukraine.
In that time, Nauseda said, "Russia has escalated from clandestine operations and limited warfare in eastern Ukraine to massive military operations, mass killings, and ultimately the largest drone attacks against civilian infrastructure the world has ever seen."
He noted how the full-blown war, starting with Russia's February 2022 invasion, had now lasted longer than the first World War. Nauseda said that despite massive casualties, Russian progress had slowed to a snail's pace and Ukraine's culture, language and institutions stood tall.
Nauseda said that only a Ukrainian victory could safeguard ideals like the UN Charter.
"What we cannot allow is brute force prevailing over international law," he said. "We cannot tolerate any longer Moscow's colonial aspirations."
He said these aspirations reached far into "Europe, Africa and Asia," and said that no country should consider itself immune.
In Lithuania's case, he said Russia's war of aggression had led to "numerous violations of our airspace by combat drones," to intensified hybrid attacks, disinformation and sabotage efforts.
He said that where Russia advanced in opening this "new Pandora's box of new techniques for destablization, other hostile actors follow, learning new skills and ideas."
Qatar's emir says Gulf going through 'one of its most dangerous phases'
Qatar's Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said the current crisis in the Gulf "should come as no surprise to anyone" as he took to the podium in New York.
"It is the cumulative result of years of postponing crisis management through temporary solutions and unrealistic policies," he said of the war between the US and Iran which has sprawled to impact a series of Gulf states.
"At the heart of the dangerous situation we are witnessing lies an absence of a regional system of collective security," Al Thani said. "One that respects the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of states. One that promotes the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-interference in the internal affairs of states."
He said Qatar had recently called "from this very podium" for such a system and was now reiterating the appeal "after recent events have demonstrated the urgent need for it."
The emir said, without naming Iran or the US at any point in his address, that the absence of such a regional accord had allowed "one party to drag its neighbors into a war that is not theirs, targeting their vital assets and installations, despite their strenuous efforts to avert escalation."
Iran has sometimes struck targets in neighboring Gulf countries with close ties to the US.
Al Thani said that the restrictions on passage through the Strait of Hormuz amounted to the "lifelines of the global economy" being turned into bargaining chips, "with people on every continent bearing the cost, despite being far removed from the causes of the conflict."
The 46-year-old head of state said this was driving up prices not just for fuel but also for core other goods like food and medicine.

Erased by AI: Stanford swops Hispanic student for Black woman in campus photo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:56:26 UTC
17:56:26 KST

Erased by AI: Stanford swops Hispanic student for black woman in campus photo
Alan Blinder
- Stanford University used AI to alter a photo by replacing a Hispanic student with a Black woman and making others appear thinner, violating its own AI policy.
- The university acknowledged the mistake, promised additional training, and removed the altered banners.
- This incident highlights ongoing issues in higher education marketing where racial diversity is often misrepresented, sometimes through manipulated images to appear more inclusive.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Billy Ramirez had collected a plate of noodles at a Lunar New Year party in 2024 when a Stanford University photographer snapped a picture of him alongside two other students.
The university’s dining service posted the photo online the next day. But when Stanford used the image on banners last week, a black woman had replaced Ramirez. The other students’ appearances had been altered so that they appeared thinner.
“To see me erased like that so easily was kind of very upsetting,” Ramirez, who is Hispanic, said in an interview on Sept 22.
Ramirez, a senior who is majoring in human biology, said there was “a comedic element” to the matter. Nevertheless, he said he was frustrated by Stanford’s move, which he learnt about from a friend.
Stanford acknowledged in a statement on Sept 22 that it used artificial intelligence to change the original image.
“Stanford’s AI policy is clear: The use of AI in producing or altering images of Stanford people, events, research, facilities or achievements is strictly prohibited,” the university said.
“Both the alteration and lack of disclosure in this case violate that policy,” it added. “We are working with Residential and Dining Enterprises to provide additional training and ensure proper review of all materials.”
The other students in the original photograph – an Asian woman and a man Ramirez said was also of Hispanic descent – did not respond to e-mails.
The episode comes as colleges and universities, largely because of pressure from the Trump administration, are weighing how and whether to embrace diversity efforts on their campuses.
The New York Times reported in March that the Justice Department had begun examining admissions practices at Stanford’s medical school. The next month, the Education Department said it had opened an inquiry into whether Stanford illegally used race to discriminate in a teacher training programme.
The altered photo, first reported by The Stanford Review, also underscores how AI misuse is unfolding on campuses and the lengths to which some colleges and universities go to portray themselves as welcoming.
Not the first time
It is not the first time a school has ended up in a tempest over manipulated photography.
In 2000, for example, the University of Wisconsin-Madison drew criticism after it added a black student to the cover of its undergraduate application booklet; white students had filled the original image.
The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported then that the university would spend about US$64,000 – about US$123,000 (S$157,000) today – to reprint the booklets.
The 100,000 new brochures, the university decided, would instead feature a sunset photo of a popular spot on campus.
Nearly two decades later, York College of Pennsylvania removed two white students from a photograph for a billboard and replaced them with a man of Asian descent and a woman who was wearing a head covering that appeared to be religious in nature.
In statements published at the time by a television station, the college said the imagery reflected the college’s diversity, but that school officials “should have made a better decision” while under deadline pressure.
Overtly doctored imagery, however, is thought to be only a sporadic occurrence in higher education marketing materials.
More commonly, universities select or stage photos that suggest that their campuses are more diverse than they actually are.
In a study published in the Journal of Marketing for Higher Education in 2013, researchers found that schools’ recruitment materials often hinted that they enrolled more black students than they did.
After assessing demographic data about student bodies, the researchers also concluded that white and Asian people were over-represented in the images that were a part of the study.
Hispanic students were under-represented.
The study’s authors wrote that they did not believe the schools in their sample necessarily acted “unethically” by altering the photographs with software.
Rather, they wrote that they were “suggesting that the consistency at which institutions of higher education presented misleading depictions of racial diversity leads us to the understanding that it is intentional and near universal”.
They added: “It is clear that racial diversity is being used as a commodity in the marketing of higher education and presenting an image of diversity is more important than accurately portraying the student body.”
Enrolment records show that Stanford had 17,314 students in the autumn of 2025, and that 3,406 were American citizens or permanent residents who were classified in the university’s “under-represented minority” category. Another 4,431 were international students.
On Sept 22, Ramirez said he was sceptical that the altered picture had accurately represented the university’s student body.
He also said he had not heard from Stanford about the picture.
“I’m just a little surprised that a photo from years ago resurfaced,” he said.
Hours later, Stanford said it was removing the banners.
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Turkish first lady calls for shift from 'throwaway culture' to sustainable consumption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:56:03 UTC
17:56:03 KST

Orhan Onur Gemici
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan called on Wednesday for moving away from a "throwaway culture" centered on single-use products toward sustainable consumption based on long-lasting, durable goods.
Emine Erdogan, the wife of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and chair of the UN Secretary-General's Advisory Board of Eminent Persons on Zero Waste, spoke at the International Energy Agency (IEA) High-Level Energy Transition Dialogue at UN headquarters.
She said record temperatures, heat waves, wildfires, floods, and severe storms have become increasingly commonplace, linking them to growing energy demand driven by consumption and rising greenhouse gas emissions.
"We should not limit the issue of energy transition solely to the question: How can we produce more clean energy? We should first approach the issue by asking: Why do we have to produce more energy?" she said.
She argued that lasting solutions require addressing the root causes of waste, noting that energy, natural resources, and human labor are embedded in products that are eventually discarded.
The first lady cited global food waste as an example, saying food equivalent to 5.8 trillion plates is wasted annually and that the energy used in producing, packaging, preparing, preserving, and distributing it is also lost.
"Our primary concern should be to move away from a throwaway culture shaped around single-use products,” she stressed. “For the well-being of us all and for intergenerational justice, we must transition to a culture of sustainability shaped around long-lasting and durable products.”
Erdogan said production processes can be designed to prevent waste and discarded materials can be turned back into raw materials, describing nature as a model for circularity.
 
Türkiye's Zero Waste Project
She highlighted Türkiye's Zero Waste Project, launched in 2017, as a roadmap for energy and resource security.
"Türkiye is preparing for this transformation by accelerating our zero-waste practices and clean energy investments,” she said.
“Today, we rank fifth in Europe and 11th in the world in terms of installed renewable energy capacity,” she said. “By 2035, we aim to increase our installed solar and wind power capacity to 120,000 megawatts.”
Erdogan said Ankara wants to further advance the zero-waste approach as part of its action agenda for the UN Climate Change Conference COP31, which it will host in November.
"Zero waste is the most powerful path opening the door to genuine transformation in every field, from production to consumption," she added.
Following her remarks, a roundtable meeting was held with the participation of Turkish Cabinet ministers and other officials.

Flags over Spitsbergen. What Arctic Biennale Expedition leaves on archipelago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:55:28 UTC
17:55:28 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS Correspondents Konstantin Malykh, Maria Kartuz/. The Arctic Biennale art and scientific got to the Spitsbergen Archipelago onboard the Professor Molchanov scientific-research vessel. Despite the alarming situation around Norway's arrest of the ship, over a week on the archipelago, participants in the project, organized by Alexander Ponomarev's Free Elements Arts Center, were working on all the planned installations. This material by TASS is about what the artists left in Barentsburg and with what they were leaving the archipelago.
This story has no global analogues yet. Never before have artists, scientists, philosophers, and public figures embarked on a journey to explore the Arctic waters. The project's geography fascinates imagination with its high latitudes locations - Spitsbergen, Franz Josef Land, and the North Pole - these are just some points on the map that the biennale has planned.
"One of our mottos is "Mobile Within Mobile," because this is movement, process, action...," the expedition's leader, artist Alexander Ponomarev said.
Traveling to the Arctic
The traveling began early in the morning in Moscow, when the expedition participants got onto a big bus and departed for Murmansk. The trip was two days with an overnight accommodation in Petrozavodsk. The artists did not waste time and made quick sketches during short stops. Styles differ: while Katya Sergeeva was drawing with almost photographic precision, Karina Batrachenko used lines and geometric shapes.
The Professor Molchanov departed on the expedition from Murmansk at night. The voyage was due to be about three days long. The passengers quickly coped with the rolling (got "rolled up," as sailors say), and the expedition work continued. Oceanographers Sergey Pisarev and Alexey Sokov told everyone about the seas they are passing, explained why water in those sees did not freeze up, and shared curious and smart stories. Artists Marina Belova and Alexei Politov were particularly impressed by a story about the experiment to relocate penguins to the Far North. They call themselves "penguins of the world" and were taking to Spitsbergen a light installation dedicated to these symbols of the Antarctica. It was to be installed in the Barentsburg Museum (the center of Russia's presence in Spitsbergen), and, artists hoped, it would correct the unfair situation that their beloved pets were not represented in the Arctic.
The Prowling Art Group, having received the captain's permission, was installing a big dark figure on the forecastle (the front of the ship) - that was a visual part of their Pilot project, which was to be installed on the shore later on. According to Daria Dogaeva, their pilot could find ways when all regular landmarks cannot be seen. However, the Professor Molchanov's crew did not need help - after three and a half days of travel, the ship docked at Spitsbergen.
Arts shore
It took about three to four days to install most of the objects. The archipelago has many restrictions due to the fragile Arctic environment: whatever temporary objects further on must disappear without a trace, and whatever remaining installations must fit seamlessly the laconic architecture and strict regulations. One of such objects was the Arrow of Time by architect Totan Kuzembaev at Cape Heer. The object, which is based on a crane boom and coils from cables, is about time, memory, the Arctic's industrial development and present.
The Doomsday Light Storage Facility will remain in the Barentsburg coal mine. The installation by Vladimir Nasedkin and Tatiana Badanina consists of two parts: the first part is two four-meter-high snow-white figures on a mountain that "collect" light. The second part is five massive sarcophagi, where the collected light is "stored". The authors explained: it's not about just the lighting, it is about the light, love and warmth that are inside every person - if suddenly they disappear off the face of the Earth, their supply for new generations will remain available underground.
Marina Rin, the biennale curator, installed a "stone" whale on debris of the old whaling yard at Cape Finneset. According to her, this is a topo-myth - a legend predicting the Arctic Biennale: "The whale's shape is that of an ancient rock, on which all our projects are drawn in petroglyphs," Marina explained.
Giant flags are fluttering on that cape. This is Alexander Ponomarev's Telegraph of Momentary Joy. It is installed on the communications tower's remaining fragments. The colored flags resemble polar poppies, as they are turning the radio station debris into a live communication line between land and sea, into flashes of light in the coming polar night.
The Observatory is another "communication point" for the biennale term. This is a pavilion assembled on the shore from a huge old fuel barrel and road concrete slabs, where the roof is an openwork structure resembling the famous Shukhov Tower. Over the expedition, it was an exhibition space, and later on it will become an observation deck for Barentsburg's residents and visitors.
Artist Katerina Kovaleva found herself into a difficult situation. Her project - The Camp of Lost Expeditions - was planned for the abandoned village of Piramida. There is no road to there, and the only way to get to the village is by water from Barentsburg, while the arrested Professor Molchanov was still chained to the dock. However, Spitsbergen is a special territory. The locals say, wishes made here do come true. So, here is Katerina uploading the installation into a helicopter, heading for the old village. On the return flight, she brought photos and impressions.
"In an abandoned dining room in Piramida now there is a Camp of Lost Expeditions. I have fixed a parachute under the ceiling. On it there are three schooners of the Brusilov, Sedov and Rusanov expeditions. Their fate was tragic. Under the dome, I laid a table for 40 people: metal bowls, glasses covered with granite "bread". The table is ready, but no one will sit at it," the artist said.
Interestingly, it was thanks to Katerina that Otto Schmidt's personal belongings were brought to Spitsbergen for the first time. The artist has received them from the famous polar explorer's great-grandchildren. "Unfortunately," she said, "I couldn't bring many more, and some of the items will be presented during the Arctic Biennale's second stage."
During the biennale week, in small Barentsburg everything was literally filled with art. Even the word was visualized in an art object by artist Sergey Katran. There is no word for "art" in the Russian-Nenets dictionary. The artist asked native speakers to find new words for "art." They came up with neologisms like "valeybzo", "paskoyvava", "hale of the year". The artist recorded the new words' sound vibrations and depicted them as ice figures. The material, imitating ice, highlights the language vulnerability and the risk of its disappearance, the author said.
The expedition participants brought about 30 new art objects to Barentsburg. In addition to earlier mentioned objects, those were The Ear of God by Vladimir Chernyshev, The Rooks Have Arrived by Nikolay Polissky, The Extract of Joy by Evgeny Sautkin, The Art-Arctic by Sergey Serov, Is It Really Me? By Katya Sergeeva, The Wasteland by Karina Batrachenko, The Germination by Anna Lapshinova, The Room by Yulia Nemova, We Hear Through the Wind by the Prowling Art Group, The Imaginary Museum by Katerina Kovaleva, a capsule collection of Arctic Linen by Katerina Terekhova, and The Cover by Alexander Konstantinov.
The Arktikatarsis installation by Vladimir Kuzmin was the project's symbolic unifying line. The work created from mining helmets on the village's main observation deck was based on the most recognizable architectural proportion: the golden ratio. "The symbol of labor in Barentsburg becomes part of the artistic idea and designates differently this place in the Arctic landscape," the artist said.
Right on the last day of the artists' visit to the archipelago, they opened the most complex and big-scale object - The Drunken Ship by Alexander Ponomarev. The composition, about 20 m high, is a system of masts, yards and sails on a sloop mounted on a port crane boom. The structure is made of the so-called thrown timber. "These logs have traveled a long and mysterious route in salt water. They have become strong and durable, like art that has passed many challenges," the Arctic Biennale's leader Alexander Ponomarev said.
The first part of the Arctic Biennale in Spitsbergen finished on time, despite the Professor Molchanov's arrest. All participants in the expedition have returned home safely, and now they are preparing expositions for the next stage, which is scheduled for December in Nizhny Novgorod at the branch of the Pushkin State Fine Arts Museum (Arsenal).

Last Friday morning, the Emergency Response Center was once again notified that a fox was running around the third floor of the parking garage at the Viru shopping center in Tallinn.

China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:54:00 UTC
17:54:00 KST

China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
September 23, 2026
For decades, China has faced accusations from the United States and the European Union of stealing their technology.
From robotics and advanced semiconductors to precision engineering and automotive parts, Chinese firms have recruited top engineers, allegedly spied on Western rivals and been linked to cyberattacks aimed at gaining access to valuable trade secrets.
It is perhaps ironic, then, that China is now taking steps to prevent its own high-end technologies and talent from escaping abroad.
China's Great Wall around its top brains
Last week, new entry-exit rules took effect, giving Chinese authorities the power to stop engineers, founders and other specialists from leaving the country if their expertise in batteries, rare earths or artificial intelligence (AI) is judged a threat to "industrial and technological security."
Recently, China has also tightened outbound-investment rules, cracked down on Chinese nationals holding their wealth offshore and restricted the posting of technical staff overseas.
Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University (SMU), believes that, taken together, the curbs "offer a rare glimpse into the true state of China's economy."
"These measures suggest that Beijing is deeply concerned about economic weakness and substantial capital outflows," Gao told DW, adding that authorities are also determined to stop "entrepreneurs and skilled personnel from leaving the country."
The strain on China's economy is increasingly hard to hide. While demand for exports remains strong — especially for high-tech goods — the country's property crash has severely weakened domestic consumption.
Bank lending fell to a record low over the summer, and new car sales in August dropped nearly a quarter year-on-year.
Beijing blocks deals, founders seek exit
The same anxiety now extends to people and money leaving. The most prominent recent example is Manus, an AI startup created by two Chinese nationals in Beijing. Last year, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore, partly to avoid US investment curbs and expand into global markets.
When Facebook owner Meta tried to acquire Manus last December for $2 billion (€1.74 billion), Beijing blocked the move and barred the firm's two founders from leaving the country.
Just this month, Chinese social media has been awash with rumors that Huawei founder and CEO Ren Zhengfei and his daughter, CFO Meng Wanzhou, may have left the country.
The claims were picked up by Taiwanese and Indian media outlets. On Wednesday, however, Chinese-language media shared a photo of Ren in Shenzhen a day earlier, signing a cooperation deal with a Chinese automaker.
Wealthy Chinese struggle to get capital out
Bloomberg Intelligence estimated that some $1 trillion in Chinese wealth had exited the country last year — the largest amount of "hot money" leaving since 2006, when records began.
Beijing has not tightened its annual $50,000 foreign-exchange quota that households may take out of the country. What has tightened, says Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at French investment bank Natixis, are the unofficial routes the wealthy used around that cap.
"They haven't changed the $50,000 quota. They are now squeezing the people and agents that money usually travels with," Garcia-Herrero told DW.
An entire industry has grown up, in China and abroad, to help people get themselves and their capital out. Emigration agents arrange visas and relocations, while offshore brokers and trusts help Chinese nationals to park wealth overseas.
Companies sometimes use a foreign subsidiary, a listing or a staff posting to take money and know-how out together.
New rules may spur workarounds
SMU's Gao believes the new curbs may prove counterproductive, as the more difficult it becomes to move capital or people abroad, the greater the incentive for those with the means to find other ways out.
"Over time, that could further erode confidence, accelerate capital flight and deepen the very economic problems the measures are intended to contain," Gao told DW.
Garcia-Herrero, meanwhile, thinks the block on talent will matter more than the squeeze on capital.
"You can still move money slowly, with approvals," she told DW. "You cannot easily replace a process engineer who cannot board a plane — or who will not take an overseas job because of an indefinite ban."
AI talent now needs permission to fly
The risk is already hitting China's AI firms, which are fast catching up with their US rivals in the race to produce the most advanced AI systems.
In May, Bloomberg reported that Chinese authorities now required top AI researchers, founders and executives at firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to obtain approval before traveling abroad.
Last year, some DeepSeek staff were asked to hand in their passports, according to tech news site The Information. Beijing has neither confirmed nor denied the practice.
Bloomberg reported in January last year that other tech engineers face similar pressure, including those helping foreign firms cut their reliance on China by building factories in Vietnam and India.
Lawyers and officials tighten legal advice
For foreign nationals, both Chinese and foreign firms sometimes disguise a working visit to China to avoid scrutiny and visa delays. They may suggest a trip is for tourism, business meetings or a factory tour rather than actual work.
Ahead of the new curbs, international law firms like DLA Piper advised companies to keep visa filings "truthful" and "complete," warning that a mismatch between the paperwork and the actual work could now mean an entry ban of up to five years.
The new rules state that a visitor should, in principle, be told if they are banned. However, Chinese authorities may withhold notification if it "may affect national security or the investigation of criminal cases."
In an updated travel advisory earlier this month, the US State Department went further, warning Americans to "exercise increased caution in mainland China due to ... the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru
Editor's note: This article was first published on September 23, 2026 and was updated shortly after to reflect new reporting on the whereabouts of Huawei's founder.

Airbus seeks space collaboration with Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:53:55 UTC
17:53:55 KST

Airbus Defense and Space seeks to expand its collaboration with Türkiye to benefit from the country’s existing satellite expertise and to accelerate domestic technological capabilities.
Carlo Mirra, sales director of Airbus’ corporate business growth and development unit, told Anadolu that the company monitors Türkiye’s expanding focus and growing industrial capacity in the space sector.
Mirra said the aerospace ties between the firm and Türkiye could expand further via direct industrial collaboration or intergovernmental agreements involving Türkiye, the European Space Agency (ESA), the European Commission, or Airbus’ founding nations.
These discussions came to the fore as Türkiye prepares to host the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) in the southwestern city of Antalya under the coordination of the Industry and Technology Ministry and the Turkish Space Agency, with Anadolu serving as global communications partner.
Mirra expressed strong excitement about the event, noting that he has never visited Antalya before.
Mirra noted that he began working with the IAC and the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) in 1989 and currently chairs the federation’s industrial relations committee while managing ESA business relations at Airbus.
“I'm dealing primarily with European business, although I have a past in international business, especially in the US; nevertheless, we are observing here the rapid growth of the political attention and also industrial capacity in Türkiye, and as you know, our company in particular has been present in Türkiye for quite a while,” he said.
“The release of the National Space Program, the space plan, the flight of the astronauts, the ambition to have independent access to space are all important messages that the current political administration in Türkiye are giving in order to let the local industry develop and also emerge in the international environment,” he added.
Mirra stated that the IAC serves as a springboard to achieve this goal, with over 1,800 abstracts already submitted by Turkish institutions for the technical conference.
“This is providing a direct channel for Turkish researchers and industries also to present their technologies, the progress of their studies, to a truly international environment – from green propulsion to small satellite architectures, I think that this will be a very interesting confrontation for all of them,” he said.
He noted that both established firms and startups will meet international prime contractors and investors during the event.
He emphasized that establishing space diplomacy leadership is key, adding that hosting IAC 2026 demonstrates credibility in operating within a global environment.
“Türkiye is really committed to play a major role in this area, and this is proven also by the organization and investment into these events, and I think that this is providing, in terms of international cooperation, in terms of space sustainability and security, a very strong message in order to reinforce existing relationships and create new ones,” he said.
 
Türkiye has resources, manpower to develop capacity
 
Mirra highlighted that Türkiye boasts a population of 85 million people with an average age of 33, contrasting sharply with aging European demographics.
“This is a phenomenal potential to educate the space engineers and the scientists of the next decade – you have the resources (and) the manpower to develop this capacity,” he said.
“Europe is aging fast, we have ambitions in terms of programs, but the difficulty is in finding and educating qualified engineers,” he added.
Mirra noted that Türkiye’s capacity to cultivate motivated experts will fuel its long-term economic and technological objectives.
“And I'm sure that a conference like the IAC will have a very positive effect, especially with students and young generations,” he added.
Mirra stated that Airbus representatives in Ankara work at their permanent office to advance partnership-focused models.
He confirmed that negotiations with the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TUBITAK) remain underway.
“I observe three to four areas – there are some where the cooperation may be more direct and involved, certainly in lunar exploration,” he said, referring to ongoing talks between Airbus and TUBITAK on lunar exploration, human spaceflight, and satellite communications.
Mirra noted that Airbus played a key role in boosting capacity through the Turksat satellite program, where the aerospace giant aims to broaden its footprint.
“That is certainly an area where we would like to maintain the relationship and possibly also broaden that, either as a sort of industrial cooperation, but also under a government-to-government partnership – you know, if there is a Turkish government, for example, making a deal with the European Commission or with ESA or with some of the mother countries of Airbus, namely France, Germany, Spain, and UK, that is certainly something where we have an interest, so that is a development that we are observing with a lot of attention,” he added.

Von der Leyen says Hungary 'strengthened rule of law', unlocks €4.2bn in EU funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:53:52 UTC
17:53:52 KST

The European Commission has unlocked €4.2 billion in cohesion funds for Hungary and reopened Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe access, after PM Péter Magyar's government met EU rule-of-law conditions. Brussels froze the funds in 2022 over corruption and procurement concerns under the Orbán government.
The European Commission has unfrozen €4.2 billion in previously blocked cohesion funds for Hungary, judging that Budapest has addressed earlier rule-of-law breaches. The move also clears the way for Hungary to rejoin the Erasmus+ student exchange programme and the Horizon Europe research funding initiative.
In 2022, the EU suspended €6.3 billion in cohesion funding to Hungary under the conditionality mechanism, citing shortcomings in the country's anti-corruption framework, conflicts of interest, and systemic irregularities in public procurement.
Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who won a landslide election victory in April, had campaigned on a promise to unlock EU funds suspended during Viktor Orbán's 16-year rule.
"Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the Union's financial interests," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
"Today, we are proposing to unlock €4.2 billion and reopen the doors of Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe to Hungarian students and researchers. I am glad that they will once again fully benefit from the opportunities our Union creates. This shows that reforms deliver results."
In May, Magyar and von der Leyen agreed to release €16.4 billion in EU funding on the condition that the country met key rule-of-law milestones. In total, Hungary was required to deliver on 27 so-called "super milestones" and more than 100 others.
In late August, Hungary announced it had met all of the conditions, including resolving the situation surrounding public interest trusts (KEKVA) — a legal structure the previous government had used to take control of public institutions such as universities.
Beyond the €4.2 billion released, Hungary is also seeking to withdraw €10 billion in recovery funds; the Commission's assessment of that request is ongoing.
A further €2 billion in cohesion funding remains blocked over concerns about the asylum system, child protection law, and academic freedom. Magyar has pledged to resolve these issues by the end of the year.

Belgium faces worst drought in decades as water levels fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:49:44 UTC
17:49:44 KST

Melike Pala
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Belgium is facing its driest period in decades, with prolonged rainfall shortages raising concerns over drinking water production, particularly in Brussels, according to the Royal Meteorological Institute (KMI).
The country is facing a significant precipitation deficit, with around 80% of its territory affected, KMI meteorologist Pascal Mormal told public broadcaster VRT on Wednesday.
The situation is particularly severe in southern Belgium, while some areas of West Flanders and Limburg have recorded closer-to-normal rainfall levels.
In Uccle, a Brussels municipality where the KMI maintains a long-term observation station, only around 21 to 22 millimeters of rain is expected this month, compared with a normal monthly average of about 65 millimeters.
Mormal said no substantial rainfall is expected in the short term, with significant precipitation potentially not arriving until November.
"For such a long, uninterrupted period of drought, we have to go all the way back to the 1970s," Mormal said, adding that the current situation is comparable to the drought of 2018 but could worsen if the dry conditions continue.
The prolonged drought is also affecting water production.
Vivaqua, the company responsible for supplying drinking water to Brussels and several municipalities in Wallonia and Flanders, may have to further reduce water extraction at its Profondeville facility along the Meuse River.
The facility accounts for around 30% of Vivaqua's water supply.
The drought is also affecting municipalities across the Wallonia Region.
Restrictions on drinking water consumption are currently in place in 17 municipalities, while tanker trucks have been deployed in Libramont, in the Luxembourg province, to help secure local water supplies.
In Flanders, authorities have so far maintained a code-yellow drought alert, calling for increased vigilance without introducing additional measures.
Meteorologists expect wetter conditions in November and December, but officials caution that prolonged, steady rainfall will be needed to replenish depleted water resources.
Heavy downpours alone may not be sufficient, as much of the water can run off rapidly rather than replenish groundwater and other reserves.

waiting for promotions to come.

However, over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be.
