====================================================================================================

‘powerful designs keep asking questions’ next gen winner maria gil on craft and identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:30:27 UTC
17:30:27 KST

MARIA GIL WINS DESIGNEUROPA NEXT GENERATION DESIGN AWARD
designboom speaks with Polish designer Maria Gil, winner of the DesignEuropa Next Generation Design Award honoring emerging talent in European product design. Still at a young age, Gil has already achieved major milestones, building her body of work on self-directed curiosity and hands-on manufacturing. After studying in London and Italy, she returned home to Poland to establish her design identity with loud, expressive objects that serve as an invitation to open, reflective conversations.
‘I think the most valuable out of this whole experience, is realizing that the most powerful designs are the ones that keep asking questions, even after they’re finished, and open room for a conversation instead of being just a monologue,’ Gil starts the interview.
designboom in conversation with Maria Gil, winner of the DesignEuropa Next Generation Design Award | all images courtesy of DesignEuropa Award
EXPRESSING UNTOLD STORIES THROUGH MATERIAL AND FORM
The DesignEuropa Next Generation Design Award celebrates young and emerging designers across diverse creative disciplines in Europe. Before receiving this award, Maria Gil experienced living and studying across Poland, London, and Italy, developing a multifaceted approach to design. This global trajectory helped define her personal creative identity while deepening her understanding of how history influences contemporary objects.
‘London is such a multicultural environment, introducing you to a range of attitudes all at once. When there are so many diverse voices, you’re inspired to explore your own identity. I gained so much knowledge about foreign design history, especially Italian heritage during my exchange in Milan, that I felt ashamed to admit I knew barely anything about Polish design history. I decided to take a journey around Poland and its most focal points regarding craft and design to see everything up close. That’s where I realized that one puzzle was missing, one that in Italy was my favorite moment – postmodernism,’ explains the designer.
integrating LED lighting along its central framework, the Fan Lamp extends traditional fan geometry into a functional object
Immersed in Italian cultural legacy, Gil discovered a desire to reconnect with her background, turning her move back home into a reality. Reconnecting with Poland offered both conceptual inspiration and raw material for her projects.
‘Being able to express untold stories using something seemingly as straightforward as a piece of furniture was something I didn’t realise was possible,’ Gil tells designboom. ‘My guiding rule is to not create things that already exist. That doesn’t mean inventing for the sake of novelty but rather shifting the conversation towards meaning. I don’t want to add more meaningless objects to the world.’
Post War Wardrobe emerged as an unexpected outcome of Gil’s experimental creative process
FROM SELF-PRODUCTION TO INDUSTRY COLLABORATION
Limited local resources, unlike those available in Italy or the UK, prompted a nationwide study across Poland to observe surviving craft and design traditions. Her key finding was the absence of a Polish postmodernist movement, a stark contrast to Italian Radical Design, long considered a major reference in design history. The inquiry into why this movement never emerged, and what form it might have taken, was developed into the designer’s thesis project Post War Wardrobe.
The broader experience earned her valuable industry contacts and new opportunities. After winning a design contest made by the fashion brand House of Errors with a sketch for her All Seeing Chair, Gil was challenged to bring the physical piece to life under a fast-paced studio routine, an effort that subsequently earned her top honors at the Young Furniture Exhibition.
These wins provided the validation she needed, reinforcing her confidence to push her work further, as Gil reflects: ‘ I almost didn’t submit my sketch of the All-Seeing Chair because I genuinely thought it was so obvious, that everyone must have thought of it too. I didn’t think it stood any chance for any of the prizes and yet it was recognized,’ she continues. ‘But recognizing that pattern forced me to follow my intuition now. I’ve stopped fighting that feeling and started trusting it instead.’
the All Seeing Chair earned early competition success, opening key doors for Gil’s practice
Her career has grown steadily since. In 2025, Gil showcased her work at SaloneSatellite during Salone del Mobile, an opportunity that gave her firsthand insight into how the broader design industry operates. ‘For Salone Satellite, I knew I had to recreate my prototypes to the highest possible level to match the gravity of the fair. The process, however, was hardly creative but rather administrative, logistical and simply physical. It taught me, more than any studio project ever could, how much organizational effort it takes to be a successful designer,’ she shares.
What was once a simple desire for visibility quickly took physical shape, connecting Gil to an international community and solidifying her role within the design market. The transition to production and sales was quickly recognized as an unforeseen challenge. Administrative tasks were seen as a strain on creative output, making the need for manufacturer collaborations evident over self-production.
Zyranball repurposes table tennis balls into a chandelier fixture
A year later, Gil returned to the fair to launch a sofa designed for Nicoletti Home. The experience marked a clear shift in her practice: with manufacturing and production handled in collaboration with the brand, she poured her energy directly into the core design, allowing for a far more focused creative process and engaging with the fair from an entirely new perspective.
‘At the fair I got to experience the other major aspect to the more commercial side of the industry which is that instead of reaching only a handful of collectors, you get to have a meaningful impact on a wider audience. And it’s the direction I want to explore further, collaborations that turn ideas into impact,’ Gil shares.
Maria Gil’s Fan Lamp reimagines traditional fan making as a contemporary lighting fixture
New designs often need intellectual property protection to prevent copying. When unauthorized reproductions of Gil’s work surfaced online, having her designs registered gave her a clear way to respond. What could have been a setback became, instead, confirmation of how far her design resonance had reached.
‘I have to say that after moving countries twice, I’ve come to see registering my work as part of the creative process itself,‘ she reflects. ‘I’ve registered some of my work in the UK and through the EU Design system, and each time it’s felt like an investment in my identity as a designer, a way of standing behind what I create. My pieces often involve unusual techniques, and registering them early gives me the confidence to keep experimenting and putting new work out into the world.‘
furniture where emotional and cultural resonance matter as much as physical durability
The DesignEuropa Next Generation Design Award marks a pivotal moment in Gil’s career, affirming the maturity of her process. The recognition provides a foundation for future collaborations, establishing trust while allowing her visual identity to adapt and diversify.
‘As a young designer, I know my ‘signature’ is still taking shape and I’m genuinely excited to see how collaborations will evolve it. I think working with others has the potential to make my work much more diverse. That’s why receiving the DesignEuropa Next Generation Design Award matters to me so much. I hope it works as a kind of stamp of approval that reassures clients that behind the bold ideas, there’s a deliberate process,’ notes the young designer.
expressive forms reflect Gil’s desire for her furniture to provoke conversation and emotional response
Influenced by diverse design traditions, Gil balances immediate emotional impact with long-term cultural endurance. Looking ahead, her creative vision uses loud, provocative forms to address present uncertainty while building a quiet, enduring legacy:
‘I believe my work reflects that nothing is certain today. We’re not certain about the future, nor are we certain about what’s even true in the present. Through my designs, I question and invite reflection and maybe that’s why I want them to be loud now. Today, I want my work to provoke, to make people feel something,’ Maria Gil concludes. But a century from now? I wouldn’t mind if they felt nothing extraordinary. Today we look at steam-bent chairs or flat-pack furniture as ordinary when a hundred years ago they were radical. It would be an honour to create things so present now that they leave a quiet legacy later,’ Maria Gil concludes.

award: Next Generation Design Award 2026
 organizer: DesignEuropa Awards 
designer: Maria Gil | @maria_______gil

Erdoğan urges UN to abolish Security Council veto power ahead of General Assembly address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:30:18 UTC
17:30:18 KST

Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan argued that Turkey is an indispensable part of European security architecture. Turkey has been a NATO member since 1952 but its EU accession process has been frozen for nearly a decade.
"A Europe that excludes Turkey from its security architecture cannot possibly be stronger or safer," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, seeking a more central role for his country in European security as trans-Atlantic relations remain strained under the Trump administration.
"As an integral part of Europe, our country plays a significant role in ensuring the welfare and security of the European continent," he said, referencing the NATO summit Ankara hosted in July as a "concrete manifestation" of Turkey's commitment.
"We are shaping our future with the European Union precisely through this strategic vision, and we expect the same vision from the European Union as well."
Erdoğan has repeated the same stance since at least April 2025, when he told the Antalya Diplomacy Forum that "It has become clear once again that European security is unthinkable without Turkey."
"Turkey is ready to take responsibility for European security in the future as well," he said at the time.
Europe's indispensable partner
NATO member Turkey has been positioning itself as an indispensable partner as the White House signals that Europe must take greater responsibility for its own security, including in Ukraine, where Russia's all-out war has continued well into its fifth year.
As the leader of the vast Mediterranean country of some 88 million with NATO's second-largest military and a substantial domestic defence industry, Erdoğan has preserved relations with both Kyiv and Moscow throughout the war, serving as a Black Sea broker.
"First and foremost, we are compelled to change the current mindset where international law is applied differently to the strong versus to the weak," Erdoğan said in his speech.
"Secondly, whenever international efforts fall short in resolving crises, we must harness regional ownership as an effective means of addressing those issues," he added.
"As Turkey, whenever we have acted upon this principle, as in the case of the Black Sea Grain Corridor, we have achieved results, and we have contributed to both regional and global security."
According to Erdoğan, cooperation and open diplomacy are at the core of the world's future.
"History has shown us time and again through bitter experiences that there is no winner in a political approach which is built on mistrust," he emphasised.
In his speech at UN headquarters in New York, the Turkish president also discussed his relationship with his US counterpart Donald Trump.
"I believe that our relations with the United States will flourish in every field during President Trump's second term, also with the contribution of our close friendship with him," Erdoğan said.
Turkey applied for European Union membership in 1987, but the accession process has been stalled since 2018.
A European Parliament report last year said the process could not be relaunched in current circumstances despite Turkey's geopolitical importance, citing the arrest of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, the crackdown on protests and broader democratic backsliding.
Reform the Security Council, Erdoğan says
On the UN Security Council, Erdoğan called for fundamental reform, arguing the current structure was no longer fit for purpose.
"The United Nations, established 81 years ago to maintain peace and security, has become unable to fulfil this mission, or rather, it has been made unable to do so," he said.
"Let's recognise that a system in which the will of more than 190 countries is subject to the whims of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust."
Erdoğan proposed abolishing the veto power held by the five permanent members — the US, Russia, China, the UK and France — and replacing the current structure with a council whose members the General Assembly elects for fixed terms, with no permanent seats.
"The Security Council must absolutely be reformed in accordance with the principle that the world is bigger than five," Erdoğan said.
Towards the end of his speech, the Turkish president stated that his country will "not remain silent in the face of injustice, and we’ll never consent to oppression."
"When we look at the course of the world today, we can see that there are two paths before us," he said.
"Either we’ll deepen uncertainty through fear, through conflict and isolation, or we’ll build the future together through justice, solidarity and common will."
"Of course, it is easy to punch darkness, what is difficult is to light a candle that will dispel that darkness," Erdoğan said.
"Turkey has chosen the second path, and hopefully we’ll follow it with patience," he concluded.

Opinion
Hong Kong needs social science to help deliver on its 5-year plan
Universities and academics can contribute the evidence needed to turn these commitments into better decisions
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Michael (Jinghan) Zeng is head of and a professor in the Department of Public and International Affairs at City University of Hong Kong. 
Hong Kong’s first five-year plan gives its universities an opportunity to show what their research can do for the city. Its ambitions for technology, regional development and international cooperation depend on decisions about institutions and people’s lives. Social scientists should help shape those decisions from the outset.
The blueprint explicitly addresses public governance, including civil service performance, departmental coordination and digital administration. It also provides for monitoring and assessment. Universities can contribute the evidence needed to turn these commitments into better decisions.
Artificial intelligence offers an immediate opportunity. The policy address has announced a HK$300 million (US$38.24 million) AI for Welfare Lab and proposes requirements for bidders on public-facing government AI projects to submit safety and ethics declarations.

Alibaba’s AI push reaches deeper into Europe with new cloud regions and data centres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:29:55 UTC
17:29:55 KST

Alibaba has announced plans for new data centres in Europe, alongside a more powerful AI chip and plans for much larger Qwen models at its annual flagship.
Alibaba is expanding its overseas data centres to Europe, the Chinese tech giant announced Wednesday at its annual conference.
The company said it would "establish its first cloud regions" in Finland, the Netherlands and Turkey, while expanding its data centre footprint in Germany, France, the United Arab Emirates, Malaysia and Hong Kong over the next 12 months.
“Today, the total volume of Machine Thinking is less than 3% of all Human Thinking,” said Eddie Wu, CEO of Alibaba Group.
He suggested machine thinking could eventually grow to 1,000 times human capacity.
“With this in mind, our target is that by 2032, the global data centre capacity operated by Alibaba Cloud will surpass 20GW, fueling the industry’s exponentially rising demand for AI,” Wu said.
The expansion will further increase Alibaba Cloud's global computing capacity, the company said in an announcement.
Alibaba is one of the frontrunners in China's artificial intelligence (AI) industry, with its Qwen models among the world's most downloaded AI models.
Wu said on Tuesday that it will further expand its AI’s capacity with five to ten trillion parameters, which would make it several times bigger than the current largest Chinese model.
China’s push for homegrown AI chips amid US restrictions
The Chinese tech giant also unveiled a new AI chip at the conference, which Wu called “the most powerful AI chip in China today”.
Alibaba’s new Zhenwu V900 chip, widely believed to be twice as powerful as Nvidia’s H20 designed for China, comes amid US efforts to curb China’s AI progress.
Washington’s longstanding export controls have restricted access to advanced chips, prompting Beijing to urge Chinese companies to use domestic alternatives.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to meet in Washington this week, with trade tensions, chip restrictions and AI threats to national security expected to feature in their talks.

Alpaca migration: Woolly travellers make their way down from the Swiss Alps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:29:38 UTC
17:29:38 KST

Around 70 alpacas leave their summer pasture in the Bernese Alps and make their way down to Switzerland's Kiental valley.
The video shows the herd being counted, called together and guided across bridges and along a narrow mountain road.
They pass cows and a postal bus before reaching the valley, where they are loaded into livestock lorries bound for their winter farm near Aeschi.
The Luginbuhl family has bred llamas in Switzerland for 30 years and began raising alpacas in 2000. The herd is kept mainly for breeding and wool, while some are selected for meat.
The breeder says the alpacas have adapted well to the Swiss mountains, whose conditions resemble those in South America.

For the first time in a decade, more Europeans travel by train than by bus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:28:39 UTC
17:28:39 KST

Cars remain Europe's top way to travel. However, trains have overtaken buses for the first time in a decade, while planes grew fastest of any mode of transport over the same period.
Planes, trains and cars... Are Europeans changing how they get around?
According to the latest Eurostat data, the answer appears to be yes, albeit slowly. Nevertheless, cars remain by far the continent's favourite way to travel.
Cars carried 69.2% of all passenger travel across the EU in 2024. That's still overwhelmingly the most common way to get around, but it's a share that's been slowly shrinking.
For the first time since 2014, trains have overtaken buses, coaches and trolleybuses. Rail edged ahead to 7.5% of all travel, just past buses at 7.3%.
It's a modest crossover; both modes still trail cars by a wide margin, but it's a milestone that hasn't happened in a decade. Sea travel remained the smallest slice of all, largely unchanged at 0.4%.
Look back a full decade, and the picture sharpens considerably. No mode of transport grew faster than air travel, up 3.6 percentage points since 2014.
That's well clear of rail's smaller 0.9-point gain over the same period, a second, quieter shift running alongside the trains-over-buses milestone making headlines now.
Cars, meanwhile, gave up 2.9 points over the decade, and buses lost 1.3. Put together, the direction is unmistakable. Fewer journeys are happening by road, and more by rail and by air, even as cars keep their commanding lead over everything else.
How travel habits vary by country
Zoom into individual countries, and the EU-wide averages break apart into very different national stories.
Lithuanians rely on cars more than anyone else in the EU, with 83.7% of all their travel happening on the road. The Netherlands (77%) and Finland (over 75%) aren't far behind, all three among the bloc's most car-dependent nations.
Flying, meanwhile, is close to a way of life in Croatia, where it accounts for nearly half of all travel, 45.6%, likely a byproduct of its island geography and heavy reliance on tourism. Bulgaria (30.3%) and Cyprus (25.3%) also rank among the EU's most air-dependent countries, for similar reasons.
Rail carries the most weight in Hungary, at 11.3% of all travel, and Austria, just over 10%. Buses hold their strongest ground in Malta, Ireland and Hungary, all countries where rail networks are comparatively limited.
As for sea travel, it's the island and coastal nations that lead the way: Estonia, Malta and Croatia, though even there it remains a small fraction of overall travel.

Fake videos spread fraud claims during German elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:28:27 UTC
17:28:27 KST

Videos falsely claimed the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) was omitted from postal ballots or that votes were destroyed, echoing tactics previously used by the pro-Russian influence network Storm-1516.
Fake videos alleging widespread election fraud in Germany are ultimately tied to a pro-Russian influence network, which shared posts online ahead of two key elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The footage purported to show postal ballots for the AfD being destroyed or the party being omitted from ballot papers altogether.
However, the videos, which garnered hundreds of thousands of views on X, clearly differed from official voting materials.
Some videos were amplified by accounts known to spread pro-Russian theories and resembled false election-fraud content previously linked to Storm-1516, an influence network attributed to Russia by German intelligence.
Fake Berlin postal votes
One of the videos appears to show a man opening postal-voting documents in Berlin and cutting up ballots marked for the AfD.
This was shared by Alina Lipp, a pro-Russian German blogger placed under EU sanctions in May 2025. The EU has accused her of spreading disinformation regarding Russia's war against Ukraine and of participating in coordinated information manipulation in support of the Kremlin.
She claimed on X there was no evidence the video was fake, with her post gaining more than 630,000 views.
However, German election-monitoring website Wahlrecht.de found clues that the three purported postal-voting packages were fraudulent.
To begin with, they did not contain the polling cards that voters need to return with their ballots. In addition, neither the outer electoral envelopes nor the internal ballot envelopes were sealed.
According to Wahlrecht, the packages were missing the separate ballot papers used to elect Berlin's district councils, while the papers for the Berlin House of Representatives were folded differently from genuine ballots, indicating it was not real.
AfD removed from fabricated ballots
A second video, shared across multiple accounts, claims to show postal ballots in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania without the AfD.
In one video, a male narrator claims to be a pensioner from Rostock who received a suspicious ballot that did not include the party as an option in the list of parties.
This footage was subsequently shared by multiple accounts on X, with some explicitly describing it as election fraud. Similar posts purported to show ballots from three different constituencies: 9, 11 and 33.
The names of the other candidates on the supposed constituency 11 ballot match those on the official sample ballot. However, the row containing the AfD had been removed from the version displayed in the video.
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state election chief, Christian Boden, confirmed to German news agency dpa that the AfD appeared on the genuine postal ballots.
Election officials responsible for the other constituencies shown in the posts also confirmed that the AfD was included on their ballot papers. According to Boden, the forgeries had been closely modelled on official sample ballots, with the fields containing the AfD simply deleted.
Familiar Russian disinformation tactics
Claims of election irregularities and fraud are not new: fake videos also emerged before Germany's 2025 federal election.
One of these falsely claimed the AfD was missing from ballot papers in the city of Leipzig, whilst the other appeared to show ballots being destroyed.
German authorities said the earlier videos appeared to form part of a targeted pro-Russian disinformation campaign associated with Storm-1516, which has used staged witnesses, fabricated videos and websites designed to resemble legitimate news organisations to introduce false claims into political debate.
The latest videos repeat similar election fraud narratives and closely resemble the earlier videos, with researchers linking them to the Storm-1516 campaign.
In December 2025, Germany's Federal Intelligence Service described Russia as the "central actor" behind Storm-1516.
The AfD ultimately finished first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, taking 38.2 per cent of the vote.
The false narrative casts the AfD and its supporters as victims of manipulation.
The party supports closer relations with Moscow and lifting sanctions on Russian energy, while opposing Germany's continued military support for Ukraine. There is no evidence that the party is behind this social media campaign.

A 15-year-old student detained for wounding 11 peers with a shotgun outside a high school in the western province of Manisa in Türkiye claimed he carried out the Sept. 22 attack due to severe peer bullying.
Three of the victims remain in critical condition following the shooting near İnci Üzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the Turgutlu district, while medical staff discharged one person. Education officials suspended classes at the facility for one day as authorities secured the area.

The Radio and Television Supreme Council (RTÜK) imposed a broadcast ban on the shooting. Armed violence outside school grounds remains exceptionally rare in Türkiye, although law enforcement continuously conducts operations to seize unregistered hunting rifles and combat juvenile crime across the country.

Russia increases its use of jet-powered drones eightfold in three months – Ihnat
Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department at Ukraine’s Air Force Command, said this on television, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
Russia has used a total of 7,700 these drones since it began deploying jet-powered UAVs. Their number has been increasing every month: 350 in June, 1,500 in July, 2,850 in August, and about 1,900 so far in September, according to Ihnat.

A kidney wait since 2024 ends with an Army airlift and a rare double transplant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:24:04 UTC
17:24:04 KST

NEW DELHI: An 18-year-old who had spent nearly two years waiting for a kidney, undergoing dialysis twice a week and with no family donor, received not one but two kidneys from a single brain-dead donor on Monday — after the organs were airlifted from Chandimandir to Delhi. Both kidneys were transplanted into Anil Yadav at Safdarjung Hospital, and he is doing well.The donor, 62-year-old Amar Chand, father of an Air Warrior, had undergone coronary artery bypass graft surgery last year and was on dual antiplatelet medication. He later slipped in his bathroom, suffered a head injury and brain haemorrhage, and was declared brain dead at Command Hospital (Western Command), Chandimandir. His organ donation helped save other lives. His liver was transported to Army Hospital (Research & Referral), Delhi, for transplantation, while both corneas were donated to Command Hospital, Chandimandir.His family’s decision to donate his organs set off a race against time. With Army support, the two kidneys were airlifted to Delhi and taken to Safdarjung Hospital, where doctors transplanted both into Anil, who has chronic renal failure.
“This is the first en bloc renal transplant at the hospital, in which both kidneys from a donor with marginal renal function were implanted in a single recipient. With a severe shortage of organs nationwide, accepting marginal kidneys can help expand the donor pool and give more dialysis patients, many of whom wait for years, a chance at transplantation,” said Dr Himanshu, Professor & Academic Head, Department of Nephrology, VMMC & Safdarjung Hospital.
“The patient is recovering well, with good renal function and urine output.”“The most difficult part of organ donation is counselling a grieving family to say yes within two hours,” said Col Anurag Garg, Transplant Coordinator and Palliative Physician at CHWC. “I have seen this in the Subedar’s family, a Colonel’s wife’s family and Air Warrior Ranbir’s case.”
Anil had been waiting for a transplant since 2024, with no donor available in his family. Until Tuesday, twice-weekly haemodialysis had been part of his routine.For a teenager who had spent nearly two years waiting for a donor, the journey from a brain-dead donor in Chandimandir to a transplant table in Delhi took place in time to give him a chance at life beyond dialysis.

&quot;Ukrposhta&quot; has changed the operating procedures of its branches because of air-raid alerts: how it will work
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:23:28 EEST
17:23:28 KST

"Ukrposhta" has changed the operating procedures of its branches because of air-raid alerts: how it will work
Kyiv • UNN
In urban branches, parcels will be accepted and handed out on a priority basis. The new procedure is already in effect in more than 90% of such branches.
"Ukrposhta" has introduced a new operating procedure for urban branches with multiple service windows. From now on, employees will first accept parcels, while their second priority will be handing them out — both operations will be carried out outside the general queue. This was reported by Ihor Smilianskyi, CEO of "Ukrposhta," writes UNN.
Details
It is reported that employees will give priority to accepting shipments, which can be processed outside the general queue. The second priority will be handing out parcels — this will also be done outside the queue. The company explained that the decision was necessary to speed up the movement of shipments due to possible reductions in working hours during air-raid alerts.
According to the CEO of "Ukrposhta," if a parcel is accepted before an alert is announced, it will have a better chance of being sorted and sent out on the same day.
At the same time, financial services, including pension payments and payment processing, will continue to be provided as usual. "Ukrposhta" noted that such transactions can be completed on the same day even after the air-raid alert has ended.
The new procedure has already been introduced in more than 90% of urban branches that have more than one service window. There, the "Express Window" will operate under the new rules.
The rules for branch operations during the "yellow" and "red" levels of an air-raid alert currently remain unchanged. At the same time, "Ukrposhta" is preparing proposals concerning the specifics of the national postal operator's operation during the winter period.
The company names the launch of self-service stations and an increase in the number of parcel lockers as its next step.

Miami plastic surgery boom lures Swiss dermatology giant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:21:46 UTC
17:21:46 KST

Miami plastic surgery boom lures Swiss dermatology giant
Galderma, the Swiss dermatology company, recently opened a new headquarters for the Americas in Miami, lured by the city’s mix of high-income spenders and a booming plastic surgery industry that attracts visitors from around the world.
The firm, which has a market value of about CHF39 billion ($48 billion), took a full floor at 801 Brickell Avenue in the city’s financial district. The space will allow for about 200 employees and Galderma has started with about 50 thus far, CEO Flemming Ornskov said in an interview. The new space is down the street from its prior – much smaller – Miami office.
Miami “has a lot of what we’re looking for: dynamic, multicultural, growth-focused, diverse, aesthetic focus, consumer focus, and it also has a very good scientific basis,” Ornskov said. “And it’s the one place where we can get everybody to travel to without moaning too much.”
More
‘A wild west’: how one Swiss company aims to tame the botox boom
The US is the fastest-growing market for Galderma with revenue expanding more than 30% in the first half of this year compared with last year. US sales will likely overtake the international business soon, Ornskov said.
Galderma also has US offices in Boston, California and Texas, but Miami has emerged as the prime location to “keep a finger on the pulse” of the consumer and also serve Latin America. The firm has said it plans to invest $650 million in US manufacturing through 2030.
Wealthy newcomers
Founded in 1981, Galderma was started as a joint venture between Nestlé and L’Oreal. After a few years of being entirely owned by Nestlé, it was acquired by a group of investors in 2019 before an initial public offering in 2024. Since then, the shares have posted a total return of 157% against a gain of just 29% for the SPI Swiss stock exchange. L’Oreal now owns 20% of the firm.
Galderma’s fast-growing injectable aesthetics are in high demand in clinics in Miami. Since the pandemic, South Florida has received a wave of wealthy newcomers who were initially drawn by the lifestyle and remote work and more recently by lower taxes amid proposals to slap levies on the rich in more blue states.
Add that to deep-pocketed tourists from Latin America and Europe, and the city has seen growing demand for luxury offerings – including cosmetic procedures.
Miami is also one of the world centers for itch research through the University of Miami, which adds to the appeal of having a bigger presence locally. Galderma sells prescription drugs like Nemluvio for conditions that cause itchy skin.
“When we started to look at plastic surgery, particularly injectable aesthetics, we see Miami is just moving up the ladder,” Ornskov said. “Both the influx of people but also as a medical tourism place.”

Russia pounds Kyiv with drone strikes after Zelenskiy-Trump talks
KYIV, Sept 23 - Russia pounded Kyiv with drone strikes on Wednesday, hitting railway infrastructure, warehouses and fuel stations, just hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy met US President Donald Trump to discuss peace efforts.
At least two people were killed and more than 30 were injured in the attack, which lasted for hours from the morning into early afternoon, officials said, in one of the heaviest strikes since Russia began hitting Kyiv and nearby areas with faster and high-flying jet drones that are harder to intercept.
Several explosions were heard and smoke billowed above the centre of the Ukrainian capital and other areas.
Zelenskiy said Russia had deployed many drones against the city, with a large number of them jet-powered.
"Russia continues to turn civilian and critical infrastructure into targets: pharmaceutical facilities, gas stations, railways, communications infrastructure, and shopping malls," he said on X.
A separate Russian aerial bomb attack killed at least four people and injured four others in a village in the frontline Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, the regional governor said on the Telegram messaging app.
Zelenskiy, who was due to address the UN General Assembly later on Wednesday, said it was important to keep up sanctions pressure on Moscow, including on Russian oligarchs.
In his meeting with Trump on Tuesday, Zelenskiy discussed a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets and asked for increased supplies of US Patriot air defence missiles to defend against an expected Russian winter campaign against Ukraine's electricity infrastructure. No agreements were reached, he said.
Zelenskiy said he was ready for "any format" of an energy ceasefire with Moscow, as long as Russia halted its own attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure.
On Wednesday, the Kremlin said the grounds for future peace talks with Ukraine were still not in place and there were no plans for any high-level meetings.
PETROL STATIONS HIT
"This is the view from the windows of the EU Delegation (in Kyiv) today. Buildings nearby are burning," Katarina Mathernova, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, said in a social media post.
The attacks largely targeted the neighbourhood near the main railway station, which Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said had not been damaged.
Ukrzaliznytsia's head Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said railway infrastructure came under attack and one of its workers had been injured.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a drone hit a nine-storey non-residential building, as well as a business centre and warehouses.
Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta said Russia hit one of its petrol stations in the capital, the sixth such facility attacked in recent weeks.
In total, two petrol stations came under attack, authorities said. Reuters TV footage showed one of the heavily damaged stations on a busy highway.
Energy worker Mykola Nechypurenko, one of a team repairing damage to the power network, was sceptical about the prospects for any energy ceasefire with Russia.
"I don't think they'll agree on anything. As long as the war goes on, energy infrastructure remains under threat," said Nechypurenko, 55. "I don't believe it will work. Not until the war ends." REUTERS

'We stood by our values': pro-Palestinian Stanford students speak out after charges dismissed
Students from Stanford who were part of a campus movement protesting against Israel’s war in Gaza will see their charges dismissed, it was announced this week. 
The five students, who were part of a larger group of 11 defendants, some of whom accepted plea deals, now appear to be coming to an end to a drawn-out process in which they were accused of a felony for barricading themselves in the president’s office in June 2024.
“Throughout this process, I’ve maintained that it was fundamentally unjust for a multibillion dollar institution like Stanford University to attack its own students for protesting for Palestine. Today’s outcome affirms that belief,” said defendant and recent Stanford graduate Amy Zhai in a public statement. 
"I am proud that we stood by our values and that we finally have a resolution," she said.
"For more than two years, Stanford University and the Santa Clara District Attorney’s office have taken extreme measures to attack us for speaking our minds," said Germán González, another Stanford defendant. 
"As this saga comes to an end, we are humbled by the outpouring of community support and we look again to Gaza, the compass of our struggle, to reaffirm our commitment to solidarity," he said.
The defendants will be required to complete 100 hours of community service and pay a restitution of around $52,000, which has already been paid. 
González told The New Arab that their protest movement, which began long before the sit-in at the president’s office, was widely supported by people around campus. 
"Our case started well before June 2024. On October 20, 2023, we started a sit-in to stop the genocide. It was the longest sit-in in Stanford’s history. More than 500 students came out," he said. 
"People from Gaza were holding signs thanking universities. We felt like we had no other option. We had to come through," he said. "After being ignored by the university, we took the sit-in to the president's office."
They then received a letter saying they were suspended from campus. That was the beginning of their two-year long legal battle that has come to a close this week.
Though they say they are relieved by the news of the dismissed charges, they say they will continue to advocate for Palestinian human rights and other causes.

Under new deal, U.S. military buys non-standard weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:20:08 UTC
17:20:08 KST

- Global Military Products won a spot on a new five-year, $19.5 million USSOCOM contract for U.S. and foreign weapons, ammunition, and protective equipment.
- GMP has historically supplied Soviet-pattern weapons like AK-platform rifles and RPG-7 launchers for training and partner-force support.
Global Military Products has been selected as one of several contractors on a new U.S. Special Operations Command indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract for U.S. and foreign weapons, ammunition, and personal protective equipment, the Tampa, Florida-based company said Sept. 21.
The five-year contract has a ceiling of $19.5 million, and GMP will compete against other contract holders for individual delivery orders as the command’s needs arise.
The company has not disclosed which specific weapons this contract will cover. But GMP’s business has long centered on sourcing non-standard, foreign-made military equipment through a separate line of contracts known as Special Ammunition and Weapon Systems, or SAWS, which the company has held with the Army for over a decade. Those items typically include Soviet and former-Eastern-Bloc-pattern hardware not in the standard U.S. arsenal: Kalashnikov-pattern rifles such as the AKM and AK-74, PKM and RPK machine guns, RPG-7 rocket launchers, SVD-pattern sniper rifles, and mortars in non-NATO calibers such as 82mm, along with the ammunition that feeds them. The U.S. military uses this kind of foreign-made equipment to train special operations forces on weapons they may encounter in the field, to equip foreign partner forces already using Soviet-era arms, or for testing.
This is the second consecutive USSOCOM IDIQ contract for weapons and ammunition procurement that GMP has held. The company said its work on the earlier agreement, which involved sourcing and delivering weapons and ammunition through its international supplier network, factored into its selection this time.
“Special operations forces require speed, flexibility and dependable access to equipment,” said Austin Gouveia, associate program manager at Global Military Products. “This award reflects Global Military Products’ commitment to providing U.S. and allied forces with reliable access to critical defense equipment and capabilities.”
“This award also reflects our ability to perform under the previous USSOCOM IDIQ contract, where we excelled at sourcing and delivering weapons and ammunition while leveraging our global network and supply chain capabilities to respond to evolving operational requirements and support USSOCOM missions,” Gouveia said.
GMP, a subsidiary of Global Ordnance, has built its business around supplying this kind of non-standard hardware to the U.S. military and its allies, including mortar systems, sniper rifles, assault rifles, machine guns, grenade launchers, anti-armor weapons, ammunition, electro-optics, and weapon accessories. The company separately holds a $639.8 million Army contract for 155mm artillery rounds awarded in 2025.

Climate change is &quot;driving&quot; tropical animals northward — another species has been spotted in an unusual location

Climate change is "driving" tropical animals northward — another species has been spotted in an unusual location
Kyiv • UNN
A tropical turtle has laid eggs on the western coast of the United States for the first time in history. Scientists link this to the warming of ocean waters.
A tropical sea turtle laid eggs on a beach in Southern California, marking the first time in history that this has happened on the U.S. West Coast. Scientists say it is the latest sign of warming ocean waters. The New York Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
The olive ridley sea turtle is the smallest species of sea turtle and is endangered. These animals usually live in tropical and subtropical waters off the coasts of Mexico and India. California lies farther north.
According to the publication, on September 16, the turtle dug a nest on a beach near Seal Beach and laid eggs. Three days later, the animal was spotted again several kilometers to the south, near the Huntington pier, where it was laying eggs once more. Scientists do not know whether it was the same turtle.
Video: The New York Times
"On Tuesday, scientists said that the turtle’s appearance is a sign of what is to come in California. Waters off the West Coast have been warming for many years, attracting species accustomed to warmer climates, such as brightly colored tropical sea slugs and Humboldt squid. This year, the trend has intensified because of a strong El Niño — a periodic climate phenomenon characterized by warmer temperatures in the Pacific Ocean," the publication writes.
The nest will now be monitored throughout the incubation period, which may last about two months, and the eggs will be protected with special enclosures.
Recall
In Peru, scientists discovered 27 new animal species. The finds include an amphibious mouse, a tree salamander, and a fish with an unusual teardrop-shaped extension on its head.

17:08:42 KST

The Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to bar MK Ofer Cassif from running in the October 27 election, accepting a Likud petition despite the attorney-general’s position that the evidence did not meet the stringent legal threshold for disqualification.
Nineteen committee members supported disqualifying Cassif, five opposed the decision, and two abstained.
The decision is not final. Under Basic Law: The Knesset, a committee decision disqualifying an individual candidate requires Supreme Court approval before taking effect. The court is set to hear the election disqualification cases next week.
Cassif, a Hadash member placed sixth on the Joint List slate, said after the vote that the committee was political and that he had not expected a different result. He told KAN Reshet Bet that he was convinced the Supreme Court would overturn the decision.
The Likud petition alleged that Cassif’s statements and political activity negated Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state and demonstrated support for armed struggle against Israel by a terrorist organization - two of the three grounds for disqualification under Section 7A of the Basic Law.
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara and State Attorney Amit Aisman had taken the opposite position, finding that the material submitted against Cassif - while including reprehensible statements and conduct - was insufficient to establish any of the statutory grounds for barring him.
Adalah, the legal aid center representing Cassif, said, “It is hard to believe that the Likud, when it filed this motion, genuinely thought it rested on evidence even remotely connected to the grounds for disqualification.”
It continued, “Israeli law does not permit barring a candidate from the Knesset simply for criticizing the army and the government for committing war crimes against Palestinians, and certainly not for supporting the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel.” Adalah said it was confident that the Supreme Court would accept its position.
Sohlberg cautions against overly broad use of defensive democracy
Opening the hearing, committee chairman and Deputy Supreme Court President Noam Sohlberg described Section 7A as an instrument of “defensive democracy,” allowing a democracy to protect itself against those who use its freedoms to undermine it.
He also warned that applying the provision too broadly could damage the same democratic values it was intended to protect.
“The stronger the power, the greater the caution required in exercising it,” Sohlberg said, noting that disqualifying a candidate also denies voters the ability to support that person.
The Supreme Court has interpreted Section 7A narrowly, requiring clear, convincing and unequivocal evidence that a prohibited objective is central to a candidate’s political activity. Offensive or extreme statements are not, by themselves, sufficient; previous rulings have generally required a sustained pattern of conduct.
Attorney Ilan Bombach, representing the Likud, argued that the evidence showed such a pattern. He cited Cassif’s appeals to international bodies and calls for sanctions against Israel and Israeli leaders, as well as his support for releasing Marwan Barghouti.
Barghouti, a senior Fatah figure, is serving five life sentences after being convicted for his role in terrorist attacks that killed five people. Cassif has called for his release and described him as a potential leader of the Palestinian people.
Bombach also argued that Cassif’s condemnation of the October 7 massacre did not erase his other statements and conduct. Section 7A covers support expressed “either explicitly or implicitly,” he said, and was intended to prevent anti-democratic forces from obtaining power through democratic institutions.
Legal advisory argues Cassif has not supported armed struggle against Israel
Anat Goldstein, presenting the legal advisory, told the committee that the accumulated evidence still did not establish that Cassif supported armed struggle or met either of the other disqualification grounds.
Cassif’s efforts to generate international political or legal pressure against Israel did not amount to support for armed struggle, she said. Similar allegations were considered during a separate attempt to expel him from the Knesset after he supported South Africa’s proceedings against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
That effort failed in February 2024, when 85 lawmakers voted to expel Cassif and 11 opposed the measure. Ninety votes were required.
Goldstein said one 2023 statement in which Cassif referred to Palestinians fighting the IDF as “freedom fighters” came closer to the statutory prohibition. A single statement, however, was insufficient to demonstrate the sustained and dominant political objective required by Supreme Court precedent.
Other statements attributed to Cassif, including comparisons between Israeli leaders and Nazis, were deeply objectionable but had previously been found insufficient to justify disqualification, she said.
Adalah general director and attorney Hassan Jabareen argued that the Likud had failed to connect Cassif’s parliamentary and political activity to any of Section 7A’s prohibited objectives.
“If an elected official can’t say what an ordinary citizen can, what are they doing in the Knesset?” Jabareen asked.
He said contacting the United Nations, alleging genocide in Gaza, or seeking international pressure against a government could not, without additional evidence, be equated with support for armed struggle.
Cassif says petitions meant to remove war opposition
Adalah attorney Ariel Remez similarly argued that the petition’s allegation that Cassif had aided the enemy during wartime resembled an accusation of a criminal offense. If the evidence supported that allegation, he said, the appropriate response would be an indictment rather than an election disqualification proceeding.
Cassif told the committee that the petitions were intended not only to remove Arab parties but also to silence opposition to the war and prevent voters from choosing representatives who shared their views. He called the effort fascist and an attempt to delegitimize Jewish-Arab political partnership.
The dispute will now return to familiar ground. In 2019, the Central Elections Committee also voted to disqualify Cassif, but the Supreme Court overturned the decision after finding that the evidence did not meet the high threshold under either the Jewish-and-democratic-state ground or the armed-struggle ground.
Cassif’s case was the first in two days of committee hearings on requests to bar candidates and lists from the election. The committee continued Wednesday with petitions against Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, Ra’am, the Joint List, and Balad.
Requests against Otzma Yehudit, the Religious Zionist Party-Zehut list, and the Democrats are scheduled for Thursday. The committee’s decisions will then move to the Supreme Court, either for mandatory approval of individual-candidate disqualifications or through appeals challenging its decisions concerning party lists.

UK firm tests robot sailboats to track hidden submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:08:17 UTC
17:08:17 KST

- Oshen deployed six hydrophone-equipped C-Star sailboats at REPMUS26 in Portugal to test a distributed acoustic picket line against live targets.
- The company plans to bring eight C-Stars to the Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego next month to test the concept in a U.S. setting.
Oshen, a UK maritime technology company based in Plymouth, is testing what it calls the first “acoustic picket line” built from small robotic sailboats at REPMUS26, a monthlong multinational maritime robotics exercise underway in Portugal. The company has deployed six of its C-Star sailboats, each about 1.2 meters (4 feet) long and fitted with a hydrophone, to form a distributed underwater listening network, and is testing the concept against live targets for the first time.
Passive sonar detection has traditionally relied on towed arrays, long cables carrying up to 100 hydrophones pulled behind surface ships. Those arrays give precise local detection and bearing data but cover a limited area and pick up noise from the towing vessel itself. Oshen’s approach spreads many small, low-cost sensors across a wide stretch of ocean instead, using a fleet of C-Stars to form what the company describes as an acoustic barrier that can be reshaped based on the threat picture. Because the boats are spread across a wide area rather than clustered on one vessel, the network can pinpoint a target’s location rather than just its bearing, and can help direct other sensors such as towed arrays toward it.
“A defensive network built from a host of individual hydrophone platforms behaves very differently to one built from a handful of expensive towed arrays,” said Gordon Jones, Defence and Oceanography Lead at Oshen. “It is wider, more resilient and harder for an adversary to characterise. REPMUS is the first real test of that model against live targets, and it points the way to how persistent undersea surveillance can be evolved.”
“REPMUS embodies what our technology is designed to do: take a capability that normally depends on a handful of expensive assets and turn it into something that can be deployed at scale, cheaply and continuously,” said Anahita Laverack, CEO of Oshen. “There are many potential applications, including an acoustic picket line to help protect the GIUK Gap.”
The GIUK Gap, the stretch of ocean between Greenland, Iceland, and the United Kingdom, has been a chokepoint for tracking submarines transiting between the North Atlantic and open ocean since the Cold War, when the U.S. Navy’s SOSUS seabed hydrophone network monitored the same waters.
Oshen says its C-Stars are built to survive extended missions in rough conditions, and the company has said one of its boats transmitted data from inside a Category 5 hurricane. Being small and low in the water, the boats are difficult to detect, and Oshen argues that even if individual units are spotted or lost, the wider network can keep functioning and makes it harder for an adversary to work out which vessels are carrying active sensors.
REPMUS is designed to test more than new hardware. The exercise brings together vessels ranging from Oshen’s 50-kg C-Stars to 3,000-tonne manned frigates, and organizers use it to check whether command and control systems can coordinate across that range of platforms in a congested environment. Oshen said its engineers worked with naval partners ahead of the exercise to integrate its software with NATO systems and make sure data from the C-Stars would not overwhelm communication channels.
Oshen currently runs three active projects with the Royal Navy, including one through the UK’s Defence and Security Accelerator program, and holds a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Navy covering single-beam sonar applications. The company plans to bring eight C-Stars to the Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego next month to test the same acoustic picket line concept in a U.S. setting.

BAE’s self-funded armored vehicle passes U.S. Army field tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:04:28 UTC
17:04:28 KST

- BAE Systems self-funded two AMPV 30 prototypes with Kongsberg 30mm turrets, delivered to a U.S. Army Transformation in Contact unit in April.
- The Army has not committed to procuring the AMPV 30, though it expects two more prototypes in early 2027 for further testing.
BAE Systems said it has delivered two AMPV 30 prototypes armed with Kongsberg’s Medium Caliber Turret to a U.S. Army Transformation in Contact 2.0 unit, funding the six-month development effort itself with $17 million in internal research money.
The company disclosed the delivery in a Sept. 22 release, though the vehicles reached the Army’s 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, Texas, in April.
The AMPV 30 pairs the Army’s existing Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle chassis with a remotely operated Kongsberg turret carrying a 30mm Mk 44 Bushmaster II cannon. The same turret is already in production for the Marine Corps’ Amphibious Combat Vehicle. BAE Systems built the two prototypes without a government contract or an Army requirement behind them, a point the Army has confirmed publicly since the vehicles first arrived at Fort Hood.
“Our mission was speed and innovation, and we delivered beyond expectations,” said Bill Sheehy, vice president of BAE Systems’ Ground Maneuver futures. “With today’s battlefield evolving faster than ever, it’s paramount that Soldiers have the capabilities they need to win the fight. Throughout this effort, our team demonstrated how we can integrate new design solutions in a time-effective and more cost-efficient manner for the Army.”
Since the April delivery, the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry Regiment has run the AMPV 30s through field evaluations, including live-fire testing, to compare the platform against what soldiers say they need on the battlefield. Beyond the cannon, the vehicles carry counter-drone detection systems, a cross-platform target handoff system that lets multiple vehicles share targeting data, and a 360-degree camera system that lets crews see their surroundings without exposing themselves outside the armor.
The AMPV’s open architecture lets BAE Systems swap in more than 30 different turret systems on the same common top plate, according to the company. These two vehicles bring the total number of turreted AMPV prototypes BAE Systems has self-funded to eight over the past two years. The Army has said it expects two more AMPV 30 prototypes in early 2027, with plans to run them through a rotation at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California.
Defense analyst Nicholas Drummond, assessing the vehicle on social media, wrote that the AMPV fitted with the latest Kongsberg MCT-30 turret and an Echodyne MESA radar amounts to “your XM30 right there,” referring to the Army’s long-running effort to find a Bradley Fighting Vehicle replacement. He called it “a nicely done evolutionary upgrade. Reduced risk, cost, and time to deliver. Big uplift in performance.” Kongsberg has separately announced integrating Echodyne’s MESA radar into its Protector remote weapon stations for counter-drone use, though BAE Systems has not confirmed that radar is fitted to these specific AMPV 30 prototypes.
The Army has not committed to buying the AMPV 30 or issued a formal requirement for it. BAE Systems and the Army have both described the current vehicles as company-funded prototypes under evaluation, not a program of record.

Roche obesity shot reduced body weight by 15.5% in trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:02:18 UTC
17:02:18 KST

Roche obesity shot reduced body weight by 15.5% in trial
Roche’s experimental obesity shot enicepatide cut both blood sugar and body weight in type-2 diabetes patients who were overweight or obese in a mid-stage trial.
Patients receiving the highest 24-milligram dose had a 2.65% reduction in HbA1c – a measure of blood sugar – and lost an average 15.5% of their body weight after 48 weeks with no plateau observed, Roche said.
The data “look competitive” against results for rival drugs in Phase 3 trials, Goldman Sachs analyst James Quigley and colleagues said. They cautioned, however, that they need to see detailed placebo-adjusted data and the results replicated in Phase 3 trials to confirm the benefit.
Roche shares fell 0.19% at the end of the trading day in Zurich.
The Swiss drugmaker is seeking to compete with Eli Lilly & Co and Novo Nordisk A/S with a once-weekly shot that works similarly to Lilly’s Zepbound — by simultaneously activating the GLP-1 and GIP hormones involved in regulating metabolism. The global market for weight-loss drugs is estimated to reach as much as $150 billion.
More
Can Swiss pharma giant Roche reshape the obesity market?
Roche’s discontinuation rates due to side effects were just 2% after 48 weeks. In a mid-stage trial of Lilly’s Mounjaro in patients with diabetes that was carried out over a shorter period, discontinuation rates varied from 5% to 24.5%.
The results of the trial have been very promising, Manu Chakravarthy, senior vice president and global head of cardiovascular, renal and metabolism product development at Roche, said in an interview.
“What it tells us and underscores for us is the incredible potency of this molecule,” he said. “You’re losing weight, you have no hypoglycemia, and you’re dropping your sugar in a very, very healthy range. And that to me as an endocrinologist is the greatest boon you can offer people with poorly controlled diabetes today, because they don’t really have such a solution.”
Late stage trials underway
About 62% of the people were brought within 48 weeks to the normal glycemic range, he said.
One of the strategies the company is embarking upon, especially with enicepatide, is to cover the broadest range, from obese or overweight people without any co-morbidities to very significant co-morbidities like cardiovascular disease, heart failure, type 1 diabetes and others, he said.
More
What will be the next obesity blockbuster?
Roche already has two late-stage obesity trials underway. In early 2027, it plans to expand testing to diabetes and cardiovascular outcomes.
The company also plans to test higher doses of enicepatide and is exploring combinations with other weight-loss drugs. At its half-year media conference in July, pharmaceuticals chief Teresa Graham said Roche was looking to develop the drug both on its own and in combination, particularly for patients who need “greater weight loss and/or better glycemic control.”
Enicepatide, formerly known as CT-388, was first developed by Carmot Therapeutics, which Roche acquired for $3.1 billion in 2023.
Enicepatide has a “competitive profile” in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity, Vontobel analyst Stefan Schneider said, pointing to the combination of normalised glucose levels in a meaningful share of patients and sustained weight loss. Schneider expects the drug could launch as early as 2028 and reach peak sales of CHF2.5 billion ($3.05 billion).
Previous data suggested enicepatide is “as good as rivals on weight loss,” Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Michael Shah and Christos Nikoletopoulos wrote in June. The drug is expected to win approval by 2030, the analysts wrote, and could have peak sales of $4 billion.

Families of victims of Kenneth Law to address court as sentencing hearing begins in Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:02:13 UTC
17:02:13 KST

Law admitted targeting buyers on a suicide forum and shipping his products to 41 countries, and families angry that he escaped murder charges will now tell the court how their loved ones' deaths affected them.
Relatives of people who died after buying lethal substances from Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law are due to speak in court this week, as a judge begins deliberating how long the former chef should spend in prison.
Justice Michelle Fuerst has set aside four days at a court in Newmarket, just north of Toronto, to hear victim impact statements and further evidence. It is not yet clear when she will hand down her sentence.
Law pleaded guilty in May to aiding the suicides of 14 people in Canada. Prosecutors dropped murder charges after concluding they did not have enough evidence to secure a conviction over the online forums where he advised people on how to end their lives.
Under an agreed statement of facts signed by both sides, Law admitted seeking out buyers by posting on a suicide discussion forum under a false name and offering lethal products for sale. His packages reached customers in at least 41 countries, including China, France and Brazil, with 330 sent to the United Kingdom.
Several bereaved families have said they are angry Law will not stand trial for murder, arguing he bears direct responsibility for the deaths of mostly young and vulnerable people. Legal experts say prosecutors are likely to push for a heavy sentence, potentially up to 20 years.
UK deaths under scrutiny since 2023
Britain's role in the case came to light soon after Law's arrest. In August 2023, UK authorities were investigating 88 deaths linked to Law, with the National Crime Agency working to trace people in Britain who may have bought his products.
Police in Surrey had contacted Law in October 2022 over the death of 22-year-old Tom Parfett, who died in 2021 after apparently visiting one of Law's websites, and a later inquiry into his death raised questions about why the force had not investigated Law further.
'Not a diabolical madman'
Earlier this month, Canada's Globe and Mail reported details of interviews Law gave to a psychiatrist in prison after his guilty plea. According to court documents obtained by the paper, Law said he had been "trying to serve a need that I thought was humane," adding: "I'm not a diabolical madman."
The documents show that after his arrest in 2023, Law considered himself blameless, insisting he never made the final decision to end anyone's life and was simply selling a product, the Globe reported.
Law, now in his 60s, worked as a chef at a luxury hotel in downtown Toronto before setting up his online forums during the Covid-19 pandemic. He has admitted to shipping lethal substances within Canada and abroad, typically charging around $80 per package.
Among his victims was 18-year-old Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez, who died in 2022. Speaking outside court in May, her father Leonardo Bedoya said he had found her dead in her bedroom. Describing his only daughter as the "light in my life", he called the prosecutors' decision to drop the murder charges "a disgrace."

====================================================================================================

‘Ghost patient’ policy wrongly removing at-risk people from GP lists, doctors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:00:18 UTC
17:00:18 KST

An NHS policy to remove “ghost patients” from GP lists is inadvertently leaving some of the poorest people in England without vital healthcare, analysis has found.
Under previous NHS rules, inactive patients at risk of being removed from their GP practice were given six months to respond to outreach. But under NHS England’s accelerated list validation timeline, introduced last October, patients now have only three months to reply.
According to analysis by Healthtech-1, registered GP lists in English practices declined by 483,019 patients between October 2025 and July 2026, with the most deprived fifth of practices accounting for about 138,400 of the net decline – just under 30% of the national decline.
While GP lists need reviewing as people move away or die, GPs have said the accelerated timeline has inadvertently led to patients from deprived areas being incorrectly removed, creating barriers to receiving treatment.
Consequently, GPs and practice managers have reported having to re-register vulnerable and elderly patients, creating an additional administrative burden.
De-registering patients can also cause gaps in care and disruption to treatment. Since GP practices’ income also depend on the number of registered patients, a drop can leave practices struggling to pay for running costs.
A GP at a university practice in Southampton said the accelerated timeline was causing problems because patients were being incorrectly removed from their list and were struggling to access their prescriptions and treatment.
“If you give prescriptions out to people, they’re on repeat and once they get kicked off the lists they can no longer access any prescriptions,” he said. “The risk is that if you’re unable to access your repeat prescriptions, your treatment will be affected.”
He added: “If you’re narrowing the window from six to three months, more people are going to be kicked off and therefore more people will be put into the position where they cannot access treatment.”
The GP also warned that, besides reducing a practice’s income, the policy change was hitting patients from deprived and vulnerable backgrounds hardest.
“In our case, we had around 100 people who were taken off our list who didn’t leave at all. That worked out as around £10,000 in lost income for our practice,” he said.
“We were later contacted by these patients telling us that they couldn’t access their prescriptions and that they hadn’t gone anywhere.
“The money we’ve lost hasn’t been compensated, and I know of another practice locally that has lost £100,000 that they also won’t be compensated for.
“For those who have been erroneously taken off, we’re being penalised. We’re going to have to make cuts somehow to make up the shortfalls.”
Dr Clare Bannon, the chair of the British Medical Association’s GP committee, said GPs across England support the principle of keeping patient lists accurate but the current list-cleansing process is “seriously flawed”.
Bannon said: “We have called on NHS England to pause the exercise. The approach is overly aggressive, leading to practices losing tens of thousands of pounds in income and causing active patients, including vulnerable individuals, to be removed in error.
“It is essential that active patients are not deprived of access to a GP through no fault of their own.”
An NHS spokesperson said: “There are robust checks in place to ensure that vulnerable groups are not removed from GP lists – people are contacted through multiple different channels with the thorough processes lasting up to five months before any action is taken.
“This process ensures that patient contact details are correct so that they receive vital information about screening and vaccination appointments, while ensuring NHS funding resources are allocated fairly with money no longer spent on people who do not live in England.”

Apple unveils music venue within Battersea Power Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:00:11 UTC
17:00:11 KST

Apple unveils music venue within Battersea Power Station
Tech brand Apple has revealed the 600-seat Apple Music Hall, its first live music venue, which sits alongside its offices within London's Battersea Power Station.
Set to open later this year, the venue overlooks the power station's Turbine A at the northern end of the huge brick building. It will be Apple's first permanent performance venue.
Designed by Apple's in-house team led by Apple Places vice president Kristina Raspe, the venue takes its industrial language directly from the Giles Gilbert Scott-designed power station.
The venue is flanked by brick walls, while the building's huge structural steel joists are exposed at the rear of the performance space.
As a nod to the art deco design of the original power station, a series of four illuminated, streamline-styled arches span the venue.
Bronze, art deco balconies were placed between the arches, as box-like areas overlooking the main venue space.
According to Apple, the flexible venue was designed to give artists an "unprecedented level of creative control".
The venue has an 11.5-metre-wide stage and can be arranged in multiple configurations as either an all-seated or all-standing venue, or a combination of the two.
Music will be played through a 48-speaker spatial sound system, while 16 hardwired cameras can capture performances to be broadcast.
"In short, an artist can perform an intimate live show for fans at Apple Music Hall and walk out with a finished Spatial Audio recording, a broadcast-ready mix, and multicamera video — all from a single show," said Apple.
Alongside the main venue space is what Apple describes as a "full production facility" that contains a pair of professional-standard recording and mix studios.
The venue also includes a dedicated space for Apple's radio station – Apple Music Radio, which will now broadcast from inside the building.
Apple Music Hall was built alongside Apple's Foster + Partners-designed European HQ, which occupies the centre of Battersea Power Station. One of London's best-known buildings, the power station was refurbished in 2022 by architecture studio WilkinsonEyre after being derelict for 40 years.
It now contains apartments on the upper floors, with restaurants and shops, including an Apple Store in the former turbine halls.
The photography is courtesy of Apple.

BAE’s self-funded armored vehicle passes U.S. Army field tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:04:28 UTC
17:04:28 KST

- BAE Systems self-funded two AMPV 30 prototypes with Kongsberg 30mm turrets, delivered to a U.S. Army Transformation in Contact unit in April.
- The Army has not committed to procuring the AMPV 30, though it expects two more prototypes in early 2027 for further testing.
BAE Systems said it has delivered two AMPV 30 prototypes armed with Kongsberg’s Medium Caliber Turret to a U.S. Army Transformation in Contact 2.0 unit, funding the six-month development effort itself with $17 million in internal research money.
The company disclosed the delivery in a Sept. 22 release, though the vehicles reached the Army’s 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, Texas, in April.
The AMPV 30 pairs the Army’s existing Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle chassis with a remotely operated Kongsberg turret carrying a 30mm Mk 44 Bushmaster II cannon. The same turret is already in production for the Marine Corps’ Amphibious Combat Vehicle. BAE Systems built the two prototypes without a government contract or an Army requirement behind them, a point the Army has confirmed publicly since the vehicles first arrived at Fort Hood.
“Our mission was speed and innovation, and we delivered beyond expectations,” said Bill Sheehy, vice president of BAE Systems’ Ground Maneuver futures. “With today’s battlefield evolving faster than ever, it’s paramount that Soldiers have the capabilities they need to win the fight. Throughout this effort, our team demonstrated how we can integrate new design solutions in a time-effective and more cost-efficient manner for the Army.”
Since the April delivery, the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry Regiment has run the AMPV 30s through field evaluations, including live-fire testing, to compare the platform against what soldiers say they need on the battlefield. Beyond the cannon, the vehicles carry counter-drone detection systems, a cross-platform target handoff system that lets multiple vehicles share targeting data, and a 360-degree camera system that lets crews see their surroundings without exposing themselves outside the armor.
The AMPV’s open architecture lets BAE Systems swap in more than 30 different turret systems on the same common top plate, according to the company. These two vehicles bring the total number of turreted AMPV prototypes BAE Systems has self-funded to eight over the past two years. The Army has said it expects two more AMPV 30 prototypes in early 2027, with plans to run them through a rotation at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California.
Defense analyst Nicholas Drummond, assessing the vehicle on social media, wrote that the AMPV fitted with the latest Kongsberg MCT-30 turret and an Echodyne MESA radar amounts to “your XM30 right there,” referring to the Army’s long-running effort to find a Bradley Fighting Vehicle replacement. He called it “a nicely done evolutionary upgrade. Reduced risk, cost, and time to deliver. Big uplift in performance.” Kongsberg has separately announced integrating Echodyne’s MESA radar into its Protector remote weapon stations for counter-drone use, though BAE Systems has not confirmed that radar is fitted to these specific AMPV 30 prototypes.
The Army has not committed to buying the AMPV 30 or issued a formal requirement for it. BAE Systems and the Army have both described the current vehicles as company-funded prototypes under evaluation, not a program of record.
